22694-the-international-magazine-volume-:
The International Magazine of Literature, Art, and Science offers its issue of January 1851, volume 2, number 2. The catalog record names no editor. New York's International Magazine gathered British and American writing for a growing middle-class audience, reprinting much from London journals alongside fresh work.

This number reprints Mrs. Hall's account of a pilgrimage to the homes and grave of Edmund Burke, from her series on English shrines in the London Art Journal, illustrations included. Literary biography, essays, and tales fill the rest of the pages. Magazines like this one were the internet of their day: fast, miscellaneous, and shameless about borrowing. The issue preserves the reading diet of 1851 in a single helping.
agrippa-three-books-occult-philosophy-16:
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa sums up all magic in Three Books of Occult Philosophy, here in the first English text of 1651. Agrippa was a sage, healer, and rogue of the age of print's dawn. His three books take in the magic of the earth world, of the stars and sums, and of rites and the names of God and souls in one vast scheme.

J. F. turned the Latin to English for the London press. Adepts since then have kept the book as their base. Its range has no peer in its age. It is the craft's great store.
anzus-treaty-1951:
Australia, New Zealand, and the United States signed the ANZUS security treaty at San Francisco in 1951. The pact was sealed while the Korean War raged and fear of communist expansion ran high across the Pacific. Australia and New Zealand also wanted an American promise of protection as they accepted a lenient peace with Japan.

Under the terms, each party must act to meet a common danger if another party is attacked in the Pacific area. The three also promise to consult whenever one of them feels threatened. The treaty anchored the American alliance system in the South Pacific. Ties between the United States and New Zealand later frayed over nuclear ship visits, but the pact still frames regional security.
arxiv-2510-00351:
Rohit Dilip and three colleagues published this 2025 paper presenting Kanzi, a tokenizer for protein structures. Tokenizers chop a protein's three-dimensional shape into discrete units that AI models can read and write. Existing tokenizers lean on hand-built parts that respect spatial symmetry but train awkwardly. Kanzi instead uses a diffusion autoencoder trained with one flow matching loss.

The simpler design drops frame-based representations in favor of plain global coordinates. Standard attention replaces the special symmetry-aware operations used before. Training became more stable, and the models stayed small and cheap to run. On reconstruction metrics, Kanzi beat existing tokenizers at a fraction of their size and cost. A generative model built on its tokens also beat rival token-based generators in their tests. It still trails the best continuous diffusion models, a gap the authors state plainly.
arxiv-2510-00451:
Dalal Alharthi and Ivan Garcia published this 2025 paper calling for security to be designed into generative AI from the start. Language models remain open to prompt injection, where crafted inputs hijack their behavior. The authors introduce PromptShield, a framework that validates prompts against a formal ontology before they reach the model. Standardized, checked inputs leave less room for ambiguity or manipulation.

The team tested PromptShield on an agent system analyzing Amazon Web Services cloud logs. The log set held 493 events tied to malicious activity and anomalies. Under simulated prompt injection attacks, the shielded system scored about ninety-four percent on precision, recall, and F1 alike. Security rose without sacrificing task performance in the experiment. The authors argue the modular design travels beyond cloud security to other high-stakes domains. They frame the work as groundwork for future AI safety standards and policy.
arxiv-2510-00551:
Gao Huang, Song Li, and Deanna Needell published this 2025 paper on recovering signals when only intensities survive the measurement. Phase retrieval underpins imaging from crystallography to astronomy, and noise decides whether recovery is trustworthy. Real detectors bring awkward noise: photon counts follow Poisson laws, and outliers grow heavy tails. The authors analyze two least-squares estimators under both noise models.

For bright Poisson signals, both estimators hit the best possible error rate, the first such guarantee known. For dim signals, the nonconvex estimator adapts, its error shrinking as signal energy fades. Heavy-tailed noise with a finite moment yields matching optimal rates as well. The proofs treat Poisson noise as tame when bright and wild when dim, a unifying trick. The framework extends to sparse and low-rank variants of the problem.
arxiv-2510-00651:
Bispo, Brophy, Mohandas, Scanlan, and Eising at the University of Limerick present FIN, a fast inference network for map segmentation in self-driving cars, in this paper dated June 2025. Map segmentation labels a bird's-eye-view grid around the vehicle as drivable, crossing, sidewalk, and so on, and mistakes can cause unsafe manoeuvres. Fusing camera images with radar gives rich detail plus accurate distances at modest cost, but heavy fusion models run too slowly for real-time driving.

FIN pairs that camera-radar fusion with a new lightweight segmentation head and a carefully designed set of training losses. Per-class balancing in the loss set helps rare but important classes compete fairly. On the nuScenes benchmark the model reached 53.5 mean intersection-over-union, comparable to much larger systems. Its inference speed set a new benchmark, improving on the strongest baselines by about two hundred sixty percent.
arxiv-2510-00751:
Zvonilov reviews and completes the rigid isotopy classification of real algebraic curves in this 2025 arXiv paper, part of the programme around Hilbert's sixteenth problem. A rigid isotopy class groups curves that deform into each other without passing through a singular one. The spaces split into chambers of nonsingular curves and walls of curves with one node or cusp. Enumerating those pieces, and how they touch, is the classification problem.

The paper finishes the case of curves of bidegree (4,3) on a hyperboloid, work the author began. It supplies missing proofs that sixteen classes of curves, each having a single node or cusp, form connected components. The tools are graphs of trigonal curves on Hirzebruch surfaces, worked out through dessins. Adjacency graphs of the chambers and walls are presented. The same arguments classify genus-four trigonal curves on a quadratic cone.
arxiv-2510-00851:
Salama and four co-authors apply neural architecture search to traffic prediction for open radio access networks, in this 2025 poster paper for the ACM OpenRan workshop. Next-generation wireless networks must forecast traffic to allocate resources before congestion hits. In the O-RAN design, intelligence splits between a non-real-time controller that can train models and a near-real-time controller that must answer fast. The authors let architecture search pick the right LSTM size for each situation automatically.

Architecture optimization runs as an rApp in the slow loop, while chosen models serve as xApps in the fast loop. Across six LSTM architectures, lightweight models predicted regular traffic with R-squared around 0.91 to 0.93, cheaply. Complex models reached near-perfect accuracy in critical scenarios when accuracy mattered most. Orchestrating the switch cut computational complexity by seventy to seventy-five percent versus always running the biggest model.
arxiv-2510-00951:
Hoster, Stump, and Vecchi prove a conjecture about counting polynomials for partially ordered sets in this 2025 arXiv paper on combinatorics. Their objects are finite graded posets, sets with a ranking from a bottom element to a top one. The ab-index is a polynomial that encodes how chains of elements sit inside such a poset. A recent extension folds in the Poincaré polynomial to capture still more structure.

The authors show that this extended index comes from the ordinary ab-index through a fixed operation called the omega transformation. That result settles a conjecture by Dorpalen-Barry, Maglione, and Stump. It also gives a more unified route to results about Chow polynomials, which matter in the geometry of matroids. Several earlier arguments in the literature become simpler corollaries of the main theorem.
arxiv-2510-01051:
Liu and a large team of co-authors introduce GEM in this 2025 arXiv paper, an open-source gym for training language model agents through experience. Reinforcement learning for agents needs interactive environments, much as classic reinforcement learning relied on OpenAI Gym. GEM standardizes the agent-environment interface, with asynchronous vectorized execution for speed and wrappers that make new tasks easy to add. It ships with a diverse suite of environments and integrated tools.

The authors provide baselines across twenty-four environments using REINFORCE with return batch normalization. Unlike GRPO, that algorithm handles dense per-turn rewards and gives better credit assignment in multi-turn tasks. They also benchmark PPO, GRPO, and REINFORCE head to head in single- and multi-turn settings. Single-file example scripts show GEM working with five popular training frameworks, and the toolkit doubles as an evaluator.
arxiv-2510-01251:
Bono, Belotti, and Palmonari make entity linking honest about its own uncertainty without paying for repeated model runs. Matching table cells to knowledge-base entries is core plumbing for data integration. Language models do it well, but estimating their confidence normally needs many costly generations.

The team regresses an entropy estimate from features visible in a single output. Token probabilities from final and middle layers carry the needed signal. A short warm-up phase calibrates the estimator for each deployment. Tests across several models showed the cheap estimates reliably flagging low-accuracy links. Single-shot estimation keeps the workflow's latency nearly unchanged. Knowledge bases anchor the target side of every link. Uncertainty flags route doubtful cells to human review. Self-supervision avoids labeling a separate confidence dataset. Tabular data is where enterprise linking actually lives. Cheap honesty beats expensive certainty in production.
arxiv-2510-01651:
Zhou and co-authors read ancient Chinese bronze inscriptions automatically, building a dataset and a specialized recognition pipeline. The characters are degraded, appear as photographs, rubbings, or tracings, and follow a brutally long-tailed distribution. Their corpus holds twenty-two thousand images and two hundred thousand annotated characters.

Detection first localizes inscriptions, then recognition transcribes character by character. Ladder-style mixture-of-experts adapters on a vision-language encoder let experts specialize by domain and rarity. Accuracy beat scene-text baselines across common and rare categories alike. Archaeology gains a scalable reader for its oldest documents. Six thousand six hundred fifty-eight unique categories define the label space. Head, mid, and tail characters all improved under the experts. Parameter efficiency keeps the adapter approach practical at scale. Ritual vessels carry the inscriptions and the history together. Degradation is the default condition of three-thousand-year-old text.
arxiv-2510-02051:
Ou, Huang, and Ozoliņš train neural quantum states without a pre-taught sign structure in this 2025 physics paper. Neural quantum states approximate ground states of frustrated Hamiltonians, where the wavefunction's sign pattern is the hard part. Existing methods often assume that structure in advance or pre-train a separate phase network. Both crutches limit where the methods can go.

Their modified stochastic reconfiguration evolves amplitude and phase with different imaginary time steps. A larger step for the phase lets the sign structure catch up efficiently alongside the amplitude. Phase and amplitude networks then train simultaneously in one loop. The authors demonstrate the method on the frustrated Heisenberg J1-J2 model. That model is a standard battleground for spin liquid physics. Removing the pre-training stage simplifies the whole workflow for non-stoquastic problems. The approach widens the class of Hamiltonians that neural states can attack directly.
arxiv-2510-02151:
Lee proposes a quantum version of convex optimization in a 2025 theory paper. Convex optimization is a core tool in modern computing. It finds the lowest point of a bowl-shaped cost function. Lee replaces that task with a physics problem. The new task asks for the lowest energy of a quantum system. A curved potential well plays the role of the bowl.

Lee gives a quantum algorithm called the Fundamental Gap Algorithm. The method tracks a slowly changing ground state, which is the lowest energy state. It reaches the answer within a chosen error in polynomial time. Lee then applies the method to a classic shape problem. The algorithm finds the lowest tone of a convex drum in many dimensions. No fast method for that drum problem was known before.
arxiv-2510-02351:
Pihulski and Kocon ask language models to judge offensive tweets through other people's eyes. Their 2025 paper studies political posts from the 2020 United States elections. Human readers disagree about offense by culture and ideology. The team prompted models to adopt set personas. Personas ranged from far right to progressive. Judgments were made in English, Polish, and Russian contexts. Several recent reasoning models entered the test. The set included DeepSeek-R1, o4-mini, and GPT family models.

Larger reasoning models tracked persona differences most faithfully. They stayed consistent across languages and viewpoints. Smaller models often missed the subtle distinctions entirely. Explicit reasoning improved both accuracy and explanation quality. A model that shows its steps earns more trust here. Moderation tools must serve mixed publics fairly. Persona aware judging offers one path toward that goal.
arxiv-2510-02551:
Finkelstein uses machine guided search to find tidy formulas for plasma solitons. His 2025 physics paper applies Physics-Informed Symbolic Regression. Bright solitons are wave packets that hold their shape as they travel. In magnetized plasma they follow equations too hard for exact answers. Numeric simulations give numbers but little insight. Symbolic regression hunts for short formulas that fit the data. Physics constraints and boundary rules steer that hunt. The target profiles describe vector potential and particle density. A reduced model from Maxwell-fluid equations governs both.

The search rediscovered approximate solutions matching published numeric results. Closed forms replace heavy simulation runs for this model. Cheaper answers let researchers scan conditions quickly. Formulas also reveal which terms truly matter. Plasma modeling often trades insight for computation time. This method buys back some of that insight. Other reduced models could get the same treatment.
arxiv-2510-02651:
Partovi and Iuricich organize forty years of point cloud visualization work into a task based taxonomy. Their 2025 visualization paper maps a scattered design space. Point clouds drive navigation, monitoring, and disaster response work. Seeing them clearly remains hard for several reasons. The data comes sparse, uneven, and huge in scale. Designers lack a map from goals to techniques. The taxonomy links choices along three dimensions. Data types, user objectives, and visual techniques form the axes. Four decades of published designs get classified inside it.

Strengths and limits of current approaches come into focus. Perception aware design is one open challenge named. Low level task evaluations are another gap. The framework gives newcomers a structured entry point. Tool builders can match techniques to real objectives. Better maps of the field guide better tools. Point clouds keep growing as sensors spread. Visualization research needs this kind of shared scaffolding.
arxiv-2510-02751:
Wiktorowicz and co-authors predict how many self-lensing binaries the Extremely Large Telescope can find in globular clusters. Their 2025 astronomy paper models dense star clusters. A compact companion can pass before its bright partner. Its gravity then briefly magnifies the partner's light. White dwarfs make the most common lenses in clusters. The team ran synthetic cluster populations through MOCCA simulations. Telescope and camera traits of the ELT entered the forecasts. Present day clusters should hold between one and fifty such sources. The starting binary fraction drives that wide range.

Predicted events show two brightness peaks. Typical crossings last about two hours. High binary fraction clusters outperform sparse ones consistently. Extreme magnifications happen but stay rare. Self-lensing offers a clean channel to hidden compact objects. Globular clusters concentrate those objects densely. Dedicated ELT surveys now have a quantitative case. Planning observations can start from these rates.
arxiv-2510-02851:
Park and co-authors speed up smart robots that think partly in the cloud. Future 6G networks will split robot brains across device, edge, and server. A small on-board model can draft each action. A big server model then checks and fixes the draft. Robot actions, though, depend on fresh sensor views. Each action changes what the robot sees next. Drafts cannot be checked in parallel batches.

Their method scores each action by its deviation. The score compares the action with a weighted mean of past ones. Odd actions are likely to be rejected by the server. Likely passes skip the trip to the server entirely. The team derived a threshold that balances traffic and skill. In tests, uploads and server work fell by two fifths. End-to-end delay fell by about a third. Task success stayed close to the server-only level.
arxiv-2510-02951:
Boţ and Schindler analyze a noisy, momentum-driven optimizer over long time spans. The heavy ball method rolls downhill with inertia and friction. Real gradient readings, though, come with random noise. Their system adds that noise to the heavy ball motion. The setting is a broad Hilbert space with a convex cost. They prove that solution paths exist and are unique. Almost surely, each path settles on an optimal point.

Speed also decays to zero along the way, they show. Rates for the cost gap come in two flavors. One holds almost surely, and one holds on average. A known system of Su, Boyd, and Candès turns out to match theirs. Matching parameters make the two systems the same. The second half leaves optimization for monotone equations. A correction term joins the dynamics for that wider class. Fast rates appear for a version with fading damping.
arxiv-2510-03051:
Meindl and co-authors pretrain one model to optimize many unknown functions. Black-box optimization probes a costly function point by point. No gradients are available to guide the search. Bayesian optimization leads the field, but its settings need hand tuning. Tuned settings often fail on new landscapes. Their model, ZeroShotOpt, learns the search craft itself. It trains on millions of synthetic bumpy functions. Trajectories from twelve Bayesian variants serve as its lessons.

Offline reinforcement learning distills those lessons into one policy. The policy then faces fresh problems with no tuning at all. It handled tasks from two up to twenty dimensions. Sample efficiency matched or beat strong Bayesian rivals. One trained model now serves as a reusable base. Builders can extend it instead of starting over. Limits remain clear in the paper. Mixed, discrete, and multi-goal problems sit outside its scope for now.
arxiv-2510-03251:
Cao, Yan, and Tan forecast time series inside several hypercomplex spaces at once, letting algebra do the decomposition. Forecasters often split a series by handcrafted structures and priors. Those designs grow complex and lean on fragile assumptions. The authors noticed a clean pattern in exotic number systems. Characteristic frequencies fall as the space's dimension rises. Their Numerion model exploits that law systematically. Linear layers and activations generalize to power-of-two dimensions.

A new real-hypercomplex-real perceptron block carries the computation. Several blocks work in spaces of differing dimension in parallel. Each space naturally models a different frequency band. Low-dimensional spaces catch fast wiggles, high ones catch slow swells. A dynamic fusion mechanism blends the band forecasts adaptively. Public benchmark suites returned state-of-the-art results. Visualizations confirmed the frequency split the theory predicts. Power, finance, and transport forecasting all stand to gain.
arxiv-2510-03351:
Wang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on diagnosing mental disorders from brain scans in a way doctors can inspect. About one in five teens lives with a diagnosed mental or behavioral condition. Resting brain scans reveal how regions sync with each other, and graph networks can learn from those links. Such networks, though, act as black boxes, which blocks clinical trust. The team's system, ConceptNeuro, forces choices through named connectivity patterns instead.

A large language model drafts candidate concepts from medical knowledge, and experts filter them. Each concept is a small subgraph linking named brain regions. Across several disorder data sets, concept guided networks beat their plain counterparts on accuracy. The concepts that drove decisions matched expert views of each disorder. Some patterns also hinted at fresh research questions. Transparent tools like this could help clinics adopt scan based diagnosis with more confidence.
arxiv-2510-03451:
Seeger presents a 2025 arXiv paper in probability theory pinning down how well a probability distribution can be approximated by weighted point masses. The error is measured in Wasserstein distance, the geometry for comparing distributions. Practitioners place the points at random, but chosen deterministic points can do better. Seeger derives convergence rates as the point count grows. The rates depend on the measure's moment behavior, the Wasserstein exponent, and the dimension.

In certain low dimensional regimes, and for measures with unbounded support, the rates beat what random sampling and methods achieve. Except for critical borderline cases, the rates are optimal, so no placement strategy can do asymptotically better. Quantization questions like this sit underneath simulation, compression, and numerical integration. Rates tell engineers how many points an accuracy demands. They mark where cleverness stops helping, which is as valuable as an algorithm. The paper closes several regimes that bounds had left loose.
arxiv-2510-03551:
Alvaro and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper giving the first formal treatment of metastable failures in software systems. In such failures, a brief stress spike knocks performance down, and the system stays down after the stress ends. Cloud firms treat these events as rare but catastrophic outage sources. The team models request response servers in a domain language. From those models they build Markov chains, tuned with data, that mirror the system's behavior.

Pictures of the chain's global shape turned out to be a surprisingly sharp way to spot risky settings. A formal measure based on escape probabilities ties metastability to the chain's eigenvalue pattern. Their algorithms also predict how long recovery should take, and those times balloon near metastable settings, as theory says. A tool runs the analysis in milliseconds on models drawn from real failures. Operators could screen designs for this failure mode before it strikes production.
arxiv-2510-03751:
Zaffar and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper showing that the reference map in visual place recognition is a training resource hiding in sight. Place recognition matches a query photo against a database of images of a place. Modern methods still stumble when the test environment differs from their training data. In many deployments, the reference set for the target area exists before any query arrives. The authors fine tune the model on that map, a step they call Reference Set Finetuning.

The fine tuning raised top one recall by about two and a third percent on average across benchmarks. Fine tuned models kept their generalization to data sets rather than overfitting the map. The trick worked across data sets and helped recognition methods too. Robot and vehicle localization depend on place recognition in the places training data covers worst. Using the map you have is a cheap accuracy win.
arxiv-2510-03851:
Ma and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on whether language models can design good system algorithms. Cloud engineers spend huge effort on routines like cache replacement and bin packing. Asked for designs, language models tend to copy famous generic solutions instead of inventing fresh ones. The authors call this pull toward the familiar an availability bias, and they set out to counter it.

Their framework, MetaMuse, guides the model through structured creative reflection. It scores ideas by measured performance, uses outside stimuli to steer invention, and builds working code through planned waypoints. Tested at a global cloud provider, MetaMuse produced cache policies that cut misses by roughly a third. Its bin packing designs also used far fewer bins than standard rules. Some generated designs surprised the human engineers involved. The work suggests models can contribute real algorithm design when their search is well guided.
arxiv-2510-04051:
Liao and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on evaluating language models without running every benchmark question. Full benchmark suites cost thousands of GPU hours, which prices smaller teams out of careful evaluation. Item response theory, borrowed from educational testing, can estimate ability from a small item subset. Earlier adaptations handled only right-or-wrong scores and treated each benchmark in isolation.

Their framework, LEGO-IRT, natively supports continuous scores from generative tasks alongside binary ones. It also splits each model's ability into a general part plus parts specific to each metric or benchmark. Across seventy models and five benchmarks, stable capability estimates needed only a tiny slice of all items, a few percent of the full set. Adding structural knowledge cut estimation error by up to about a tenth. The estimated abilities also tracked human preferences closely. Cheaper, trustworthy evaluation lowers the barrier to comparing new models honestly.
arxiv-2510-04151:
Qu and Zhao present this 2025 arXiv paper on the Hamiltonian geometry of rational reductions of the two-dimensional Toda hierarchy. Rational reductions carve out smaller hierarchies with rich structure, but the asymmetric types were less understood. The authors work at the full-dispersive level rather than in a dispersionless approximation.

They derive the local bihamiltonian structures of the asymmetric reductions of types (2,1) and (1,2) separately. For the (2,1) type they construct a three-dimensional generalized Frobenius manifold with non-flat unity. The authors conjecture all central invariants equal one twenty-fourth for the general family.
arxiv-2510-04451:
Nan Meng and Yun Bin Zhao wrote this 2025 paper on sparse optimization, a workhorse of signal recovery. Sparse problems seek a solution with very few nonzero entries, from as little data as possible. Thresholding algorithms solve them by stepping downhill and cutting small entries to zero. The team replaced the classic Newton step with a compressed one. Their step confines the Newton move to a small subspace, then maps it back with a stabilizing term.

That change cuts the cost of each step while keeping the speed that makes Newton methods attractive. Two algorithm families follow, one using hard thresholding and one using optimal thresholding. The authors prove both families converge under a condition on the sensing matrix. Experiments matched leading methods on success rate and solution accuracy. Uses range from compressed sensing to feature selection in machine learning. The paper gives practitioners options with proof behind them.
arxiv-2510-04751:
Xinyi Wei, Julian Braun, Yangshuai Wang, and Lei Zhang wrote this 2025 paper on simulating crystal defects inside smaller computer models. Dislocations, line defects in a crystal, set how metals bend and break. Atomistic simulations must box them into finite cells with edges. Standard boxes converge slowly, so results carry size errors unless cells grow. The authors design boundary conditions of higher order accuracy. Their recipe expands the field of the defect in a multipole series.

Predictor solutions come from a ladder of singular equations solved by a spectral method. Discrete corrections use force moment identities with controlled error. Coupling the two parts makes the boundary scheme improvable order by order. Tests on screw and edge dislocations confirmed the predicted convergence rates. Errors in shape and energy norms fell as theory said they should. Size effects shrank while computing cost stayed moderate. Better boundaries mean smaller cells and faster materials studies.
arxiv-2510-04851:
Dongge Han and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on giving teams of AI agents a memory of how tasks get done. Office workflows repeat: the same plans and tool moves recur across days. Teams keep that know how in habits and manuals. LEGOMem stores it as units cut from past task runs. An orchestrator agent plans and delegates, while worker agents execute the steps.

Memory units can be handed to either level, in plans or pieces. The authors used the framework to study where such memory helps most. On an office task benchmark, orchestrator memory proved vital. Planning and delegation improved when past plans were at hand. Memory for workers improved how accurately they executed steps. Teams of smaller models gained a lot from stored experience. Their gap to stronger teams narrowed as they reused prior traces. The study is a design guide for memory in multi agent systems.
arxiv-2510-04951:
Jayanta Mandi, Marianne Defresne, Senne Berden, and Tias Guns work on decisions under uncertainty in this 2025 arXiv paper. Many planning problems first predict unknown values, then optimize with those guesses. When the guessed values sit inside the constraints, a small error can make the plan impossible to carry out. Their method trains the predictor with that risk in view.

Their framework, called Odece, uses two new loss functions built from maximum likelihood ideas. One loss punishes predictions that lead to infeasible plans. The other punishes predictions that rule out the truly best plan. A single dial blends the two losses to taste. In experiments, turning the dial let decision-makers favor either safety or quality. It beat existing baselines on whichever goal they chose.
arxiv-2510-05251:
Chenghao Yang and five co-authors improve how reasoning models explore during training in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards teaches models by trial and error. Fixed sampling temperature forces a bad trade-off: hot sampling degrades quality, cold sampling limits discovery. The authors observe that early tokens set a response's whole direction.

Their method, exploratory annealed decoding, starts generation hot and cools it step by step. The schedule explores boldly at the beginning, then exploits to protect quality and stability. It plugs into existing training algorithms without extra machinery. Across algorithms and model sizes, it beat fixed-temperature sampling on sample efficiency. A tuned schedule also improved ordinary test-time generation. The lesson: match exploration to the natural flow of sequence generation.
arxiv-2510-05351:
Jinghao Cao and four co-authors reconstruct the Sun's three-dimensional magnetic field with a neural operator in this 2025 arXiv paper. Solar physicists model the corona as a nonlinear force-free field. Traditional solvers iterate slowly, which blocks real-time space weather forecasting. A learned model could jump straight from surface measurements to the full field.

Their model, PIANO, combines a Fourier neural operator with channel attention and dilated convolutions. Attention prioritizes the input channels that matter most for field variations. A physics-informed loss enforces the force-free and divergence-free conditions during training. On the ISEE benchmark, PIANO beat other neural operators on accuracy. It also matched the physical characteristics of real fields across several active regions best.
arxiv-2510-05451:
Machot and his co-author tackle a safety problem in sorting aviation incident reports. Pilots and controllers file these reports in the Aviation Safety Reporting System, run by NASA. One report can carry several labels at once, such as a runway event plus a communication failure. The 2025 paper asks how a classifier can respect expert safety rules while it learns.

Their system, NASP-T, pairs a transformer model with logic rules written in Answer Set Programming. The rules help in two ways, by creating extra training examples and by guiding training itself. On the safety report test set, rule violations fell by up to 86 percent. Scores for label accuracy also improved over a strong plain baseline. The work shows how logic checks can make language tools more trustworthy in high-stakes fields. The authors next want the logic solver to check rules during training itself.
arxiv-2510-05551:
Boussim tackles a bias that haunts surveys and field studies in economics. Outcomes are often seen only for a self-selected slice of the population. When the outcome is a category, like job status or health grade, standard corrections fit poorly. His 2025 paper builds a correction that needs no ranking among the categories.

Classic fixes lean on strong assumptions about error distributions. A recent framework avoids those assumptions but only handles ordered outcomes. Boussim extends that idea with a local logistic representation of joint chances. Each category gets its own association term, which shows how selection tilts that outcome. He proves the hidden distribution can be pinned down without strong assumptions. He also adds a practical two-step estimator and its large-sample theory. The tools suit labor, health, and education studies where categories rarely come ordered in practice.
arxiv-2510-05851:
Chandarana and colleagues chain classical and quantum optimizers into one workflow. Hybrid sequential quantum computing runs stages in sequence, each exploiting complementary strengths. Classical heuristics explore broadly but trap in local minima. Their 2025 testbed sandwiches a quantum stage between classical ones.

Simulated annealing opens by mapping the solution landscape. Bias-field digitized counterdiabatic quantum optimization then tunnels through barriers. A memetic tabu search finishes by recovering nearby optimal states. On a 156-qubit superconducting processor, the pipeline solves dense higher-order problems. Ground states come back consistently within just a few seconds. Quantum bitstrings seed the final classical stage toward better basins. Decoherence explains why the quantum stage alone rarely finishes optimally. Estimated speedups reach seven hundredfold over annealing alone. The framework accepts any stage sequence that beats its components.
arxiv-2510-06151:
Justus and Baber of the University of Birmingham test language models as stand-ins for human teammates in a 2025 artificial intelligence study. Training agents to cooperate with people is hard because human policies stay hidden and shifting. Human data collection is expensive, so they propose language models as policy-agnostic proxies generating synthetic human-like decisions.

They ran three experiments in a grid-world capture game inspired by the Stag Hunt. The first compared thirty human participants and two expert judges with LLaMA 3.1 and Mixtral outputs. The models matched the experts more closely than the participants. Prompt tweaks in the second made the models swing between risk-averse and risk-seeking play, mirroring human variability. In the third, model movement paths resembled human trajectories. The proxies lack full human adaptability, yet they offer a scalable base for team training.
arxiv-2510-06251:
Bagdonaviciute and Vineet run a failure-mode analysis of vision–language models on physics tasks in a 2025 computer vision study. Benchmarks record what models answer correctly, not why they succeed or fail. The authors wanted diagnostics that separate genuine physical understanding from lucky pattern matching.

They tested six frontier vision–language models on Physion, Physion++, and CLEVRER. Custom subtests factored performance into distinct capabilities: perception skills like object, color, and occlusion recognition, plus motion prediction and spatial reasoning. Counterintuitively, subtest mastery correlated only weakly with overall benchmark accuracy. Models often answered correctly without grounding in perception or physics at all. In other words, strong scores sometimes happen for the wrong reasons. Aggregate metrics therefore hide failure modes that matter for deployment. The study argues for diagnostic benchmarks that expose which capability breaks, so developers can fix causes rather than chase leaderboard points.
arxiv-2510-06351:
Naveed, Agrawal, and Panagou extend the gatekeeper safety architecture to dual control with active exploration in a 2025 robotics paper. Planning under model uncertainty forces a trade-off. Robust planning stays safe but ignores uncertainty reduction, becoming overly conservative. Exploration bonuses help, yet usually without formal safety guarantees.

Their framework explores only when it verifiably improves the mission without compromising safety. The extended gatekeeper generates trajectories both safe and informative. Such trajectories reduce uncertainty and mission cost, or keep cost within a user budget. Exploration becomes a gated privilege, not a constant temptation. Simulations test online dual control of a quadrotor under parametric uncertainty. The vehicle flies its mission while learning its own uncertain parameters. For safety-critical robots, curiosity should be earned through verification, not tuned in by weight.
arxiv-2510-06451:
Wang and Levin build a microscopic theory of superconductivity in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Twisted graphene superconductivity is a major recent discovery, yet its pairing remains unsolved. Recent tunneling experiments report Kekulé ordering in the superconducting state. The theory starts from that clue.

Their pairing lives within a single valley and carries finite momentum. It forms a pair-density wave intrinsically bearing a Kekulé modulation. Four signatures follow. It breaks threefold rotation symmetry, producing nematic order. Its pairing is triplet, not singlet. Its density of states evolves from V-shaped to fully gapped U-shaped as attraction grows. Its zero-bias conductance varies systematically with temperature, matching tunneling data. Modest interactions already place the state near a BEC-like phase. That explains the extremely short coherence lengths experiments observe.
arxiv-2510-06651:
José Frías and three colleagues in Mexico build new ways to tell three-dimensional spaces apart. Their 2025 paper works with closed, orientable 3-manifolds, which are spaces that locally look like ordinary 3D space. Telling two such spaces apart is a classic hard problem in topology. The authors turn pictures of the spaces into polynomials, which are easier to compare.

They start from Heegaard diagrams, a standard way of splitting a manifold into two handle-like parts. Each diagram yields a graph drawn on the splitting surface. Only finitely many minimal graphs occur for a fixed manifold, which makes the scheme well defined. Applying known graph polynomials to those graphs produces manifold invariants. For lens spaces, the graphs can be fully classified, matching the classical classification. Computer evidence suggests the polynomials may even be complete invariants there. A test on the Poincaré homology sphere gave matching polynomials across different diagrams.
arxiv-2510-07151:
Cherepanov, Kovalev, and Panov give robot brains a memory that lasts far beyond the present moment. Their 2025 paper presents ELMUR, a transformer design with built-in external memory. Robots often see only part of their world at any time. A cue may matter long after it appears. Normal models forget such cues because their viewing window is short. ELMUR stores notes at every layer instead.

Each layer reads and updates its own memory store through attention. Old notes are swapped out by a rule based on recent use, or blended with new ones. The design stretched useful memory to spans vastly longer than the viewing window. In a maze test with million-step corridors, the agent scored a perfect success rate. On robot arm tasks with sparse rewards, it nearly doubled strong rivals. Long memory is vital for real-world machines.
arxiv-2510-07251:
Hughes and Horak show that reshaping one mirror can rescue a simple optical cavity design. Their 2025 paper concerns cavities that boost the interaction between light and a single emitter. A flat-plus-curved mirror layout tolerates misalignment and needs only one curved mirror. Its weakness is poor focusing at the cavity center. The authors ask whether a smarter mirror profile can fix the focus without losing the layout's virtues.

Simulations say yes, emphatically. Even simple, manufacturable mirror shapes raised coupling to a central emitter by about tenfold. The shaped design rivaled delicate two-curved-mirror cavities in achievable strength. It kept modest sensitivity to cavity length and its trademark tolerance of misalignment. Such gains could raise the rate and fidelity of single-photon sources and qubit readout. Quantum hardware may benefit from cavities that are strong yet forgiving to build.
arxiv-2510-07551:
Rajgarhia and co-authors present RECAP, a hybrid system that hunts personal data in text across thirteen low-resource locales. Their 2025 paper addresses a compliance necessity. Privacy laws demand that names, numbers, and identifiers be found and protected, but low-resource languages lack the labeled data that train standard detectors. RECAP pairs deterministic pattern rules, precise for structured identifiers, with a language model that reads context for the ambiguous cases. A three-phase refinement pipeline disambiguates and filters the merged candidates.

Benchmarked with a standard entity evaluation tool, RECAP beat a fine-tuned named-entity model by a wide weighted margin. It also beat a zero-shot language model baseline by a clear margin. Region-specific and complex entities, where pure rules and pure models both stumble, drove the advantage.
arxiv-2510-07751:
Li, Wu, and Deng wrote this 2025 operations research paper on scheduling pumped storage hydropower. Such plants pump water uphill when power is cheap and release it when demand peaks. Grid operators fold them into day-ahead unit commitment plans. The standard model treats each turbine separately. When several identical units share one reservoir, that model creates symmetric copies of the same choices. Solvers then waste effort exploring equivalent plans.

The authors propose two reformulations based on aggregating variables across units. One handles fully identical units that share a reservoir. The other covers units with equal generating and pumping efficiency. Both break the harmful symmetry before the solver starts. Even three or four units could slow a solver badly when symmetry went unhandled. Numerical tests on instances showed efficiency gains from the new formulations. Cleaner models should help operators schedule flexible storage on renewable-heavy grids.
arxiv-2510-08151:
Luza, Alard, and Barraquand wrote this 2025 ecology paper stress-testing a species occupancy model against the messy data ecologists actually collect. Occupancy models estimate where species live while correcting for missed detections. Newer versions add spatial and temporal autocorrelation to cope with sparse repeat visits. The authors asked whether such models survive datasets where many sites get one visit or none. A butterfly dataset motivated the study.

The model proved robust to uneven survey effort and shared covariates. Severe spatiotemporal gaps broke it. With gaps, predicted occupancy shrank toward the average, and that average was itself overestimated. Random effects could not repair the damage, because the relevant parameters became unidentifiable. Two real butterfly species confirmed the pattern. The warning is sharp: autocorrelation buys robustness to messiness, not to absence.
arxiv-2510-08251:
Maria Titova and Kun Zhang study persuasion games in a 2025 arXiv paper in economic theory. One player, the sender, knows the facts and sends messages that can be checked for truth. The other player, the receiver, then picks an action from a fixed set. The sender's tastes do not depend on the true state, only on the action chosen. The authors ask which outcomes can arise when neither side can commit in advance.

They characterize the full set of equilibrium outcomes for this verifiable-message game. They then compare those outcomes with the results under commitment, the standard information design setup. The paper gives conditions under which a commitment outcome can also hold as an equilibrium. It also finds settings where the sender gains nothing from commitment power. These results clarify when proof and commitment can stand in for each other.
arxiv-2510-08351:
Qingxiu Liu and co-authors put file system metadata inside network switches in a 2025 arXiv paper called FMCache. Distributed file systems split file and folder data across many metadata servers. Looking up paths is constant work, and caching on each client adds consistency headaches as clients multiply. Programmable switches, which process packets with custom logic, offer a shared middle point.

FMCache serves metadata requests directly in the switch data plane, before packets reach a server. Unlike earlier in-switch caches for simple key-value data, it handles path dependencies between folders and files. It also respects the tight memory limits of switch hardware. The team built it on Hadoop HDFS and tested it with a Tofino switch on real workloads. Throughput rose by up to 181.6 percent over plain HDFS, with low latency and modest switch resource use.
arxiv-2510-08451:
Jon Nelson, Joel Rajakumar, and Michael Gullans prove that Clifford-only quantum circuits cannot hold information for long, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Clifford gates are a restricted, well-behaved family that many error correction schemes rely on. Under steady depolarizing noise, which randomly scrambles quantum states, these circuits forget their input. The authors show this memory fades exponentially fast, even given an endless supply of fresh qubits in any state.

That help matters, because an older protocol stores data indefinitely in general circuits using fresh qubits. No such protocol can exist within the Clifford family alone, the authors prove. Non-Clifford gates are therefore fundamentally required for long-term quantum memory. This draws a sharp line between gate sets that look similar in other tasks.
arxiv-2510-08651:
Somasekhara Goud Sontti and co-authors simulate gas bubbles in shear-thinning liquids inside microchannels in a 2025 arXiv paper. Segmented flow, alternating gas slugs and liquid slugs, underpins many microfluidic devices. Shear-thinning liquids flow easier under stress, complicating bubble formation. The team studies polyacrylamide solutions at three concentrations as the continuous phase in a square microchannel.

Their simulations use the coupled level set and volume of fluid method, called CLSVOF, to track the gas-liquid interface. Gas slug length and volume shrank, as did unit cell length, as polyacrylamide concentration rose. Velocity and non-uniform viscosity patterns inside liquid slugs are reported for each concentration. Raising the contact angle shortened gas slugs and flipped bubble shapes from convex to concave. Surface tension and velocity ratios were varied systematically as well.
arxiv-2510-08851:
Mao and co-authors help robots learn where to explore by giving them concepts to aim for, in this 2025 arXiv paper on reinforcement learning. An agent learning by trial and error wastes enormous effort wandering at random, especially when it sees only camera images. A vision-language model can name the objects that matter for a task, but its guesses are noisy. Trusting those guesses directly, as reward signals, can mislead training.

Their method, Concept-Driven Exploration, uses the guesses more carefully. The robot's controller is trained to reconstruct the suggested concepts from its own internal features, and how well it reconstructs them becomes its exploration bonus. The outside model is consulted only during training, not afterward. Across five hard simulated tasks the agent explored in a targeted, efficient way and shrugged off noisy suggestions. A real robot arm then hit an eighty percent success rate on a physical task.
arxiv-2510-09051:
Shafique and co-authors build a strong language model for Urdu on a shoestring budget, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Urdu is spoken by hundreds of millions yet remains low-resource for AI, with scarce quality data. Simply translating English material imports errors, misses cultural nuance, and costs heavily. The team's model, Alif, instead trains on synthetic data generated with a modified self-instruct method, where a model drafts its own training tasks under careful seeding.

Each task drew a unique prompt and seed from a global pool, producing data with native-style reasoning chains, translation pairs, cultural grounding, and safety alignment. Built on an open eight-billion-parameter base, Alif beat that base model's tuned version on Urdu tasks. It also outperformed three leading multilingual rivals of similar size. The whole training budget stayed under one hundred dollars, which the authors offer as a recipe for other underserved languages.
arxiv-2510-09551:
Gavriel Di Nepi, Federico Siciliano, and Fabrizio Silvestri revisit a Google memory model in a 2025 arXiv paper. Titans, introduced at the end of 2024, is a neural memory architecture that learns during testing and reported strong results on many tasks. Yet no public code appeared, and ambiguities in the original description blocked reproduction.

The authors wrote a lightweight reimplementation and evaluated it thoroughly on masked language modelling, time series forecasting, and recommendation. Titans did not always beat established baselines, and they trace part of the gap to chunking, the splitting of input into blocks. Its neural memory component, however, consistently improved performance compared with attention-only models. The team concludes that the idea holds genuine promise, while its practical limits and open questions deserve attention. Their analysis gives later researchers a firmer base for judging test-time memory.
arxiv-2510-09851:
Haci Ismail Aslan and co-authors present QONNECT in this 2025 arXiv paper on distributed computing. QONNECT is an orchestration system for Kubernetes clusters spread across cloud, fog, and edge sites, the three layers where modern apps now run. It is built to respect quality-of-service goals, the performance promises users set for their apps.

The team notes that the standard Kubernetes scheduler ignores user goals such as saving energy, cutting cost, or raising global performance. Operators are then left placing workloads by hand, cluster by cluster. QONNECT instead makes placement decisions with those stated goals in view. The system aims to adapt placement as deployment contexts change across the cloud, fog, and edge sites it manages.
arxiv-2510-09951:
Lin, Yuk Hoi Yiu, and Christian Leibold model visual navigation in the brain in this 2025 arXiv paper in computational neuroscience. As an animal moves, place cells in the hippocampus fire in sequence, each cell tuned to one spot. The standard reading says the sequence simply mirrors the places the animal passes.

The authors build on newer theories that treat these sequences as serving abstract goals, such as planning a route. Their model links egocentric vision, what the animal sees from its own viewpoint, to the hippocampal sequences that form during navigation. The work tests whether sequences can arise from goal-driven processing rather than passive input alone. That shift changes what the firing pattern is thought to represent.
arxiv-2510-10051:
Gong and co-authors improve audio-visual segmentation in this 2025 arXiv paper in computer vision. The task is to mark, pixel by pixel, the objects in a video that are making the sound. Transformer and CNN methods have raised accuracy, but older CNN designs fused sound and vision with crude padding or multiplication.

Such basic fusion is limited by the small receptive field of CNNs, the patch of image each unit can see. The authors bring in complementary and contrastive learning, techniques that teach the model what belongs together and what must be told apart. Their aim is cleaner interaction between the audio signal and the visual features. Better fusion should sharpen the masks on sounding objects.
arxiv-2510-10451:
Keisuke Fujii and eight co-authors build a simulator that learns how groups of animals move, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Biologists use simulators to study behavior, but the true rules of animal movement are rarely known. Models written by hand therefore miss much of the real motion. Their data driven simulator instead learns from recorded trajectories, using deep reinforcement learning paired with counterfactual simulation, which asks what would happen under changed conditions.

The team treats missing parts of the movement model as actions the learner can choose. A distance based reward keeps the simulated animals close to the real ones. They validated the simulator on artificial agents, flies, newts, and a silkmoth. It reproduced species specific behavior more faithfully than standard imitation and reinforcement learning methods, and it earned higher rewards. It could also predict behavior in new settings and generate what if trajectories for several animals.
arxiv-2510-10551:
Baris Ardic, Quentin Le Dilavrec, and Andy Zaidman watch how novice programmers use generative AI to write software tests, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Tools like ChatGPT are entering engineering workflows and may raise productivity on tasks like writing unit tests. They may also change the developer's role, raising worries about control and learning. The team ran an observational study with 12 undergraduate students doing unit testing tasks with AI help.

They identified four interaction strategies, defined by whether the test idea and the test code came from the AI or from the student. Prompting styles, one shot versus iterative, often matched the broader strategy. Students praised time savings, lower mental load, and help with ideas. They also reported weaker trust, quality worries, and less sense of ownership. Notably, strategy and prompting style changed how work flowed but did not significantly change test effectiveness, measured by mutation scores or test smells.
arxiv-2510-10751:
Ningna Wang and six co-authors compute the medial skeleton of 3D shapes with better structure and mesh quality, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The medial axis transform describes a shape through interconnected sheets, seams, and junctions, giving a natural decomposition of its volume. Producing a clean medial mesh is hard. Their framework, MATStruct, is a particle based optimization guided by the restricted power diagram, which partitions the volume into convex cells whose dual encodes the mesh connectivity.

A spherical error metric constrains how medial spheres may move, enforcing structure awareness, while a Gaussian kernel energy spreads particles evenly. Compared with feature preserving methods such as MATFP and MATTopo, the approach yields cleaner, more accurate medial structures with much better mesh quality. The authors claim it is the first framework to build structural awareness into the optimization itself, with gains in fidelity and correctness.
arxiv-2510-10951:
Eitan Klinger, Vivaan Wadhwa, and Jungyeul Park argue that punctuation deserves respect when preparing parse trees for computation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Binarization converts treebank trees into binary form for parsers. Standard pipelines drop the marks before choosing head words, which warps constituent shape and harms head identification. The team releases a pipeline that instead preserves punctuation as sibling nodes before binarization, plus the derived artifacts needed to reverse the process.

Their evaluation suite covers head child prediction, reversibility after a round trip, and structural fit with CCGbank, a derivational resource. On the Penn Treebank, punctuation aware preprocessing lifted head prediction accuracy to 91.85 percent with the same classifier, up from 73.66 percent with Collins rules and 86.66 percent with a neural baseline in their experiments. Alignment against CCGbank derivations was competitive. All code is released so others can replicate and extend the resource.
arxiv-2510-11151:
Language models write code quickly, but their output often hides subtle security flaws that matter in mission-critical systems. Alexander Sternfeld, Andrei Kucharavy, and Ljiljana Dolamic present TypePilot in this 2025 arXiv paper, an agentic framework for safer model-generated code. The idea is to route generation through a strongly typed, verifiable language, using Scala as the working example.

The team evaluates TypePilot in two settings: formal verification with the Stainless framework, and general-purpose secure code generation. Experiments with leading open-source language models show that direct code generation often fails to enforce safety constraints. Simply prompting the model to write more secure code does not fix the problem either. The experiments covered both settings with the same set of leading models. Their type-focused agentic pipeline, by contrast, substantially reduces input validation and injection vulnerabilities, suggesting a route to more trustworthy automated code generation in high-assurance domains.
arxiv-2510-11351:
Galaxies in the epoch of reionization hold neutral hydrogen that fuels stars and blocks ionizing light, yet measuring that gas has been nearly impossible. Lucie E. Rowland and a large collaboration use a window on it in this 2025 arXiv astronomy paper. They analyze James Webb Space Telescope spectra of twelve ultraviolet-luminous galaxies from the REBELS-IFU program.

The team modeled the damping wings of Lyman-alpha absorption to derive neutral hydrogen column densities for galaxies at redshift around seven. Eight galaxies show strong damped absorption from neutral gas. Hydrogen masses estimated this way correlate with masses inferred from ionized carbon emission, though the emission-based values run larger. Dust-to-gas ratios from the two methods do not correlate directly. Combined with lower-redshift samples, the ratio of dust extinction to hydrogen column tracks metallicity strongly, suggesting these galaxies already host enriched gas and dust.
arxiv-2510-11851:
Shuo Chen and a large team warn that Deep Research agents, AI systems that plan and write long reports, carry deeper safety risks than ordinary chatbots. A standalone language model refuses clearly harmful queries. The team's 2025 arXiv paper shows the same query, fed to a research agent, can return a polished report full of forbidden detail. Biosecurity is their starkest example.

Jailbreaks built for chatbots miss what makes research agents special: their planning. The authors craft two attacks aimed at that core. Plan Injection strips safety steps from the agent's plan and inserts malicious sub-goals. Intent Hijack reframes a harmful request as an academic research question. Across models and safety benchmarks, three findings stand out. Alignment often fails inside agents, multi-step planning weakens safeguards further, and agent outputs are more coherent and professional than chatbot answers, hence more dangerous. The team calls for agent-specific alignment methods.
arxiv-2510-12451:
Mason-Williams and colleagues argue that sharp minima in neural network loss landscapes are not the enemy they seemed, in a 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Flat minima were thought to generalize better, but counterexamples and exceptions have accumulated. The authors propose that sharpness is a property of the function being learned, not a reliable badge of poor generalization.

Across studies from single objective optimization to modern image classification, they find that sharper minima often appear exactly when models are regularized. That happens through methods such as sharpness aware minimization, weight decay, or data augmentation. Those sharp minima frequently coincide with better generalization, calibration, and robustness. Baselines without regularization tend to settle in flatter minima yet perform worse on every safety metric measured. They conclude that function complexity, rather than flatness itself, governs the geometry of solutions, and call for a function centric reappraisal of how loss landscapes are read.
arxiv-2510-12651:
Janson and Andén recover a signal from many noisy, randomly shifted copies of it while using far fewer copies than classical methods need, in a 2025 arXiv paper. This multi reference alignment problem appears wherever objects are imaged in unknown orientations, from astronomy to cryo electron microscopy.

Frequentist methods recover the signal accurately even at very low signal to noise ratios, but demand large sample counts. The authors instead take a Bayesian route, using a diffusion model as a data driven prior plugged into posterior sampling. Conditioning on the sample power spectrum, a statistic unchanged by shifts, lets them sample plausible signals and quantify uncertainty at the same time. Simulations show the prior greatly reduces the number of observations required, and comparisons against expectation maximization and bispectrum inversion are favorable. The authors propose the framework for other orbit recovery tasks such as cryo electron microscopy.
arxiv-2510-12951:
Domínguez Tubío and colleagues design a satellite quantum key distribution network for the Iberian Peninsula in this 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum key distribution exchanges encryption keys with security guaranteed by physics, but fiber networks lose photons exponentially over distance. A satellite carrying an entangled photon source can link distant ground stations instead.

Their setup uses a low-Earth-orbit satellite to connect Madrid with Barcelona, Bilbao, and Lisbon. Accounting for satellite vibrations, they optimized the beam waist, the narrowest width of the light beam, to raise transmission probability and improve the secret key rate. The resulting rates proved enough for real applications, such as secure communication between hospitals run through hybrid classical-quantum protocols. The authors conclude that national-scale satellite quantum networks are viable with near-term technology.
arxiv-2510-13051:
Srivastava and colleagues examine blind spots in randomized benchmarking in this 2025 arXiv paper. The method measures a quantum processor's average gate fidelity from the decay of sequence fidelity over random gate strings. It is prized for how well it scales. It also shrugs off preparation and measurement errors. Its standard theory, though, assumes that errors stay uncorrelated in time.

The authors derive exact formulas for the observed decay under fully correlated noise. In that regime, the method always overestimates it. They give operational criteria for telling whether a processor's noise is correlated in time at all. Partly correlated noise leaves the method blind to correlations when those criteria hold. The authors explore this effect in a classical environment model.
arxiv-2510-13151:
Lin, Kam, Sun, and Akşit hide more data in images by exploiting human vision in this 2025 arXiv paper, a SIGGRAPH Asia posters contribution. Steganography embeds payloads such as metadata or watermarks inside pictures, but capacity and accuracy trade against visible quality. Human vision is sharpest at the center of gaze and blurrier at the edges, a property called foveation that rendering systems already exploit.

The authors trained models combining efficient latent representations with a foveated rendering loss, which tolerates more change where viewers are least sensitive. Their models raised capacity limits from one hundred to five hundred bits while improving accuracy to as few as one failed bit out of two thousand across a large test set. Visual quality stayed comparable to prior work on standard metrics, which the authors present as evidence that perceptual design can expand what steganography carries.
arxiv-2510-13351:
Karthik Avinash and colleagues at FutureAGI introduce Protect, a guardrail model for large language models used by companies. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses a gap in safety tooling for these systems. Most current guardrails check text alone and work in isolation, which leaves image and audio inputs exposed.

Protect handles text, image, and audio within one system built for production use. It uses small fine-tuned adapters, each trained for one safety dimension: toxicity, sexism, data privacy, and prompt injection. A teacher-assisted labelling pipeline uses reasoning traces to produce detailed, context-aware labels across all three input types. In experiments, Protect beat existing open and commercial systems, including WildGuard, LlamaGuard-4, and GPT-4.1, on every safety dimension. The authors present it as a base for safety systems that firms can audit and run at scale. Real-time oversight and clear explanations shape the design throughout.
arxiv-2510-13451:
Bai and co-authors present SHAPOOL, a framework that makes inference attacks on machine learning models cheaper to run. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets shadow models, stand-ins that attackers train to mimic a target model. Attacks such as membership inference need many shadow models, which makes them costly. Training each stand-in separately is the main source of that waste.

SHAPOOL instead trains many shared models jointly inside a single process. A mixture-of-experts design links the models so they share some sub-networks. Three new modules keep the shared models faithful stand-ins for independent ones. They route data randomly, push the models to stay diverse, and align their behaviour with target models. Tests across several membership inference attacks show large cost savings in shadow model construction. Attack performance stayed comparable to the expensive independent approach, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-13851:
Lyu and co-authors edit language model knowledge repeatedly without new edits wiping out the old ones. Their 2025 arXiv paper, EvoEdit, addresses sequential model editing, where updates arrive over time. Locate-then-edit methods find the responsible weights and patch them directly. Stacked patches interfere catastrophically, corrupting earlier edits and untouched knowledge alike.

EvoEdit aligns each incoming edit with the null space left by previous ones. Updates land in directions that leave preserved representations unchanged. Output on protected knowledge stays invariant even across long edit chains, by construction. Benchmarks of real-world sequential editing show performance matching or beating prior methods. Editing also runs up to about three and a half times faster than the state of the art. The authors supply theoretical guarantees backing the stability claims. Dynamic information settings, where facts change continually, are the target use.
arxiv-2510-13951:
Jiayin Gu and co-authors build a framework for tracking how quantum coherence fades in high-energy particle collisions, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Decoherence, the loss of quantum information to the environment, matters as physicists begin measuring quantum effects like entanglement at colliders. Here the environment is the spray of radiation emitted after a collision.

Combining soft-collinear effective theory, a tool for radiation at extreme energies, with open-system methods, they make a move. They show the evolution of a spin density matrix acts like a quantum channel. That channel steadily erases information. The flow parameter of the renormalization group, a scale-setting device from field theory, plays the role played by time. Applied to a pair of fermions with photon-like radiation, their method gives the first sharper prediction for decoherence as a function of detector resolution. It identifies the mechanism as a phase-flip channel.
arxiv-2510-14151:
Saeed Moradi, Koosha Esmaeilzadeh Khorasani, and Sara Rouhani present a framework for linking permissioned and permissionless blockchains, the private ledgers and the public open networks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Linking the two kinds is hard because they differ in access control, design, and security needs, yet connecting them would turn lone networks into joint ecosystems.

Their chain-neutral design uses relay nodes and crypto techniques to exchange data, with a lightweight design meant to ease upkeep. The Clover and Dandelion++ protocols, techniques that obscure where a transaction originated, add anonymity during forwarding. The authors test performance by measuring resource use, forwarding time, throughput, and uptime across mixed blockchain ecosystems. They report that the framework achieves secure, efficient linking. The design avoids tying itself to any single chain, so the same approach can bridge different network pairs.
arxiv-2510-14451:
Thomas Klatzer and co-authors show how to compress the time dimension of system planning models when energy storage couples decisions across hours, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Time series aggregation replaces thousands of hours with representative periods. Storage breaks the tricks: charge now, discharge later means periods cannot be treated independently. Existing methods cannot guarantee the aggregated model gives the same answer.

Their approach uses constraint sets and dual information, the shadow prices of an optimization, to achieve exact aggregation of models with storage time-coupling. To make the theory practical, they use machine learning, classification and clustering. These inform aggregation in models that co-schedule renewables and storage. Results show improved performance relative to the full-scale model. They maintain a favorable tradeoff between solution accuracy and complexity. This advances beyond methods that rely on iteration or unguaranteed accuracy.
arxiv-2510-14651:
Tipler studies, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a class of geometric objects called toric sheaves, in the first part of a series. Sheaves are bookkeeping devices that attach algebraic data to regions of a space. Toric ones are tied to spaces with strong symmetry, here the complex projective spaces. The paper focuses on rank two, torsion-free sheaves that respect that symmetry, and on their Chern classes, which are basic numerical fingerprints of such objects.

For reflexive sheaves, a well-behaved subclass, Tipler derives a simple formula for the Chern polynomial. For the general case he gives an iterative construction based on elementary injections, which lets him prescribe the Chern classes in advance. This yields infinite families of explicit examples in dimensions four and five, and existence in every dimension from three upward. The examples respect all known constraints, and the paper adds simple obstructions to smoothability.
arxiv-2510-14851:
Bichler, Matoses Gimenez, and Alonso-Mora present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a scheduler that assigns tasks to teams of different robots in real time. Mixed teams, where robots differ in speed and skills, complicate assignment, especially when tasks must happen in a set order and coalitions of robots can share a job. Solving such problems exactly is too slow for live operation.

Their system, SADCHER, learns from optimal solutions instead. It is trained by imitation learning on a quarter-million optimally solved small instances, which the authors also release as a dataset. A graph attention and transformer model predicts each robot-task pairing's reward, using positions, durations, and remaining processing times. A relaxed matching step then turns the predictions into schedules with feasibility guarantees. On randomized unseen problems for small and medium teams, SADCHER beat other learning-based and heuristic methods, at speeds suitable for real-time use.
arxiv-2510-14951:
de Sousa, Fan, and Ku offer, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a way to say what makes a Mott insulator a Mott insulator, without leaning on broken symmetries. Mott materials insulate because electrons repel each other too strongly to move, though band theory says they should conduct. Traditional phase labels, built on symmetry breaking, do not capture this. The authors characterize phases by dynamics.

In their many-body renormalization group framework, they track long-lived eigen-particles and the repulsions between them at different momenta. The essence of Mott-ness, they find, is a change in how the repulsion scales with system size, which encodes bound states in the high-energy sector. It yields a uniform signature: Mott insulators occupy every momentum singly, while Mott metals do not. The description extends to topological Mott insulators and to bosonic versions: a paradigm for phases defined by dynamics.
arxiv-2510-15251:
Yingrui Zhuang and four colleagues help planners make decisions under uncertainty without drowning in possible futures. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns stochastic optimization with conditional value-at-risk, a method that weighs the worst outcomes heavily, common in power system planning. Checking every scenario is too slow, so analysts shrink the set, but older shrinking methods favor typical cases and drop the extremes that matter most.

Their framework instead judges scenarios inside the problem itself, projecting the full set into the problem's own space. An iterative method then picks representative scenarios that best match what the original set would decide, while keeping tail risks in view. The selection is cast as a mixed-integer program, a standard solvable form, and new evaluation scores grade the result afterward. In numerical tests the method cut the optimality gap below one percent within acceptable computing time, beating existing approaches.
arxiv-2510-15351:
Long Chen, Ruchi Guo, Jingrong Wei, and Jun Zou speed up the solving of nonlinear partial differential equations, the equations behind many physics and engineering models. Their 2025 arXiv paper proposes a method called DualTPD. Hard nonlinear terms make such equations slow to solve on fine grids, and faster solvers must first split the problem into friendlier pieces.

Duality theory does the splitting. Using Fenchel-Rockafellar duality, the method decouples the nonlinear terms so they can be handled with discontinuous finite elements, giving simple closed-form updates. A transformed primal-dual dynamic then drives the resulting saddle-point system toward its solution with strong, steady convergence. Custom preconditioners, built for the elliptic-type pieces left over, pair with multigrid solvers for extra speed. Tests on a p-Laplacian problem and a nonlinear curl problem showed large efficiency gains. Convergence stayed global and did not degrade as the mesh grew finer.
arxiv-2511-00051:
Da Chang, Peng Xue, and Yu Li build a unified weight conditioning framework for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, starting from a diagnosis of why the DoRA method works. DoRA decomposes weight updates into magnitude and direction and improves on plain low-rank adaptation, but its mechanism was unclear and its overhead significant. They identify increased singular value entropy of the update as the source of its success.

Higher entropy means a more uniform update distribution, closer to full fine-tuning. Their reformulated framework pursues that effect more directly. Machine learning readers get both an explanation and a cleaner method. Understanding why an adapter works guides better designs than trial and error.
arxiv-2511-00151:
Snehalata Sahu, Pier-Emmanuel Tremblay, and Detlev Koester re-evaluate Lyman alpha wing opacities as a possible cause of the low-mass problem in cool white dwarfs. Gaia data suggested masses from optical photometry fall a tenth to two tenths of a solar mass below single-star evolution expectations. Opacity in the red wing of Lyman alpha, from hydrogen collisions, strongly affects the blue end of cool white dwarf spectra, where the mass inference is sensitive.

Revisiting those opacity calculations in the quasi-static approximation tests whether atomic physics, not stellar evolution, is at fault. Stellar astrophysics readers get a careful check of a systematic error with wide consequences for white dwarf populations.
arxiv-2511-00251:
Felix Bartel and Pascal Schröter present a Fourier-based method for approximating functions with many input variables. Their starting point is the ANOVA decomposition, which splits a function into parts that depend on single variables and small groups. Real targets are smoother in some directions than others, and the method learns that uneven smoothness, called anisotropy, from scattered data points.

The learned smoothness shapes the algorithm's frequency boxes, whose tuned proportions raise accuracy. Fast transforms for unevenly spaced points keep the computing cost low. Dozens of parameters can be tuned with little overhead. Numerical tests confirm the method works well in practice, a useful step for high-dimensional problems in science and engineering.
arxiv-2511-00351:
Amir Ziashahabi and five co-authors question a strict rule in speculative decoding. That trick speeds up language models by drafting tokens with a small model and checking them with a big one. Standard decoding demands the output match the big model's sampling distribution exactly, which rejects many good drafts and caps the speedup. The authors argue the real goal is task performance, not distribution matching.

Their method, pivot-aware speculative decoding, rejects only pivot tokens, the drafts that would actually lower final quality. A light classifier learns to spot those tokens. Since non-critical drafts pass freely, acceptance rises sharply. Across several datasets the method reached up to about two and a half times speedup while keeping utility comparable to the target model.
arxiv-2511-00651:
Chenhua Shi and six co-authors automate telecom network troubleshooting with a team of AI agents. Networks keep growing in scale and complexity, while faults still send human experts hunting across data sources for root causes. Narrow AI tools need much labeled data and generalize poorly across deployments.
