The proposed multi-agent system activates specialists once monitors detect a fault: an orchestrator, a data retriever, a root-cause analyzer, an executor, and a solution planner.

The planner is the key component, drafting remediation plans grounded in internal documentation. A small language model, fine-tuned on proprietary troubleshooting documents, supplies those domain-grounded plans. Experiments show the framework significantly accelerates troubleshooting across both radio access and core network domains. Expertise that once lived in a few heads becomes a repeatable, automated workflow.
arxiv-2511-01251:
Qi-Chun Feng and colleagues improve how physicists image the fireball created in heavy ion collisions. Pions emitted from the collision carry information about the source's shape, but the standard analysis works in each pion pair's own center of mass frame. The boost between that frame and the source's true rest frame distorts the reconstructed image.

Their approach performs the correlation analysis directly in the global source rest frame, the physically meaningful frame of the fireball. The kinematic contamination disappears, the spurious non-Gaussian tail in the image is dramatically suppressed, and the reconstructed source matches clean model source functions far better. The authors present the method as a more direct probe of the collision fireball's space time properties.
arxiv-2511-01451:
Jiacheng Wang and colleagues jointly tune sensing, communication, and computing in low altitude wireless networks, the systems planned for urban air taxis and aerial surveys. Integrating all three functions is the core of such networks. But the open low altitude airspace invites eavesdropping and detection. That degrades the whole system.

They define three performance metrics: beam pattern error for sensing, secrecy rate for communication, and age of information for computing freshness. Then they pose a multi objective problem. It balances sensing and computing output while keeping the chance of the communication being detected below a set threshold. A deep Q-network based evolutionary algorithm searches for solutions. It adapts its operators to the evolving objectives. Simulations show it beating the rivals tried.
arxiv-2511-01551:
Elnaz Rostampour and Badie Ghavami propose the layered material lithium iridate, Li2IrO3, as a platform for high-temperature superconducting Majorana fermions, the exotic quasiparticles sought for topological quantum computing. The material combines strong spin-orbit coupling and a honeycomb lattice. It also sits close to a quantum spin liquid phase. Those are features the Kitaev model prizes.

Using a model built on the Kitaev-Heisenberg Hamiltonian, the authors describe the spin couplings in the material. They show topological zero-energy states exist. They also spot their signs in spectral weight piled at the edges, the mark expected of Majorana edge modes. A device concept based on the material closes the study, aimed at spintronics, magnetic field sensing, and topological quantum memory.
arxiv-2511-01851:
Sébastien Martineau and Christoforos Panagiotis prove that percolation, the mathematics of connectivity in random media, is a local affair on a broad class of graphs. Their graphs are transitive with polynomial volume growth: grids and their kin. The question is whether supercritical percolation on one such graph can be understood from another. The second graph merely looks the same out to some large radius.

The answer is yes, in uniform quantitative forms: supercritical sharpness and the Kesten-Zhang bound on large finite clusters hold with constants depending only on the reference graph and parameter. The density of the infinite cluster is an analytic function of the percolation parameter. This holds throughout the supercritical regime. Its analytic extension on one graph is uniformly approximated by the other's. The proof leans on new results about minimal cutsets and settles a question Babson and Benjamini posed in 1999.
arxiv-2511-02151:
P. Tutt and six colleagues at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams report progress on cleaning accelerator cavities with plasma while they stay installed in their modules. Plasma processing had already improved superconducting cavities at other laboratories by reducing field emission. The Michigan facility's quarter-wave and half-wave resonators pose a catch: their power couplers are deliberately weak, which badly mismatches the plasma process at room temperature.

Driving the plasma with higher-order modes instead reduces the mismatch and raises plasma density. A spare cryomodule was processed in January 2024, and the first in-tunnel trial followed in September 2025. Cold tests before and after showed some cavities reaching notably higher accelerating gradients before field emission began, and a dual-drive variant is being explored to strengthen the effect.
arxiv-2511-02251:
Robin Mader, Terry Gannon, and Arturo Pianzola develop a foundational tool for an algebraic structure used across modern mathematics and string theory. Vertex algebras are usually studied over a field. They can be defined over any differential commutative ring, and changing the base raises a descent question: which objects over a bigger base are really objects from a smaller one in disguise? The authors build the general descent theory for this setting.

Two applications follow. First, the theory classifies twisted forms of two cornerstone families, the affine vertex algebras and the Heisenberg vertex algebras, which are the versions that look standard only after extending the base. Second, it reinterprets and generalises a correspondence due to Li. The short paper lays the groundwork rather than chasing examples, giving later classification work a common language.
arxiv-2511-02451:
Kentaro Ueda, François Portet, Hirohiko Suwa, and Keiichi Yasumoto ask whether a specialist language model can be assembled by merging other specialists instead of training from scratch. General models stumble in finance, which demands domain knowledge, mathematical reasoning, and multilingual skill at once. The team continually pretrained separate expert models for finance, mathematics, and Japanese. They then merged them with three established techniques and judged the results in stages: knowledge recovery, complementarity, and emergence of new combined skills.

Merging an expert back with its base model recovered general knowledge that specialisation had erased. Merging the experts with each other lifted performance on a finance benchmark built from eighteen tasks and sometimes produced cross-domain abilities none of the parts had shown alone. One merging method was strongest but sensitive to its settings, another steadier; the authors frame the study as the first foundational analysis of merging continually pretrained models.
arxiv-2511-02551:
Alan Pearse, David Gunawan, and Noel Cressie build Bayesian models for maps of messy environmental data: large, noisy, incomplete, and stubbornly non-Gaussian. Their approach puts a copula, a device for joining distributions, at the heart of a spatial random effects model. New copula constructions keep a low-rank form so computation stays feasible. The copula process sits inside a hierarchical model whose data layer handles measurement error and missing observations.

In simulations the fully Bayesian method gave accurate, fast inference for both parameters and spatial prediction, beating several benchmarks including fixed rank kriging. The real test maps atmospheric methane over the Bowen Basin in Queensland, Australia, using retrievals from the Sentinel-5P satellite. The model class is offered as a general tool for spatial inference when the data refuse to be Gaussian or complete.
arxiv-2511-02651:
Apriel-H1 is a family of language models built for business reasoning, described in a 2025 technical report by Oleksiy Ostapenko and many colleagues. Large models based on transformers reason well, but their attention step grows costly as text gets longer. The team sought a design that keeps reasoning skill while running much faster.

Their models mix transformer attention with Mamba blocks, a leaner kind of sequence layer drawn from state space models. They built the hybrids by slowly swapping attention layers in a trained 15-billion-parameter model for Mamba blocks. One tuned variant ran more than twice as fast in a standard serving tool, with only a small drop in reasoning quality.
arxiv-2511-02951:
Sheida Rabeti and Hessam Mahdavifar improve the decoder for a promising family of quantum error-correcting codes. Their 2025 paper works on quantum low-density parity-check codes, especially the bivariate bicycle codes recently built in hardware studies. Decoding must be fast and accurate, since every uncorrected error threatens the stored quantum information.

Their decoder extends a multiple-bases belief-propagation method and adds list decoding with a new decision rule for picking the final answer. On a leading bicycle code, it cut the logical error rate by up to 40 percent against the best rival decoder, while keeping the plain method's linear-time cost. They also define a simpler univariate bicycle family with lighter checks, which shrinks the search for good codes, and show it performs well under several decoders.
arxiv-2511-03151:
A Osin, A Levchenko, and M Khodas study how electric current bends sideways in a class of magnets called altermagnets. Their work separates two sources of that sideways flow, one built into the material and one caused by scattering. The question matters because the two parts are often assumed to differ greatly in size.

Scattering turns out to matter far more than expected, matching the built-in part in about half of the magnet groups studied when the internal splitting is large. Where a certain magnetic interaction is present, the scattering part stays important even in very clean samples. Elsewhere it fades away. The authors trace both effects to how weak spin effects lift a matching of spin states inside the material.
arxiv-2511-03251:
Zhibin Wang and co-authors propose GMoPE, a way to make graph learning models work across many fields without retraining from scratch. Standard graph networks shine on one task but carry poorly to new domains, and tuning them can cost a lot. GMoPE mixes a team of expert modules with small prompt vectors that steer each expert toward a niche.

Routing that senses graph structure sends each job to the experts best fit for it. A soft rule keeps prompts distinct, so experts do not all collapse into the same role. Only prompts are tuned for new tasks, which keeps adaptation cheap. The authors argue the design fights harmful transfer while scaling to larger, more varied graph collections.
arxiv-2511-03351:
Saba Latif and colleagues give object-centric event data a semantic encoding built on web standards. That data model records business processes around both events and the objects they touch, aiming to be a common ground across providers. Merging sources and drawing inferences from merged records remain hard when meanings stay informal.

Encoding the model with semantic web tools adds machine-readable links, type labels, and ontology ties between records. Processes from different sources can then be combined with their meanings intact. Reasoning over the enriched data can surface links that plain records hide. The authors present the encoding as a step toward process data that travels well and supports stronger automated analysis.
arxiv-2511-03451:
Haida Li and Xiangdong Zhang study how a spinning black hole bends the path of massive spin-half particles. Neutrino mass is still known only within bounds, and fresh testing grounds for it are prized. A polarized beam passing a Kerr black hole has a critical radius tied to particle traits, which the authors compute from the quantum Dirac equation.

Their derivation yields a motion equation much like the classic one for spinning bodies, with the beam's own quantum spin in the spin slot. That match confirms the classic equation can serve genuine quantum particles here. Deflection near that critical radius could, in time, offer an astrophysical probe of neutrino and other ultralight particle masses.
arxiv-2511-03551:
Christian Laudage and Jorn Sass adapt a risk-level matching tool to the regulator's view across many insurers. European rules grade insurer safety with Value-at-Risk, though Expected Shortfall is widely seen as the better measure. Switching measures needs a principled way to pick the matching shortfall level for one firm's payoff.

PELVE supplies that match for a single insurer by equating the two measures. The authors extend the idea to a whole market under one regulator. Existence and uniqueness of the joint levels are analyzed, with formulas for elliptical payoffs and limits for heavy-tailed ones. A case study warns that the extension method chosen matters greatly when firms' payoffs differ in kind.
arxiv-2511-20251:
Ruan, Hsiao, Lo, Wu, and Shuai restore variety to images made from long prompts. Their 2025 paper studies text-to-image models under detailed instructions. Long prompts add content, layout, and style detail. Fidelity rises, but outputs grow repetitive and dull. The team measures that trade-off systematically.

A new benchmark, LPD-Bench, scores fidelity and diversity together. Four leading models were tested on it. SD3.5-Large, Flux, CogView4, and Qwen-Image all showed the slump. Diversity fell clearly as prompts grew longer. Their fix, PromptMoG, needs no retraining at all. It jitters the prompt embedding before generation. Samples come from a mixture of Gaussians around it. Sampling entropy rises while meaning stays anchored. Diversity improved across all four models consistently. Semantic drift stayed in check throughout tests. Theory links prompt rewriting to higher entropy. Creative tools regain range without losing obedience. Other media may adopt the trick later.
arxiv-2511-20451:
Fang, Wei, and Zheng construct heat flows that explode at chosen spots. Their 2025 mathematics paper studies a nonlinear heat equation on a half-space. Heat spreads inside a four-dimensional region above a flat boundary. Along that boundary, outward flow feeds back as the square of temperature. Such feedback can drive temperatures to infinity in finite time.

The authors prove blow-up solutions exist for any small time horizon. Pick any number of distinct boundary points in advance. Suitable starting data makes the solution blow up exactly there. Near the blow-up moment the profile decomposes into bubbles. Each bubble is a rescaled copy of one universal shape. That shape comes from a fractional Yamabe problem. A smooth background term stays negative at the blow-up points. Bubble scales shrink to zero at a rate with logarithmic corrections. Centers drift toward the prescribed points as time runs out.
arxiv-2511-20751:
Minju Lee and a large team unveil in 2025 ECOGAL, a project mining the ALMA radio telescope's public archive for galaxy data. Instead of new observations, they reprocessed archived data wherever the Webb and Hubble telescopes had already mapped the sky. From those overlaps they built two catalogues, one anchored to known optical galaxies and one blind, from ALMA detections alone.

This first release covers the CANDELS fields COSMOS, GOODS-S, and UDS, taking in about 130,000 optically selected galaxies. Together the methods found 1,288 detections, 622 of them unique sources. Of those, 307 have spectroscopic redshifts, placing them across most of cosmic history. Adding the UDS field and public Webb data pushes past the earlier A3COSMOS and A3GOODS-S projects. The team releases the catalogues as science-ready products for studying cosmic gas, dust, and hidden star formation.
arxiv-2511-20851:
Mousam Sinha, Tirtha Sarathi Ghosh, and Ridam Pal put in 2025 a feature-selection folk trick on firm statistical footing. Faced with thousands of candidate predictors, analysts often add random noise features and keep every real feature ranked more important than the strongest noise one. The trick works but has no theory and no principled stopping rule. Their method, NABFS, keeps the noise calibration and adds a non-parametric bootstrap hypothesis test for each feature.

Every candidate is tested against the maximum importance among the noise features, with resampling supplying the significance judgement that heuristics lack. In controlled simulations the method recovered signal more consistently than Boruta, the random-forest wrapper it most resembles, and than Knockoff-based methods. On real-world datasets it surpassed Boruta, Recursive Feature Elimination, and Extra Trees. The authors argue principled stopping matters as datasets grow: a selector should certify which rankings mean something.
arxiv-2511-21151:
Marco Alecci and colleagues document in 2025 how the same Android app quietly becomes a different app depending on where it is downloaded. They name one phenomenon GeoTwins: look-alike apps with shared branding released under different package names in different countries, like the game Unison League's Japanese and English editions. Despite the identical storefront face, twins diverge in privacy disclosures, requested permissions, and third-party libraries. A second finding cuts deeper: even the base.apk inside Android App Bundles, assumed identical everywhere, varies by region.

The consequences are practical. A malware study can call an app benign while another calls it malicious, purely because of download geography, silently biasing years of research. Users, meanwhile, consent to one product and receive another. The team built a multi-region collection pipeline, analysed thousands of apps, and released a curated dataset of 81,963 GeoTwins. Their advice targets researchers, developers, platforms, and regulators alike.
arxiv-2511-21751:
Single author Mohsen Soltanifar classifies every real-valued sequence by its long-run behavior, in 2025. The space of all such sequences is usually studied as an infinite-dimensional vector space. Soltanifar instead sorts each sequence by a pair of numbers: its limit inferior and limit superior, the floor and ceiling its values approach.

That simple profile partitions the whole space into seven mutually disjoint blocks, running from finite convergence through bounded and unbounded oscillation. Each block gets explicit closed-form examples. Every class holds as many sequences as there are real numbers. The paper maps how blocks connect at two scales: an idealized graph from injective mappings, and a finer relation from pointwise multiplication. The finite-convergence block emerges as the only true subspace and a global attractor with no outgoing links. The product structure realizes about two-thirds of all possible connections between blocks.
arxiv-2511-21851:
Rodriguez and colleagues revisit ADE minimal string theories, simplified two-dimensional string models. The A-series is understood through solvable two-matrix models. The D- and E-series are conjectured to correspond to unsolvable four-matrix integrals nobody can solve directly. The team instead computes observable amplitudes, scattering-like quantities, by direct numerical integration over the moduli space, the space of possible surfaces.

They calculated sphere four-point and torus one-point amplitudes for the A, D, and E minimal strings, confirming some results, disproving others, and supplying new data where matrix models make no prediction. From amplitudes with conformal boundaries they found evidence for multi-matrix structure in the D-series, including a ramp behaviour in cylinder diagrams and departures from the instanton pattern expected of two-matrix models. They also ran a preliminary positivity bootstrap fencing in the D-series critical points.
arxiv-2511-21951:
Wang and colleagues demonstrate a quantum machine learning advantage that grows as the system gets bigger, using light. Photons are robust, work at room temperature, and keep their quantum states for a long time, but how their large state space helps learning was unclear until now. The combined team proves that the learning capacity of linear optical circuits grows polynomially with the number of photons, so more photons mean learning from less data.

They then ran real experiments on a fully programmable integrated photonic chip, training it online, on the device, for unitary learning and metric learning tasks. The experiments confirmed the theory: higher photon numbers reached lower test loss and needed smaller training datasets to generalize, exactly the scaling their proofs predict for this platform. Adding photons becomes a reliable dial for better performance, not fragility.
arxiv-2511-22251:
Hojny and Roy, optimization researchers, bring symmetry handling to Benders decomposition. A workhorse method that solves large mixed-integer programs by projecting out some variables and reintroducing their effect through cuts generated on demand by a separation oracle. Symmetry techniques turbocharge ordinary solvers, but they never transferred systematically to Benders setups because the cuts are not written down anywhere; they exist only inside the oracle. So the symmetry of the whole problem was invisible.

The authors build a tailored family of graphs capturing the symmetry information of both the master problem and the oracles. Once graph symmetries are computed by established tools, classical symmetry handling becomes available inside the decomposition. They add separation and aggregation techniques for symmetric cuts that substantially cut the number of oracle calls. Numerical tests on bin packing and scheduling problems show the combined effect, .
arxiv-2511-22351:
Bagaria, a machine learning researcher, builds a deepfake detector that also explains itself, even on heavily degraded images. Detectors usually emit a bare verdict and collapse under compression, downsampling, and domain shift, which undermines trust exactly where verification matters. INSIGHT super-resolves the image to amplify forensic traces, localizes suspicious regions with Grad-CAM heat maps. Aligns them with CLIP semantics, then has a vision-language model reason step by step over what it found.

A dual-stage check screens explanations for hallucination. Across test scenes, down to 16 by 16 pixel resolutions in their evaluation, the system improves detection robustness and explanation quality over prior baselines. The framework aims at forensic workflows where an unexplained flag is not enough. Each explanation names the artifact it relies on, so a human reviewer can verify the claim against the image instead of trusting the model.
arxiv-2511-22751:
Papazov, D'Angelo, and Flammarion ask whether gradient learning can master an algorithm exactly. Neural networks fail at length generalisation in arithmetic, memorising patterns that break on longer inputs. Their framework uses Differentiable Finite-State Transducers, a Turing-complete model family avoiding earlier architectures' traps: constant precision, constant time per step, and end-to-end log-parallel differentiable training. Training data are policy-trajectory observations, an expert's intermediate steps, not just inputs and outputs.

Trained on tiny datasets, the transducers learn binary and decimal addition and multiplication, then generalise without error to inputs thousands of times longer than any seen in training. That is exact learning in the strict sense: the correct rule applied to every input, achieved by ordinary gradient descent. They present it as evidence that differentiable agents given structured intermediate supervision can acquire precise algorithmic skills, toward systems whose arithmetic can be trusted rather than checked.
arxiv-2512-00051: Amelia Fernández Seguel, an undergraduate engineering student at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, studies how magnetic forces act between tiny robots. Her project covers modeling those forces and using them to control the robots' motion. Microrobots are small machines that can be steered without direct contact, and magnetic fields are a common way to move them. The surviving record gives the topic, the author, and the program setting, but no abstract text. Her methods and results therefore cannot be described in more detail here.
arxiv-2512-00251:
Internet-of-things networks are easy targets for denial-of-service attacks, because their devices are many and often weak. Henry Onyeka and co-authors propose SD-CGAN in 2025, a framework for spotting such attacks at the network edge. Traffic there is dynamic and heavily imbalanced.

SD-CGAN is a conditional generative adversarial network enhanced with Sinkhorn divergence, tailored for anomaly detection in edge environments. It is designed to catch sophisticated attacks and zero-day exploits that known signatures miss. Reliable detection protects everyday connected devices, from cameras to sensors, that owners rarely monitor themselves. Edge deployment keeps detection close to the devices under attack, cutting response time. Generative models help because attack traffic is too varied for fixed signatures alone.
arxiv-2512-00451:
Voice calls over satellite, maritime, and tactical links are expensive because bandwidth is scarce. Siyu Wang, Haitao Li, and Donglai Zhu present STCTS in 2025, a generative semantic compression framework for speech at ultra-low bitrates. Traditional codecs struggle below one kilobit per second.

Earlier semantic approaches convert speech to text and back, sacrificing prosody and speaker identity. STCTS decomposes speech explicitly into text, prosody, and timbre, then regenerates natural voice from that compact description. Keeping the speaker's tone and identity at very low rates could change communication wherever bandwidth is precious. The target rate, around eighty bits per second, is far below ordinary telephony. Prosody carries emotion and emphasis, which text-only schemes throw away.
arxiv-2512-00551:
Equal sums of like powers form a classical Diophantine puzzle: two pairs of numbers whose powers match. Valery Asiryan studies the equation under an extra linear constraint in 2025, calling the approach the linear slicing method. The variables are nonnegative integers and the exponent is real and greater than one.

Modular and geometric constraints narrow where solutions can hide. Linear slicing cuts the search space with a condition linking the pair sums, turning a wild problem into a structured one. Such equations connect to taxicab numbers and Euler's sum of powers, small questions that have driven number theory for centuries. The linear constraint is the slicing move that gives the method its name.
arxiv-2512-00651:
Mohammed Latif Siddiq, Arvin Islam-Gomes, Natalie Sekerak, and Joanna Santos examine how repeatable recent software research really is. Their 2025 study covers papers that use large language models to help with software engineering tasks. Repeatable work lets other teams check results and build on them with trust.

The team mined and reviewed hundreds of papers from top venues in software, machine learning, and language work, spanning 2020 to 2025. They pulled structured details from the papers, code stores, and project notes. Their large survey gives the field a clear baseline on what authors share, and what they leave out.
arxiv-2512-00851:
Du Wenzhang wrote a 2025 paper on forecasting traffic across many cities at once. Traffic patterns differ sharply by city: road networks vary in size and shape, and data volume can differ by orders of magnitude. New cities may join with only a few weeks of logs.

Most deep traffic models are trained for one city and one backbone model at a time. Keeping a separate predictor for every city is costly. The author's city-conditioned memory gives one model a store of city-specific patterns it can draw on. That design aims to help forecasts transfer to new cities with little data.
arxiv-2512-01151:
Dong Liu proposes Fiber Bundle Networks in a 2025 machine learning paper. Most deep networks fit functions as black boxes, powerful but hard to interpret. Liu instead combines differential geometry with machine learning, recasting classification as a geometric optimization problem on fiber bundles.

In a fiber bundle, points of a base space each carry a fiber, a small space attached above them. Here, categories form the base space, and wavelet-transformed features lie in the fibers above each category. Classification then becomes a structured geometric choice rather than a blind fit. Interpretable geometry could help users see why a model sorted an item as it did.
arxiv-2512-01551:
Yunfeng Jiang and co-authors extend the rational Q-system to spin chains without U(1) symmetry. The Q-system solves Bethe ansatz equations in full. It has been a fast, complete tool. Its use was stuck to systems with that symmetry, though.

Their extension covers closed XXZ-type chains that lack it. Removing the symmetry cap widens the tool a lot. Many real integrable models lack U(1) symmetry. A complete solver for them helps in condensed matter work on magnets and cold atoms. The closed XXZ case is a proving ground, chosen since its spectrum is known well enough to expose any gap in the new frame.
arxiv-2512-01751:
Christian Bonatti and Theo Marty build foliations from pre-laminations on a circle. A singular foliation on the plane has a circular boundary at infinity. That boundary carries a pre-lamination structure. The forward link was known. The converse was open.

The pair solve the converse in full. They state which pre-laminations arise from a foliation. They then build the unique matching foliation. Both regular and prong-singular cases are covered. The result completes a dictionary between plane dynamics and circle data. Uniqueness matters as much as existence, since a boundary that matched two foliations would leave the dictionary ambiguous at its core.
arxiv-2512-01851:
Nishil Savla rebuilds the PMNS matrix with a classical pendulum system. Neutrino oscillations come from interference between mass states. The PMNS matrix governs that mixing. The effect is quantum at its core. Its math mirrors coupled classical oscillators, though.

Savla builds three pendulums linked by springs as an analog. The pendulum modes mimic three-flavor oscillation traits. A tabletop analog makes abstract mixing tangible for students. It also offers an intuitive check on how mixing angles shape oscillation patterns. Spring constants map to mixing angles, so turning a lab knob sweeps the analog through the same space neutrino fits explore.
arxiv-2512-01951:
The Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3 has an infrared detector whose response bends slightly as signals grow, and astronomers correct that bend pixel by pixel. Sachindev Shenoy and co-authors revisit the correction in 2025, which rests on ground test data gathered during a thermal vacuum campaign before launch.

In the current reference file, each pixel's correction coefficients are averaged across the detector's four quadrants, smoothing away pixel-level detail. A per-pixel correction promises cleaner measurements of faint infrared sources. Work of this kind quietly underpins the accuracy of every infrared image the camera delivers, long after its ground tests ended.
arxiv-2512-02051:
If two whole-plane functions share enough values, must they be one and the same? Jeet Sarkar and Debabrata Pramanik chase this question in 2025. They compare a function with a shifted form built from its own rate of change.

Such sameness theorems are core tools in the study of how functions spread their values. They tell when data pin a function down in full. The pair prove three results. Each one sharpens and broadens a 2011 theorem by Qi. Stronger rules help analysts see when shifted forms, common in difference equations, cannot pose as each other.
arxiv-2512-02151:
Integrating an increasing function once gives its accumulated area; integrating the result again and again builds a tower of smoother curves. Maxim Burke and co-authors characterize in 2025 exactly which triples of values those repeated integrals can take at the endpoint, for increasing functions on the unit interval.

The question grew out of a problem about approximating smooth functions by entire functions in a comonotone way, keeping the same increasing pattern. Knowing the reachable set of first, second, and third integral values draws the boundary of what such functions can do. Results of this kind are the fine print of approximation theory, where they decide which approximation schemes can exist.
arxiv-2512-02251:
Farmers adapting to climate change need answers that are both scientifically accurate and readable, and those answers are scattered across papers and government data feeds. Liangji Kong, Aditya Joshi, and Sarvnaz Karimi present CAIRNS in 2025, a question-answering system for climate adaptation that tries to hold both virtues at once.

Adaptation strategies for sustaining food production live in unstructured literature and in structured climate data from official sources. A system that can draw on both must phrase findings plainly without flattening their accuracy. Balancing readability against precision is the central design problem, and it decides whether farmers and advisors can actually use the answers.
arxiv-2512-02351:
Unified multimodal models pack understanding and generation into one system, but most tasks use only a slice of that bulk. Shwai He and three co-authors study in 2025 how sparsity, running only the needed parts, can cure the inefficiency that unification creates.

A question about a picture may not need the model's generation machinery, and a caption may not need its deepest reasoning. Identifying and harnessing that sparsity means routing each task or sample to the capacity it actually requires. The work points toward unified models that keep their versatility without charging every user for all of it.
arxiv-2512-02551:
Songqiao Su and five co-authors attack matrix multiplication, the core math inside large language models. Fast multiplication kernels are hard to tune by hand. Each matrix shape rewards a different strategy, and tricks that help on one graphics chip often fail on another.

Their system, CUDA-L2, uses reinforcement learning to search for fast kernels on its own. The learning agent tests variants and keeps what runs fastest, aiming past the standard cuBLAS library. Automatic tuning at scale could speed up AI training and serving, where multiplication dominates both time and energy cost. Speed gains here flow straight to the cost of each task a firm runs on its chips.
arxiv-2512-02751:
Rakib Ahsan and three co-authors spot methane plumes from space with an attention based neural network. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and fast detection of leaks allows timely repair. Satellite images from Sentinel-2 already watch the whole planet on a regular cycle.

AttMetNet adds attention layers that teach the network where a faint plume is likely to hide. The framework targets plumes in Sentinel-2 imagery specifically. Automated detection at scale could help governments and firms find super emitters, a small set of sources behind much of the methane problem. Most leaks come from a few bad sites, so a fast sky scan is the quick way to find the worst ones first.
arxiv-2512-03051:
Ocean models stumble at coastlines, where their grids simply end. Treating fields near domain boundaries is a long standing problem in signal processing. New convolution based coarse graining methods and machine learned parameterizations have revived it, since both create artifacts at ocean boundaries.

The proposed method extends fields beyond the boundary by solving a Laplace boundary value problem. That harmonic extension is general and principled, not an ad hoc patch. Cleaner boundaries improve multiscale analysis and learned ocean models, where coastal errors now leak into open water forecasts. Coasts are where most of us live and work. Coast wise marks in a sea model are worth more than their share of grid points would first suggest to a glance.
arxiv-2512-03551:
Groups of users may need to prove membership all at once. Oylum Gerenli, Gunes Karabulut-Kurt, and Enver Ozdemir present a user centric group authentication scheme in this 2025 work. Group schemes verify many users simultaneously without a certification authority.

Past schemes fall into three generations based on their math foundations. The authors aim for a scheme centered on user needs for secure communication. Efficient group checks matter for chat, IoT networks, and shared workspaces. Removing a central authority can cut cost and single points of failure. User centric design aims to ease enrollment, a common pain point in group schemes.
arxiv-2512-03951:
Tensor products multiply mathematical objects together, and algebraists have long wanted a version that works inside abstract categories, not just for vector spaces. Bo Shan Deval, Manfred Hartl, and Tim Van der Linden build one in a 2025 category theory preprint. Their product is defined intrinsically for objects of a semi-abelian category, using a construction called the cosmash product.

Applied to abelian objects, the construction recovers the classical tensor product in many cases. A recognition theorem then characterises exactly which pairing operations arise this way for varieties of algebras. The authors develop the product's basic properties, compare it with the older Brown-Loday non-abelian tensor product. They go on to prove a categorical analogue of Ganea's six-term sequence. They also give explicit descriptions for representation categories. There, their product of modules generalises how group and Lie algebra representations are combined.
arxiv-2512-04051:
Training large models in low precision saves enormous computing, but the usual recipe computes updates in full precision and rounds them afterwards. Paul Wilson, Fabio Zanasi, and George Constantinides propose cutting out the rounding step in a 2025 machine learning preprint. In their schemes, the update rule itself is discrete, producing integer steps by design rather than by discretising a continuous update.

The authors prove that a general class of such schemes converges. As a concrete member, they present a multinomial update rule, backed by empirical evaluation. The framing matters most for models whose structure is inherently discrete, where pretending updates are continuous wastes effort. The work connects to a wider push for efficient training under hardware constraints. Giving discrete rules a rigorous footing may open design space that quantisation cannot reach.
arxiv-2512-04251:
A bilayer of the material Td-MoTe2 does something remarkable: flipping its ferroelectric polarisation with a displacement field switches its superconductivity on and off, with hysteresis. Yanfang Li, Xin-Zhi Li, and Wen-Yu He explain that coupling in a 2025 preprint. Why it happens matters because such switching promises low-power, non-volatile memory, yet its origin was poorly understood.

Their explanation centres on pairing between p and d orbital electrons within each layer. The effect sorts them into distinct layers, suppressing the intralayer pairing and killing the effect. A Landau-Ginzburg model shows hysteretic switching requires the remanent value to sit below a critical pair-breaking value, itself below saturation. The scenario makes testable predictions: an anisotropic, momentum-dependent pairing gap, and a possible transition into a pair density wave when the chemical potential is tuned.
arxiv-2512-04751:
Junhao Wei, Yanzhao Gu, Ran Zhang, and co-authors pair an improved whale-inspired optimizer with a gradient boosting model to flag promising computer science students early. The base Whale Optimization Algorithm mimics how whales circle prey, but it searches narrowly, converges slowly, and can stall in local traps. Their 2025 arXiv paper upgrades it into NAWOA with several new strategies for exploration and balance.

Good-node-set starts, leader-follower foraging, dynamic encircling, and triangular hunting widen the search. A nonlinear factor steadies the landing. On standard test functions, NAWOA beat the classic optimizer in strength and robustness. The tuned XGBoost model then trained on records of hundreds of computer science undergraduates across a decade at Macao Polytechnic University. Early flags of academic potential could help advisors steer support to students before small struggles grow into failure.
arxiv-2512-04851:
Yirong Fang, Changfu Shi, and Jianwei Mei study one of the most violent events the universe allows: two black holes colliding at near light speed. Such head-on relativistic crashes could expose cracks in general relativity, since no merger of spiraling pairs reaches their energy. Nature rarely arranges them. Their 2025 arXiv paper finds a plausible stage: a triple system, where a massive black hole's gravity whips two smaller companions to relativistic speeds.

The team models collisions in the heavy hole's background and computes the gravitational wave signals they would emit. They then grade which current and future detectors could catch such a signal. The waveforms differ sharply from ordinary merger chirps. A detection would open a window on gravity at its most extreme, and even a null result across surveys would bound how often triple systems stage these crashes.
arxiv-2512-05051: Alberto Merici's short note computes a basic invariant for logarithmic motives, an advanced framework extending the algebra of geometric shapes to spaces with a chosen boundary. For a smooth, proper variety over a perfect field, he shows how to compute the zeroth homotopy group of its motive directly. He also proves the result is unchanged by the theory's standard homotopy deformation. Applying the method to the projective line, he shows the functor that forgets the logarithmic structure loses no information.
arxiv-2512-05151: Bojan Žunkovič's lecture notes introduce quantum machine learning to an audience of computer scientists. Quantum machine learning applies quantum computing ideas, superposition, interference, and quantum circuits, to the tasks of machine learning, and it is usually taught to physicists. These notes take the other door in, presenting the subject for readers whose home ground is algorithms rather than laboratory physics. As lecture notes, they form a structured teaching text meant to be worked through, lowering the entry barrier for computer scientists who want a route into the field.
arxiv-2512-05951:
Teofil Bodea and nine co-authors present Omega, a platform for running AI agents in the cloud without trusting the cloud too much. Agents read sensitive data, call tools, and talk to each other inside systems where some components may be hostile. Confidential virtual machines protect single programs, but say nothing about trust between the many parties an agent serves, nor about the graphics accelerators agents think with.

Omega builds a Trusted Agent Platform inside one confidential machine, using nested isolation to host many agents at once. Trust across principals is established by differential attestation. Every outside interaction is supervised under stated policies governing data access, tool use, and agent to agent talk, with provenance recorded. Built on AMD and NVIDIA confidential hardware, the system secures agent state end to end while staying fast and dense. The aim is cloud agents a bank could sign off on.
arxiv-2512-06351:
Zhiying Yang and five co authors present Luca, a scheduling system for smart factories that weighs both speed and carbon cost. In a flexible job shop, each job can run on several machines, and plans must shift as orders and conditions change. A plan that is fast but dirty, or green but late, fails the twin goals of modern plants.

Luca fuses two views of the shop floor. A graph network reads the web of jobs and machines, while a large language model, steered by a home grown prompt plan, adds context about the current state. The fused picture feeds a learning policy that issues scheduling choices in real time. Its score rewards both short total run time and low emissions. On made up and public data sets, Luca beat rival methods, cutting run time at the same emission level and gaining on both counts in public tests.
arxiv-2512-06551:
Jonas Britz and Monique Laurent study how to tell whether a quantum state shared by two parties is entangled or merely separable, a split that decides what quantum tasks it can power. Testing separability is a known hard problem. A hierarchy of semidefinite tests, the DPS hierarchy, approximates the set of separable states from outside, level by level, but can be too heavy to run.

The authors exploit structure to make it lighter. For states unchanged by diagonal unitary twists on both sides, they show the hierarchy breaks into blocks, which, joined with a moment based reading, gives a far cheaper implementation. For states with Bose symmetry, they characterize the dual hierarchy through sums of squares of polynomials. Two cones from optimization, the completely positive cone and its dual, turn out to run through both settings. The work brings a hard detection problem closer to routine computation.
arxiv-2512-06651:
Hayk Lekdar Gevorgyan revisits how to model a radio frequency helical deflector, a device that steers charged particles with a rotating field. Two helical conductors carry a radio frequency voltage, and the field they make sweeps an electron beam around in a circle or spiral. That sweep turns the time structure of a beam into a spatial pattern, which makes the device a fine timer for time of flight measures, with resolution reaching picoseconds.

Textbooks model the deflector one way; an older proposal by Shamaev models it another. Gevorgyan proposes a capacitor model, sets the three side by side, and works out what each really assumes. From his analysis come formulas for the electric field, the size and tilt of the ellipse the beam traces, and how much beam duration each stretch of the pattern encodes. He also treats the resonant case, where the pattern closes into a circle.
arxiv-2512-06851:
Ruijiang Ji, Yunbo Zhang, Shu Chen, and Zhihao Xu ask a counterintuitive question: can random disorder create orderly quantum behavior instead of destroying it? Their test bed is a chain of paired sites, the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, where links inside each pair vary at random. The randomness follows a flexible pattern whose values and odds can be tuned separately. In such chains, disorder can switch on a protected state known as a topological phase.

As the disorder grows stronger, the authors show, the region of that protected phase can split into several separate windows. The count, width, and place of the windows follow directly from the settings of the random pattern. Exact formulas for the window edges match computer checks using two other measures. A moving signal called mean chiral displacement can also spot the windows in real time, giving experimenters a practical handle on disorder-made order.
arxiv-2512-06951:
Ilia Larchenko, Gleb Zarin, and Akash Karnatak report the winning entry in the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge, a contest for robots that do household work in realistic simulation. The benchmark holds fifty long tasks that need two-handed handling, moving around rooms, and decisions that depend on context. Their entry builds on a vision-language-action policy called Pi0.5, which turns camera views and instructions into movement.

The team's main trick concerns the noise used while training the policy's action generator. By correlating that noise, they train faster and can patch action sequences smoothly, keeping motion coherent. Learnable attention that mixes layers helps too, as does a stage tracker that notes which step of a task the robot is on. Extra sampling during training calms erratic outputs, and compression plus hand rules tidy the final actions. The system topped both public and private leaderboards across all fifty tasks.
arxiv-2512-07051:
Adnan Munir, Muhammad Shahid Jabbar, and Shujaat Khan present DAUNet, a lean network for outlining organs and lesions in medical scans. Such segmentation guides diagnosis and treatment planning, but leading models are heavy, which shuts out clinics with modest computers. DAUNet reshapes the classic U-shaped design with two frugal additions: convolutions that deform their sampling grid to fit anatomy, and an attention scheme that needs no extra learned parameters.

The deformable kernels sit at the network's bottleneck, where they adapt to varied shapes, while the attention modules refine the decoding path and the skip connections that carry fine detail. On two demanding data sets, fetal ultrasound and chest scans for lung clots, DAUNet beat state-of-the-art rivals on overlap and boundary scores alike. It did so with fewer parameters than the competition. Tests removing each addition confirmed both pieces earn their place.
arxiv-2512-07351:
Sayeem Been Zaman and co-authors hunt deepfakes with a committee of agents rather than a single detector. Faked video now tampers with face and voice together. And detectors that fuse both senses inside one model can be thrown off when the two streams disagree, or when noise and manipulation hit unevenly. DeepAgent splits the work. One agent reads each video with a compact convolutional network, hunting the visual signatures of manipulation.

The second agent attacks from the audio side: it combines sound features, speech transcripts from a recognition system. And text read off the frames, looking for inconsistencies between what is said, heard, and seen. A random forest meta-classifier then weighs the two agents' decisions, exploiting the fact that they fail in different places.
arxiv-2512-07651:
Yuanye Liu and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 medical imaging report on liver fibrosis. Scarring of the liver is a heavy global health burden. Staging that scarring correctly decides how each patient should be managed.

The report introduces LiQA, a dataset built for the CARE 2024 challenge. It gathers MRI scans from hundreds of patients across several centers. The scans come in multiple phases and reflect messy real-world conditions. Domain shifts, missing scan types, and misaligned images all appear in the data. Algorithms are benchmarked on two tasks against that backdrop. One task segments the liver; the other stages its fibrosis. The report also describes the challenge's top-performing method in detail. It pairs semi-supervised learning with outside data for sturdy segmentation. For staging, it seeks agreement across views and regularizes with activation maps. Using many data sources and anatomical rules clearly boosts robustness.
arxiv-2512-07751:
Shoham Letzter and Arjun Ranganathan wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on cycles in hypergraphs. A Hamilton cycle visits every vertex of a graph exactly once before closing. In hypergraphs, edges hold many vertices, and cycles can overlap in varied patterns.

The authors seek the exact density that forces such a cycle to exist. Their condition is a new flavor called minimum supported co-degree. It counts, for sets of vertices inside an edge, how many edges contain them.  Under that condition, large enough hypergraphs must contain the desired cycle. The bound they prove is tight for infinitely many parameter choices. For all other choices it misses the truth by at most one. Earlier work had only an asymptotic version of the statement. One special case settles a conjecture from a recent team of five authors. A new tiling method powers the proof.
arxiv-2512-07851:
Sansrit Paudel wrote this 2025 paper on cleaning up biological signals before machines learn from them. Heart and body sensors produce streams that real life constantly corrupts. Motion artifacts and wandering baselines spoil stretches of otherwise good data.

Some corrupted segments are too degraded for any filter to rescue. Paudel's goal is to sort the stream rather than save every piece. The sorting runs in two stages of increasing detail. First, clean segments are separated from noisy ones as a binary call. Second, the noisy pile is divided by kind: motion, sensor failure, and others. The tool is K-means clustering, an unsupervised method needing no labels. It groups clean segments from noisy ones with notable reliability. Clean data, in particular, is identified with strong consistency. Keeping only high-quality segments sharpens the features fed to later models. Downstream learning on biosignals should then grow more precise.
arxiv-2512-08151: Jeremie Brieussel and Ryokichi Tanaka, mathematicians, posted a short research paper on arXiv in December 2025. They study random walks on virtually abelian groups, a family that behaves almost like a grid of integers. Their question is noise sensitivity: does a tiny random disturbance to the walk change where it ends up, measured in total variation? They prove a clean criterion: such walks are noise sensitive exactly when the group has no nonzero homomorphism onto the integers, tying a probability property to a purely algebraic one.
arxiv-2512-08351:
Ngoc Tan Nguyen, Thi Thu Hoang, and colleagues, wireless researchers in Vietnam, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is jamming, where an attacker floods a wireless channel to block communication. Drones make the threat worse: a flying jammer can move, aim with line of sight, and adapt, while defenders run on tiny power budgets.

Their defense turns the attack into a resource. A transmitter in an ambient backscatter system learns through deep reinforcement learning. It chooses when to transmit actively, when to harvest energy from the jamming signal, and when to backscatter data using the jammer own emissions. The team models the choice as a Markov decision process and solves it with a deep Q network. In simulations, the learned policy converged faster than plain Q learning and beat a greedy defense on throughput, packet loss, and delivery ratio.
arxiv-2512-08751:
Kuniko Paxton and coauthors present a pruning method to shrink large vision models for skin lesion work on edge devices, while learning across sites without sharing data. Top vision models can beat specialists at lesion classification, but they are too large and compute heavy for small devices. Privacy rules also block central collection of medical images, which motivates federated learning.

Their method prunes parts of a multimodal Swin transformer based on the skewness of output distributions, targeting attention and feed forward layers. In a horizontal federated test, the pruned model keeps its accuracy while its size falls by about a third. That balance matters for real deployment. The study shows that careful compression and privacy preserving training can coexist for multimodal medical systems that must run on limited hardware at the point of care.
arxiv-2512-09151:
Anna Chlingaryan, Arman Melkumyan, and Raymond Leung address a practical problem in mining: estimating the chemistry of rock underground from drill samples. Blasthole samples do not measure a single point. Each one averages the rock along a drilled interval, and standard models that treat them as points lose that information.

Their method, IntegralGP, uses Gaussian processes, a statistical model that predicts values with uncertainty, built to handle interval data directly. They work out the changed mathematics the idea requires, including the formulas needed to train the model and the numerical care it demands. The method then merges blasthole results with an existing block model of the deposit to forecast iron grades in the bench of rock below. In validation tests, the fused model predicted grades more accurately and made fewer costly mistakes, such as calling waste rock high-grade ore.
arxiv-2512-09751:
Keyu Wei and colleagues use gate tuning to settle a debate about tantalum nickel selenide. It may be an excitonic insulator, a state where electron-hole pairs condense and open an insulating gap. Proving that mechanism has been difficult because a structural change occurs alongside it, and the two are hard to separate. The team studies flakes from bulk to a layer with Raman spectroscopy.

It survives to the monolayer limit. Its temperature rises as the material gets thinner. In bilayer samples, electron and hole doping both suppress the insulating state, though they shift it in opposite ways. The quasi-elastic scattering signal blamed on exciton effects grows across the doping range, opposite to what screening of exciton links should do. The authors conclude it is a coupled electronic and structural change, not excitonic, and offer doping as a test for such insulators.
arxiv-2512-09851:
Yuyang Li and colleagues build a robot sensor that sees and feels at the same time. Their see through skin sensor pairs a camera view through soft material with touch signals from the contact surface. Earlier designs could not capture both senses at once, and their touch tracking was unreliable. The new sensor, called TacThru, uses a transparent elastomer, steady illumination, and keyline markers. A matching system, TacThru-UMI, feeds both signals into imitation learning.

The learner uses a transformer based diffusion policy, a method that generates robot actions from demonstrations. On five hard real world tasks, the combined system succeeded about eighty-five percent of the time on average. That clearly beat a touch only policy and a vision only policy. It did especially well where contact sensing is decisive, such as detecting contact with thin or soft objects, and in precise tasks needing vision and touch together.
arxiv-2512-10351:
Georgi Bebrov asks a basic question about quantum key distribution, the method that uses quantum physics to share secret keys. How can anyone tell whether a given system is running as well as it possibly could? His 2025 paper sets out to give that question a precise, testable answer.

Bebrov defines a quantity he calls optimality, the best total efficiency a key distribution setup could reach under any settings, judged in the long-run limit of many uses. He then shows how that best case could be reached by pairing a top-performing quantum channel with a fully compressed classical channel. He closes by giving optimal versions of two known protocols, BB84 and twin-field distribution.
arxiv-2512-10451:
Le Tuan Minh Trinh and co-authors borrow a concept from human psychology: metacognition, knowing how much to trust your own judgement. Deep learning models give confidence scores, but those scores are often badly calibrated, claiming certainty where the model is actually weak. Their paper, presented at a NeurIPS 2025 workshop, asks whether a model's self-trust can be measured and then put to work.

The team defines a sensitivity measure, drawn from cognitive science, for how well a model's confidence tracks its own accuracy. That score then guides a bandit-style arbiter that picks, task by task, which of several expert models to believe at test time. Across varied datasets and model pairings, including image networks and vision-language models, the metacognitive route beat simply using any single model on its own.
arxiv-2512-10751:
Charlie Lloyd and Robert Dorrell simulate what offshore wind turbines do to layered seawater. New wind farms are pushed into deep, seasonally stratified water, where a turbine's foundation sits in a two-layer sea and its wake stirs the layers together. How much mixing follows, and by what mechanism, was poorly understood, caught between crude field-scale models and sparse measurements.

The authors ran the first structure-resolved direct numerical simulations of two-layer stratified flow past a vertical cylinder. Two wake regimes emerged, set by the flow's Reynolds and Richardson numbers. Weak stratification gives a narrow, energetic wake ruled by horizontal shear, the regime of today's wind farms. Under strong stratification, a recirculation cell spans the layer boundary. Strong vertical motions develop there. They launch large stationary internal waves, which carry a real share of the energy far downstream. That explains puzzling field reports about wake persistence.
arxiv-2512-10951:
Samuel Goldstein and J. Colin Hill report the first robust evidence that galaxy clusters rotate, seen through a faint signal in the cosmic microwave background. As background light scatters off hot gas inside a cluster, the gas motion leaves a two-sided pattern aligned with the cluster's spin. Finding that pattern required careful separation from much stronger background noise.

The team combined Planck satellite measurements with galaxy redshifts from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey for a sample of massive nearby clusters. The dipolar signal lined up with each cluster's estimated angular momentum and was very unlikely to be chance. Its size and shape matched advanced simulations, giving astronomers a new tool for probing how clusters move and evolve.
arxiv-2512-11251:
Yunkai Zhang and a large team build Insight Miner, a multimodal model that explains time series data in plain language across many domains. Charts of measurements drive decisions in fields from farming to finance, but extracting insights usually takes scarce expert time. Their system generates detailed descriptions enriched with domain knowledge, after training on a new paired dataset.

The companion dataset joins one hundred thousand time series windows from twenty forecasting collections with written trend descriptions. An agentic workflow built it by first extracting statistical features with tools, then having a large model weave those features into coherent narratives. After instruction tuning, Insight Miner beat leading multimodal models, including a top commercial system, at describing series and drawing insights. The authors frame the work as a first step toward models that read time series as a native input.
arxiv-2512-11451:
Joshua Althüser, Ilya Eremin, and Götz Uhrig report an unexpected strengthening of superconductivity when many electronic states pile up near the Fermi energy. In the standard BCS theory, phonon mediated attraction between electrons matters mainly right at the Fermi surface, so the superconducting order away from it is usually tiny and ignored. A closer derivation shows the attraction acts whenever two electron energies differ by less than the phonon energy.

When the density of states has a peak close to the Fermi level, that neglected region lights up. The order parameter near the peak can exceed its Fermi level value at moderate coupling strengths. A softening collective mode announces the effect, resembling a second phase transition. The authors predict concrete signatures in thermodynamic and spectroscopic measurements. Their analysis turns a textbook approximation into a search strategy for enhanced superconducting behaviour.
arxiv-2512-11751:
Andy A Shen and co-authors improve a causal inference tool by letting outcomes choose what to balance. In observational studies, fair group comparison needs balanced background traits. Kernel balancing picks a similarity measure, then balances a summary of it, but that summary is chosen blind to the outcome.

Their forest kernel balancing uses random forests and BART, two tree based learners. Trees group units that land in the same leaf, and that grouping defines a kernel shaped by outcome relevant patterns. In simulations and real examples the method beat standard kernel balancing on speed and accuracy. It offers a practical way to fight hidden bias in health and policy studies.
arxiv-2512-12251:
Saneesh Babu, Gabriele Di Stefano, and Aparna Lakshmanan S study graph coloring in a 2025 math paper. Their version uses mutual visibility: points with the same color must be able to see each other along a shortest path with no other same color point in between. The goal is the fewest colors that can do this.

They prove that finding that number is NP-complete, a sign of a hard problem, even for graphs with diameter four where the answer is just two. They also find exact values for glued binary trees and glued t-ary trees. Such exact cases help map where the problem stays tractable.
arxiv-2512-12451: Vladimir Guletskii presents a claimed proof of the Bloch conjecture, a statement in algebraic geometry first made by Spencer Bloch in 1975. The conjecture deals with smooth projective surfaces. In plain terms, these are curved two dimensional shapes that are cut out by polynomial equations and have no sharp edges or gaps. The conjecture says that the Albanese kernel of such a surface is zero. That holds as long as the second cohomology group of the surface is algebraic in nature.
arxiv-2512-12551:
Dewen Suo and four co-authors test Android security tools against anti-runtime analysis tricks in a 2025 paper. Android draws many new apps each year, and malicious apps increasingly use anti-runtime analysis, or ARA, techniques to block dynamic examination. Such tricks detect analysis setups and hide bad behavior, complicating the work of security professionals who run apps to watch what they do.

Their empirical study measures how well widely used dynamic analysis tools bypass varied ARA techniques. Results reveal a critical gap: current tools often fail against these countermeasures. The authors call for more robust solutions and offer their findings as a map of where existing tools fall short, to guide improved defenses.
arxiv-2512-13651:
Taishi Sano and Yuki Yokokura study Schrödinger symmetry in small, simplified gravity models with matter fields. Such mini-superspace models keep only a few degrees of freedom of a full spacetime. Past work found this symmetry emerging in a fluid limit, and the authors test how robust that emergence is.

They study two spherically symmetric, static models at the classical level: one with a Maxwell field and a cosmological constant, and one with many massless scalar fields. For the first, 3D symmetry emerges and the solution is the de Sitter Reissner-Nordström spacetime. For the second, symmetry in 2+n dimensions appears, with a generalized Janis-Newman-Winicour solution. They also offer a physical reading of what the symmetry generators do.
arxiv-2512-14051:
Mengzhang Cai and the OpenDataArena team introduce OpenDataArena, an open platform for benchmarking the value of post-training data sets for large language models. Model quality depends on post-training data, yet that data is usually a black box: opaque composition, uncertain provenance, and no systematic evaluation. That blocks reproducibility and hides how data traits drive model behavior.

The platform combines a unified training-evaluation pipeline, a multi-dimensional scoring framework, an interactive data lineage explorer, and an open-source toolkit. Experiments cover over 120 training data sets, 22 benchmarks, more than 600 training runs, and 40 million processed data points. Findings include trade-offs between data complexity and task performance, plus redundancy in popular benchmarks found through lineage tracing.
arxiv-2512-14251:
Nat Sothanaphan improves a lower bound for a classic distance problem in a 2025 note. Erdos, Herzog, and Piranian asked whether, for points in the plane with a fixed largest distance, a regular polygon makes the product of all pairwise distances as large as possible.

For even counts, a regular polygon was recently shown not to be best, but the gain was tiny. Sothanaphan proves the best arrangement beats the regular polygon value by a factor above 1.037 for large even cases, settling a stated conjecture. Some other arrangements look even better but lack proofs. Whether the ratio can grow without bound remains open, and no such arrangements are known.
arxiv-2512-14651:
S. Saoud and four co-authors study quintessential inflation inside the inert doublet model, a particle physics setup with an extra scalar doublet. A quintessence field with an exponential potential is coupled in, with the aim of covering both early inflation and today's accelerated expansion in one story.

Using a conformal transformation from the Jordan frame to the Einstein frame, they derive an effective Starobinsky-type potential reshaped by an exponential factor. They then test the scenario against the swampland bounds, conjectured limits on which theories can sit inside quantum gravity. The paper links a concrete particle model to those wider consistency checks.
arxiv-2512-14851:
Aslak Djupskås and two coauthors test a popular shortcut for judging how unsure a neural network is. The shortcut, Monte Carlo dropout, runs a network many times with random parts switched off and treats the spread of answers as uncertainty. It is widely used because full Bayesian methods are too slow for big networks.

The team compares the shortcut with Gaussian processes and Bayesian neural networks on test problems. Monte Carlo dropout often failed to show more doubt in the zones where doubt should grow, such as far from the training data or between clusters. Bayesian methods did show that growth. The authors conclude that, as tested, dropout based doubt is not as trustworthy as classic Bayesian doubt, a caution for safety critical uses.
arxiv-2512-15051:
H. M. Florez gives the first microscopic account of how hot atomic vapor can create entangled light in many spatial modes at once. Multipartite entanglement, links among many parties, is a resource for quantum information work. Earlier experiments showed alkali atoms could generate it in a single device through four wave mixing, a nonlinear process where pumps trade photons.

Florez extends a double Lambda model of single pump mixing to a two pump setup in dense vapor. A Floquet expansion solves how the modes gain strength and how much noise they carry. The model captures how the output depends on angle and on pairs of photons, and describes the quantum correlations among modes. It matches the main traits of past experiments, and can predict gain patterns and correlations across the range of settings labs actually use.
arxiv-2512-15151:
Yuki Nakayama and three coauthors release a large corpus of hotel reviews for language research. The Rakuten Travel Reviews collection holds 7.29 million customer reviews spanning 16 years, from 2009 to 2024. Each record pairs the review text with the hotel's response.

Records also carry an anonymized reviewer ID, the date, IDs for the hotel and the plan, the room type and name, the trip purpose, and who traveled along. Guests rated six aspect categories plus an overall score. The authors present statistics for the corpus and study how the data drifted between 2019 and 2024, using statistical tools to find what drove the shift. A long, rich, and openly described dataset like this supports work on sentiment, dialogue, and changing travel taste.
arxiv-2512-15451:
Addhyaya Sharma and co authors report a new way to build polaritonic circuits that work at room temperature in a 2025 paper. Polaritons are hybrid states of light and matter that can carry signals, and they may serve in analog computing. Older ways of shaping the host cavity gave designers little freedom after the fact.

The team etches circuits of chosen shapes into a finished organic microcavity using a focused ion beam. They show polaritons condensing and moving through straight and trapezoid guides at room temperature. Test devices include a ring guide, a Y splitter, and a Mach Zehnder interferometer. The work is an early step toward full polariton circuits.
arxiv-2512-15851:
Naoto Nakatsuji, Jennifer Cano, and Valentin Crepel present a high throughput workflow for twisted moire homobilayers in a 2025 paper. Stacking two layers of the same material with a twist creates moire patterns that can host designer quantum phases. Experiments have sampled only a narrow slice of the possible materials and angles.

The workflow pairs small scale density functional theory with perturbation theory to extract moire band gaps, valley Chern numbers, magic angles, and relaxation thresholds quickly. It also parameterizes a continuum model for each material for deeper study. The survey flags chromium based dichalcogenides for high temperature quantum anomalous Hall effects, nitride halides for mixed superconducting and moire physics, and thin III-V semiconductors for room temperature scale effects.
arxiv-2512-15951:
Shih-Yu Chang advances a theory program in this 2025 arXiv paper on quantum mathematics. It is the third part of a project building a unified algebraic foundation for operator theory and quantum processes. The language is multicategories and operads, tools for describing how operations with many inputs combine.

Chang introduces n-adjoints, a ladder of generalized adjoint operations for multi-input settings, and proves a version of Stinespring's theorem with them. He then shows that standard quantum channels, the allowed transformations of quantum states, form algebras of a single monad built from an interaction operad. Finally, he encodes famous no-go rules, such as the ban on cloning quantum states, as algebraic constraints. The results tie operator theory, category theory, and quantum information into one framework.
arxiv-2512-16051:
Sidharth Kannan and three co-authors apply graph neural networks to gravitational wave hardware in an arXiv paper made public in 2025, presented at a NeurIPS 2025 workshop. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, detects ripples in spacetime with complex optical instruments. Simulating those optics with standard software is accurate but slow.

The team trained graph neural networks to mimic the simulations for three interferometer layouts. The networks captured the intricate light physics well while running 815 times faster than state-of-the-art simulation packages. The authors also released their high-fidelity simulation data as a benchmark for future work. The study opens a new use for these networks: helping design scientific instruments, not just analyzing the data they produce.
arxiv-2512-16351:
Anshu Kumar and three co-authors survey water simulation in a paper published on arXiv in 2025. Computer models of fluid flow are now a cornerstone of water engineering. They help predict and manage rivers, pipe networks, and treatment systems. The survey reviews the math models and numerical methods behind that practice.

Coverage runs from shallow water equations to full three-dimensional Navier-Stokes models. The history and math structure of each model are explained. The authors compare the main ways to solve them on a grid. They also cover practical headaches. These include source terms, wetting and drying fronts, turbulence, and free surfaces. Data assimilation, uncertainty estimates, and machine learning add-ons get their own sections. Case studies from large water systems show how modeling choices change outcomes. The survey is a unified reference for researchers and practitioners.
arxiv-2512-17051:
Haoye Lu, Yaoliang Yu, and Darren Lo study how to restore a true distribution from many noisy, partial samples when clean samples are rare and dear. The corruption process is known only as a black-box generator.

They frame the task as one-sided entropic optimal transport and solve it with an EM-like algorithm. A test tells whether the true distribution can be recovered under the given per-sample loss, and in lost cases a few clean samples can make it largely recoverable. Their bridge model, SFBD-OMNI, maps corrupted samples back to ground truth for arbitrary measurement models, past Gaussian cases. Benchmarks show clear gains in quality and scores.
arxiv-2512-17251:
Madhava Gaikwad designs AlignDP, a guard meant to stop people from copying what a large language model knows. Attackers can extract training data, distill a model into a cheaper copy, or fine-tune it without permission. Older defenses such as watermarks only react after the leak has already happened.

AlignDP acts earlier, at the point where data enters or leaves. It splits fields into rare and common kinds and treats each kind in its own way. Rare fields get a strong shield that hides them almost fully, while common fields get measured noise so counts stay useful. A global tracker watches the total privacy budget. In a small test, rare groups stayed hidden and common groups were recovered with little error.
arxiv-2512-17451: Noam Berger, Anders Johansson, and Anders Öberg settle a threshold question for the Dyson model. In that model, a chain of spins feels every other spin, with a grip that fades with distance. The team proves the freezing point is the same either way. Stated as a critical inverse temperature, it matches whether the chain stretches one way or both ways. The proof covers fade powers between 1 and 2. They conjecture the same match holds at the borderline power 2.
arxiv-2512-17651:
Andreas Kirchner and three co-authors ask whether one fluid story can cover a nuclear smash from first touch to final spray. When heavy ions collide, they melt into quark-gluon plasma, and modelers usually start their fluid math a heartbeat after impact. Everything before that moment gets guessed, and those guesses are the biggest error source in the field.

The team tests whether a second-order fluid theory can stretch backward to cover the incoming nuclei themselves. They set out the needed equations and check how entropy grows along the way. The results are first steps, not a finished model. The larger prize is a single description where the only unknowns left are the plasma's own material traits.
arxiv-2512-17751:
Dimitrios Chatzis, John M Marley, and Daniel C Thompson revisit a claimed bridge between theories in six, four, and two dimensions. A diagram nicknamed the twistor diamond links a six-dimensional theory at the top to integrable two-dimensional models at the bottom. Coupling two copies of the top theory was proposed to switch on gaugings, extra symmetries, all the way down, but the proof covered one special case.

Recast in Cartan geometry, the mechanism now works for generic setups, the hidden gauge structure made plain. Applied to the lambda-deformed WZW model, the coupling does induce gaugings, with a twist: extra multiplier fields force the gauged connection flat. The two-dimensional children are thus non-Abelian dualisations, not mere gauged models. The diamond's plumbing needed relabeling, and dualities gain.
arxiv-2512-17951:
Kaijie Chen, Zhiyang Xu, Ying Shen, Zihao Lin, Yuguang Yao, and Lifu Huang presented SuperFlow, a faster way to train flow based image generators with reinforcement learning. The framework varied how many trial images each prompt received and scored credit step by step, matching the flow of the model. Reported tests used far fewer training steps and beat a strong base model by wide margins on text and layout tasks.

Readers should know that this paper has been withdrawn from arXiv. The withdrawal note states it was submitted without the consent of all listed authors. Because the submission itself lacked full author approval, the reported gains should not be relied on. The entry is kept as the record of a withdrawn submission.
arxiv-2512-18151:
Cesar Fierro Cota studies six dimensional supergravity theories that come from F theory built on elliptically fibered Calabi Yau threefolds. For such a theory to make sense, its gravitational, gauge, and mixed anomalies must cancel, and that demand ties geometry to counting problems.

The counting side is the Gromov Witten theory of the fiber curves, and its generating series are quasi Jacobi forms.
