Few officials leave so clear a trail from their desk to a president's signature.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d151:
Relations with the London Poles would be no more than “correct,” Stettinius cabled Harriman on 13 December 1944. His secret and urgent instruction, number 2828, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It sets the line Harriman was to hold in Moscow on Poland.

The present Polish cabinet, Washington judged, could not work out any agreement with the Soviet government. Ambassador Lane would stay in Washington until January, and no meaning was to be read into that. Harriman was to make clear that the United States still recognizes the London government. If it helped, he could add that Washington would not look kindly on Soviet recognition of the Lublin Committee. Should the London cabinet fall, Mikolajczyk might yet form one that backed his own policy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d251:
Harriman arranged a Friday meeting to draw Stalin out on the Pacific war. His report to the President of 11 October 1944, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, describes the plan agreed with Churchill the night before. Presidential approval was still to come.

Stalin and his military men would face Churchill, Brooke, Ismay, Deane, and Harriman. The chief aim is to learn two things. How soon after Germany's collapse will Stalin be ready to act against Japan? And what, in general, can Russia bring to that war? The picture gained would clear the way for the detailed talks between Deane and the Red Army Staff. Those, Harriman insists, should be Soviet-American only, with the British kept informed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d351:
Of this meeting, nothing said survives at all. The editors' note reports that no record of its substance has been found in the files. What is known of the session — its time and who attended — comes from the official trip log alone. The log shows the talks went on after lunch until 3 p.m.

Gaps like this run through the Yalta record, and the volume marks them rather than hiding them. A reader learns where the paper trail ends. Whatever passed between the leaders that afternoon stayed with the men in the room. The note stands as a warning against over-reading the famous record.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d451:
Agreement on Poland leads Eden's report in Bohlen's minutes of the plenary of February 10, 1945. Eden told the leaders the foreign ministers had settled the future government of Poland. Two questions within it he would refer to later. He then read the new formula, with one correction he admitted Molotov had made.

A new situation, the formula begins, has been created by Poland's complete liberation by the Red Army. A Polish provisional government, more broadly based, must follow. The session's list runs on: French participation in Germany's control commission, Yugoslavia, the world body, reparations, and the Dardanelles. Bohlen records the conference reaching its harvest day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d51: From Moscow on 11 January 1945, Harriman sent Roosevelt a report that stands as document 51. It belongs to the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, issued by the Department of State. Written three weeks before Yalta opened, the report helped the president judge what the Soviet leadership might demand, and what it might accept, once talks began.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d151:
Churchill showed Truman his reply to Stalin about the Balkan states in telegram number 83, sent June 10, 1945. The message is document 151 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stalin had written on May 27 that the time had come to restore diplomatic relations with Romania, Bulgaria, and Finland, and perhaps soon with Hungary.

Churchill's quoted reply thanks Stalin for the news. Britain has been weighing its own future relations with those states, he writes, and hopes very shortly to put full proposals before Stalin and the United States government. He hopes the three can then discuss them when they next meet. The exchange touched a sore point: the ex-enemy states of Eastern Europe were falling under Soviet control, and recognition was one lever the West still held.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d251:
A briefing paper set American aims on Soviet support for the Cairo Declaration, in extracts dated June 29, 1945. The paper is document 251 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It formed part of the annexes to the State Department's agenda memorandum for the President.

The minimum objective is to win Soviet adherence to the Cairo Declaration. That would give Moscow's backing to the pledge that Korea in due course shall be free and independent. It would also bar any one power from setting up a friendly government on its own in the territories concerned. The maximum objective goes further: an agreement among the three powers, with China's expected cooperation, to jointly support the measures best suited to grow a strong, democratic, independent Korean nation. The full text appears later in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d351:
German central offices form the third topic in Dunn's extracts of his July 14, 1945 talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan at Potsdam. Cadogan cited a memorandum by Field Marshal Montgomery, approved by the Prime Minister. It urged restoring central German ministries so the Control Council could handle problems that touched Germany as a whole.

Cadogan doubted Berlin could house such agencies. Dunn answered that the United States favored building German central administrative agencies, though under a less imposing title than ministries. The exchange shows both allies groping toward the same need: some German machine, under allied control, to run railways, food, and finance across zone lines.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d451:
MacVeagh's letter to Prime Minister Voulgaris, written at Athens on July 13, 1945, carries the Greek election proposal to the Greek government itself. Under his instructions, he informs the Premier of allied obligations to Greece, the undertakings at Yalta, and Article Nine of the Varkiza Agreement. America and Britain have agreed on a joint step.

If the move is agreeable to the Royal Hellenic Government, the two powers will approach the Soviet Union and France. Their proposal: that the approaching Greek national elections be held under the supervision of the four allies named. Voulgaris returned the letter at once, with his signed agreement written on it that same morning.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d51:
President Truman settled the argument over dates in a top secret reply to Churchill on June 5, 1945. The message is document 51 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, answering Churchill's plea for an earlier Big Three meeting. Only part of the telegram is printed, but its decision is complete.

Truman says that after full consideration, July 15 is the earliest date he can manage. Plans are therefore going ahead for him to travel to the area near Berlin and arrive on that day. Churchill had warned that delay would let Soviet power harden in central Europe, but the President held firm. The exchange fixed the opening date of the Potsdam Conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d551:
A top secret briefing paper on Yugoslavia was drawn up for the Potsdam Conference on July 5, 1945. It is document 551 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers. Its subject is how Marshal Tito had dealt with the Crimea, or Yalta, pledges on his country.

The paper says Tito has not carried out those pledges. A regency and a joint government were set up in March 1945 under the Tito-Subasic deal. But the wartime assembly was never widened as promised, and six new federal states are all run by partisans. It cites seized property, attacks on clergy, and U.S. firms put under state control. It urges the three powers to restate the pledges and offer to consult.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d651:
A top secret briefing paper on the future of the Tangier zone was dated June 29, 1945. It is document 651 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Tangier, in Morocco, had been run under an international statute since 1923.

Spanish forces seized the zone on June 14, 1940, by a one-sided decision of Spain's government. Madrid said the move guarded the zone's neutrality during the war. Spain now wished to regularize the situation, the paper says. France and Britain had invited the U.S. to informal talks in Paris on the zone's future. The first task was to shape a provisional regime for the span after Spanish forces and officials left. A full international conference would later settle a permanent regime.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1051:
Britain's delegation proposed this supply plan for the occupation zones at Potsdam on July 30, 1945. Its general rule is that each zone, Greater Berlin included, should draw supplies from the parts of Germany it drew on before the war, so far as practical.

On food, the Soviet zone may have no surplus for the west until the 1946 harvest. Even so, it should feed itself and all Berlin up to the Control Council's minimum standard. From that harvest on, it should supply Berlin and the west at roughly the old scale. On coal, Polish-run land within the 1937 borders would send five million tons a year west for three years.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1151:
Washington's team tabled this proposal on 29 July 1945, as Potsdam entered its final days. Late papers served a new purpose. The broad choices were made; now the teams fought to turn them into exact, signed language that would hold.

Each American paper in this stretch was a bid to shape the Potsdam Protocol, the summit's official record of its choices. Words fixed there would govern Germany and Europe for years. A proposal of 29 July belongs to that drafting fight. It shows the United States driving to close the summit on terms it could defend at home and abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1251:
Hurley wrote to the President and the Secretary of State on 26 July 1945. The date was heavy with news: Britain's count changed its government that day, and the Allies issued their terms to Japan. Hurley's dispatch from China entered that stream at the top level.

His reports kept China's crisis before the men who could act on it. The republic he dealt with was fraying as victory neared, and his cables said so in his own blunt style. This message is one of his summit-week reports. It shows the China file claiming its share of the leaders' crowded day.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1351:
Norman Armour, the American ambassador in Spain, answered the acting secretary of state on 18 July 1945. Two days earlier, Washington had sent Armour fresh instructions. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

An ambassador's reply shows how guidance from home plays out on the ground. Armour dealt with Franco's Spain, a state the winning powers kept at arm's length while still needing to talk. Read with the instruction that came before it, this cable forms a small pair: order and report, question and answer. Pairs like that are the basic rhythm of the whole Foreign Relations series.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-151:
Cohen's notes for July 31, 1945 capture the Potsdam talks on their last full day. Benjamin Cohen had recorded the sessions since the opening week. His final sets were printed in the second Potsdam volume. The closing hours turned on exact phrases, and Cohen's legal ear was built for them.

In these notes the reader hears the talks winding down. Old arguments return in shorter form. New wording gets tested word by word. Cohen's care lets us watch commitments being nailed down. The pages close his run as one of the most useful witnesses the American side produced.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-51:
Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 21, 1945, record a midday session on basic objectives, strategy, and policy. The top secret extracts are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Potsdam papers. Much of the debate turned on a shipping paragraph in the joint strategy paper.

Admiral Leahy proposed a point of clarity first. Wherever the draft said this war, it should say the war against Japan. General Somervell then read the cargo shipping wording Lord Leathers was expected to propose. He recommended the U.S. chiefs oppose the change, since it ignored shipping problems of concern to the United States alone. Admiral Gardner saw no reason to single shipping out for the objectives statement. Food and petroleum, he noted, were matters of the same nature and might claim a place on equal grounds.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d751:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff addressed the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee on July 17, 1945, in document 751. The committee joined the three services' work with the State Department's. Potsdam's opening day found the chiefs feeding military views into that shared channel. The paper entered the second Potsdam volume.

This channel mattered because Potsdam's choices mixed war and policy. Occupation, surrender terms, and force levels crossed every desk. The chiefs wrote to the one body built to join them. Readers see the American system aligning its parts at the summit's start. The document shows coordination as a daily act, not a slogan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d851:
Major Harold Zink of the Political Division, United States Group, Control Council for Germany, wrote this memorandum on July 16, 1945. Document 851 brings a staff officer's view from inside the occupation. Zink was a scholar of government serving in uniform. His memo joined the second Potsdam volume.

A major's memorandum can carry an expert's weight. Zink knew German administration from study and from the ground. Readers get the occupation analyzed by a man inside it. The document shows the Control Council's own staff thinking about their task on the summit's eve. Their questions would outlast the conference: how to govern a beaten land justly and well.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d951:
Edwin Pauley sent President Truman a staff analysis of Marshal Zhukov's charges on July 29, 1945. Zhukov had accused American and British armies of stripping factories in the Soviet zone. Pauley calls the report a smoke screen. Soviet teams, he writes, were already shipping whole plants to Russia before any reparations plan won approval.

His Committee I, chaired by Robert Sproul of the University of California, found Zhukov's facts largely correct but trivial. Western removals, they say, were mostly war booty and new German technology. Damage came largely from looting by freed slave laborers. Soviet removals, by contrast, took farm gear, sewing machines, and textile machines that were no war potential at all.
frus-1977-80v09Ed2-d51: A 1977-1980 FRUS document from the later Arab-Israeli dispute volume. Camp David's aftermath. This entry preserves that record. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
gao-gaoreports-b-298651: 2B Brokers and others took their November 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firms said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Group filings get the same full hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298751: Philadelphia Produce Market Wholesalers took its December 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firms said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Even produce fights get full hearings.
gao-gaoreports-b-309751: The Borenstein Group challenged a federal communications contract in 2007, and GAO's ruling settles it. The marketing shop said the award was unfair; the call measures the claim against bid law. In the niche market for government ad and media work, the ruling marks where the creative pitch meets the legal rulebook.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-151: The E-Rate program needed a stronger FCC hand in 2005, and GAO's report says greater involvement was required in management and oversight. The review calls for the chairman's attention. The school internet dollars deserved the watch. The involvement had to grow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-251: Anthrax test swabs needed proof in 2005, and GAO's report says the crews had to back their clean bills. The review demands the evidence. The mailrooms deserved the certainty. The certainty had to be earned. The proof was demanded. The evidence was demanded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-351: Treasury's currency manipulation checks found nothing in 2005, and GAO's report says the assessments came up empty, though exchange rate concerns continued. The review reports the clean bill with caveats. The trading partners were watched. The concerns remained. The trading partners were watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-551: RFID in the federal government got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines the tracking technology's use. The findings take the measure. The report shows the radio tags were being weighed. The technology had to be understood. The radio tags were being weighed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-851: Train riders' safety needed a federal steer in 2005, and GAO's report says the feds had to lead the charge. The report demands the direction. The findings warn that the train riders deserved protection. The train riders deserved protection. The feds had to lead the charge.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-51: IRS filing season services improved somewhat in 2005, and GAO's report says some services got better, though long-term goals would help. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the taxpayers deserved reliable help. The goals had to be set.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-151: Small firms loved the Pentagon's mentoring program in 2007, and GAO's report says the proteges valued the help, though the yearly reports to Congress needed work. The findings praise the program and prod the paperwork. The mentorship was real; the metrics were not.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-351: The bank insurer's cyber program needed staying power in 2007 — GAO's report says the FDIC had to keep up its security gains. The findings press for persistence, not one-time fixes. The report's message: the deposit guardian's own vault must stay locked tight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-451: The Pentagon's back-office blueprint was getting a redesign in 2007 — GAO's report lays out the plan for shaping the business systems map. The findings sketch the new concept in plain terms. The report's hope: draw the firm's nervous system before you start rewiring it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-51: The Navy's giant intranet needed a report card in 2007, and GAO's report says the Pentagon had to ensure the program met its goals and satisfied users. The findings demand the proof. The report warns that the sailors' network should actually work for sailors. The intranet had to deliver.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-651: Katrina's poison lingered in 2007 — GAO's report says the EPA's environmental work on the Gulf could do more by facing its information gaps. The findings press the agency to fill the data holes. The report argues that cleanup without good maps is just expensive guessing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-851: The Pentagon's personnel overhaul was flying without instruments in 2007 — GAO's report says it needed better controls and cost visibility. The findings target the management fog around the new HR system. The report demands a dashboard for one of the largest workforce experiments ever tried.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-251: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at homeland Defense: US Northern Command Has Made Progress but Needs to Address Force Allocation, Readiness Tracking Gaps, and Other Issues. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-351: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on somalia: Several Challenges Limit US and International Stabilization, Humanitarian, and Development Efforts. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-51: This 2007 Government Accountability Office report reviews NASA's Ares I rocket — the planned crew launcher for the post-shuttle era. GAO found the agency had taken steps toward sound investment decisions but still faced major gaps in what it knew about cost, schedule, and technical risk. The report reads as an early warning about a program that would later be canceled amid exactly the problems GAO flagged.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-851: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on defense Critical Infrastructure: Adherence to Guidance Would Improve DOD's Approach to Identifying and Assuring the Availability of Critical Transportation Asse. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gesner-historia-animalium-lib1-1551:
Conrad Gesner, a Swiss doctor and tireless scholar, began his Historiae animalium in 1551 with this first volume. It treats the viviparous quadrupeds, the live-bearing four-footed beasts, mammal by mammal. Scholars call the whole work the founding text of modern zoology.

Gesner names each animal in several languages and reports its habits, uses, and lore. Fine woodcut portraits made the books famous across Europe. He includes tales he doubts alongside facts he trusts, and often says which is which. The scale of the labor still stuns readers. Volume one set the pattern for three centuries of animal books.
glauber-furni-novi-philosophici-1651:
Johann Rudolf Glauber published Furni Novi Philosophici in 1651, a work on new philosophical furnaces. Glauber was a German-Dutch chemist known for Glauber's salt and for skill with furnaces and distillation. Better ovens, he argued, meant better chemical work.

Designs and directions show how to build furnaces and use them to draw spirits, oils, and salts from many materials. Glauber treated wine, metals, plants, and minerals, and he hinted at uses in medicine and trade. He guarded some secrets while printing enough to prove his skill. The book captures a moment when craft knowledge of fire and vessels was becoming modern chemistry.
govdocs-archive_org-SeptuagintBrenton185:
Sir Lancelot C. L. Brenton published his English translation of the Septuagint in London in 1851, through Samuel Bagster and Sons. The Septuagint is the ancient Greek version of the Hebrew Bible, the form of scripture used by the early church.

Brenton's edition includes the Apocrypha alongside the Old Testament books, giving English readers the full Greek canon in one volume. His translation stayed close to the Greek text and became the standard English Septuagint for generations. It is still the version many readers reach for when they want the Greek Bible in English.
gregory-letters-candid-inquirer-1851:
William Gregory systematized animal magnetism in Letters to a Candid Inquirer, printed in 1851. Gregory, a chemist at Edinburgh, wrote the letters as a manual for the open minded. Magnetic sleep, clairvoyance, and mesmeric cure receive ordered treatment. He gathers the evidence claim by claim, with cases in support.

The book became the standard British manual of the subject for mid Victorian readers. Through it, many households first met mesmerism in sober form. Gregory answers doubters while granting the field its share of fraud. His order and calm made the strange seem studyable. The letters preserve how Britain learned mesmerism. They remain a clear window on the practice.
hawthorne-house-of-seven-gables-1851:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The House of the Seven Gables in 1851, his romance of inherited guilt. The tale turns on the Pyncheon curse and a Salem house built on stolen land. Hawthorne called it a romance, free to bend fact toward mood and moral truth in prose.

Colonel Pyncheon seized Matthew Maule's lot and saw him hanged for witchcraft in old Salem days. Maule cursed him from the scaffold, and Pyncheons die strangely for two hundred years after in turn. Hepzibah, a faded gentlewoman, opens a shop in the house while her brother Clifford returns from prison. Young Phoebe's cheer and Holgrave's secret soften the gloom toward a late, guarded hope in love. The book probes how class, guilt, and old wealth decay in a young republic.
hawthorne-snow-image-1851:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Snow-Image, and Other Twice-Told Tales in 1851, a full story collection. The volume holds famed tales like The Great Stone Face and Ethan Brand among its pieces. It gathers his later magazine work into the last tale book of his lifetime in print.

A father shapes a snow child who cannot live in a warm room by the fire. A lime-burner hunts the Unpardonable Sin and finds it in his own cold, watchful heart at last. The Great Stone Face teaches a valley poet to match the profile he reveres on the mountain. Hawthorne mixes whimsy and dread, children and sinners, in tales of rare finish and quiet power here. The collection rounds out the story art that first made his American name.
hawthorne-wonder-book-1851:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys in 1851, his retelling of Greek myths. The book fixed the classical myths in the Anglophone imagination for generations of young readers everywhere. Hawthorne wrote it fast, for money, and it became his most popular book in his lifetime.

Student Eustace Bright tells six myths to children at Tanglewood, in the Berkshire hills of Massachusetts. Perseus slays Medusa, Midas turns his child to gold, and Hercules and Pandora fill the set. Hawthorne softens the myths' cruelty and pagan edge for the nursery without killing their wonder and strangeness. His frame of child listeners keeps the old tales warm, present, and full of questions. The book set the pattern for children's myth retellings in English ever since.
hero-of-alexandria-pneumatica-woodcroft-:
Hero of Alexandria, a Greek engineer of the first century, wrote the Pneumatics on machines moved by air and water. Bennet Woodcroft's English version came out in 1851, in the Taylor Walton and Maberly edition. All 78 sections are here, with the editors' opening matter.

Hero describes siphons, fountains, temple doors that open by fire on an altar, and singing birds worked by water. His aeolipile, a ball spun by jets of steam, is the first known steam engine. The book is the base text for the study of ancient machines. Engineers still rebuild his devices to test how they worked.
hobbes-de-cive-1651:
Thomas Hobbes published De Cive in Latin in 1642, and the English translation of 1651 gives it as Philosophical Rudiments Concerning Government and Society. Three parts treat liberty, dominion, and religion in turn. The book stands between his Elements of Law and the Leviathan of 1651, where his political philosophy reached its famous form.

Hobbes argues that men in nature, without a common power, live in fear and war. Peace requires a sovereign set up by covenant, whose commands are law. Religion, in the third part, must answer to that sovereign within his realm. De Cive states the case more briefly than Leviathan, and scholars prize its clarity.
hume-enquiry-principles-morals-1751:
Hume called An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals, from 1751, his own favorite among his works. Nine sections, two appendices, and a closing Dialogue make up the book. Its question is plain: why do we praise some traits of character and blame others, in every age and land?

Hume's answer is the moral-sense theory in its ripest form. We approve what is useful or agreeable, to ourselves or to others, and sentiment, guided by reason, does the approving. Benevolence, justice, and politeness all fall under his calm survey. The Enquiry reads more smoothly than any other of his books. It remains a founding text of modern moral philosophy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenstein-l-h-:
L. H. Löwenstein, a Hebrew scholar who died at Frankfort-on-the-Main about 1850, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer. He worked as reviser in the publishing house of Isaac Lehrberger at Rödelheim, a post afterward held by Seligman Baer. His own books joined careful editing with German translation.

The article lists his 1838 editions of Proverbs and Lamentations, each edited from manuscripts with a Hebrew commentary and a German translation in verse. It also records “Damascia” (1840), his book on the Damascus persecution and the old ritual-murder charge, an ode to Moses Montefiore, and a two-volume Pentateuch with Targum Onḳelos and Rashi’s commentary. Readers get a full publishing record for a scholar who defended Jews in print while editing their classic texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-madrid-10251:
Madrid, the capital of Spain, is given a Jewish history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews lived there as early as the twelfth century. The old town law gave them the same privileges as other inhabitants, with one odd exception. Christian butchers were fined for selling meat slaughtered by Jews.

The article works from charters and council records. A vineyard sale by a Madrid Jew is documented from 1336. Tax figures from 1474 show a small community in the city and nearby villages. In 1391, as across Castile, Jews in Madrid were plundered, murdered, or forcibly baptized. The city council demanded punishment for the rioters. The Jewry, rebuilt afterward, stood by Synagogue street and was walled in by royal order in 1480. The entry also names Jewish physicians appointed by the council, one allowed to live outside the Jewry for night calls.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandelkern-solo:
Solomon Mandelkern, a Russian Hebrew poet and scholar, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Mlynov, Volhynia, in 1846, he trained as a Talmudist at Dubno. There he moved among the Hasidim and studied philosophy and Cabala. Later he joined the Haskalah, the Jewish enlightenment movement. He died at Vienna in 1902.

The article follows a restless education. Mandelkern graduated from Wilna's rabbinical school and studied Oriental languages at St. Petersburg. A gold medal rewarded his essay on parallel Bible passages. At Odessa he became assistant rabbi and the first to preach there in Russian. Jena gave him a doctorate, and Leipzig became his base around 1880. His writings fill many languages and forms: Hebrew epics, a history of Russia, and Byron's Hebrew Melodies in Hebrew dress. The czar once gave him a ring set with brilliants. The entry honors a tireless man of letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marx-jacob-1045:
Jacob Marx, a German physician of the eighteenth century, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar. Born in Bonn in 1743, he took his medical degree at Halle in 1765, traveled in Holland and England for science, and there met the noted Dr. John Fothergill. He settled at Hanover, where he became much loved, and died on January 24, 1789.

The entry lists his medical books in Latin and German, from his dissertation on spasms and convulsions to a three-part set of medical observations and a treatise on consumption. Two late works argue the diet and medical uses of acorns. It also notes the criticism he drew for defending Jewish burial customs of the day against the reformer Herz, in his 1787 book on burying the dead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-megillah-10551:
Megillah, the tractate about reading the scroll of Esther, is described in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Solomon Schechter and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach. It is the tenth treatise of the order Mo'ed in the Mishnah, with four chapters and thirty-three paragraphs, and it exists in the Tosefta and both Talmuds as well. Its first chapter fixes the days of Adar for the reading: the fifteenth for walled cities, the fourteenth for open towns, with village readers allowed earlier days when they gather in town.

From calendars the article moves to practice. The second chapter rules how the scroll may be read, in what language, for hearers who know no Hebrew may use their own tongue, and how much must be read and when. The third turns to the selling of sacred objects and to a ruined synagogue, whose holiness, the tractate holds, does not simply vanish.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahot-meat-of:
Menahot is the Talmudic treatise on the meat-offerings, or meal-offerings, of the Temple. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach summarize it chapter by chapter in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Second in the order Kodashim, it runs to thirteen chapters and ninety-three paragraphs. It works out, across Mishnah, Tosefta, and Babylonian Talmud, the precise rules for the offerings named in Leviticus and Numbers.

The summary follows the tractate's logic. First come intention and its failures. An offering becomes "piggul," an abomination, if the priest means to eat it after its time. It becomes "pasul," unfit, if he means to eat it in the wrong place. Then come the handful from the flour, the oil and incense, and the waving and bringing near the altar. Offerings burned whole are regulated in turn. The entry serves as a map to one of the most technical corners of the sacrificial law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-david-ams:
David Amsel Meyer, born in Copenhagen on January 18, 1753, was a Danish financier whose rise is told in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer. He started in business very young, and by the prosperous 1790s his trade reached across the ocean. With his nephew S. S. Trier he founded the house of Meyer and Trier.

The firm weathered the Copenhagen fire of 1795 and the panic of 1799 without real injury. Meyer publicly attacked reckless paper currency in 1806, and King Frederick VI consulted him during the Napoleonic-era money crisis; in 1811 he judged loan requests for the government itself. He retired with a royal title, and his will left large sums to Jewish schools and charities in Copenhagen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monreal-10951:
Monreal is a small city in Navarre, three miles from Pamplona. It is not its Aragonese namesake. It kept a little Juderia whose history Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling piece together in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its known moment is violent. In 1320 the Jews of Pamplona, threatened by the shepherds' bands, fled here. They fought beside Alfonso of Aragon's men.

A hundred and seventy of them were killed anyway. The community dwindled to fourteen Jews by 1366. They were taxpayers to the local abbot by 1380. By 1477 so few were left that worship moved into a private house. One bright detail closes the entry. Juze Orabuena, chief rabbi of Navarre and the king's own physician, received houses in the Juderia as a royal gift.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-blessing-:
The Blessing of Moses is the name for the thirty-third chapter of Deuteronomy, where Moses blesses the twelve tribes. Four scholars wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it: Joseph Jacobs, Schulim Ochser, Morris Jastrow, and Wilhelm Nowack. Moses speaks the words at the border of Palestine, before the tribes enter the land.

The article walks through the blessings tribe by tribe: a short prayer for Reuben, long praise for Levi, and the fullest blessing for Joseph. Simeon is passed over in silence. A critical section then argues that the verses picture the tribes as they stood in the author's own day. It dates the blessing to the Northern Kingdom and later than the core of Jacob's blessing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-myrtle-myrtus-c:
The myrtle, an evergreen aromatic shrub, is covered in this Jewish Encyclopedia article by the editorial committee and Immanuel Löw. In the Bible it is named plainly only in the later books, in Isaiah, Zechariah, and Nehemiah. Tradition reads it into the boughs of thick trees commanded for the Feast of Tabernacles.

The article works through the rules for the festival myrtle: leaves must cover the wood, ideally in triple whorls. It then follows the shrub into the Habdalah blessing, where its scent refreshes the soul as Sabbath departs. Myrtle also appears at weddings, circumcisions, and funerals in the sources. A saying of Rabbi Johanan ends the survey: who learns but does not teach is a myrtle in the desert.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-de-zuzit:
Nathan de-Zuzita was an exilarch wrapped in legend. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One tradition names him as Ukban b. Nehemiah. He lived in the first half of the fourth century. He was remembered as a sinner who repented.

His surname drew several rival explanations from Rashi. It might mean sparks, from light seen around his head. It might mean hair, from curls he wore when young. Or fire was said to flash from his fringes. The sources also clash on his date and family line. The entry weighs two Nathans against three in one list. Readers see how hard ancient Jewish chronology can be.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nethinim-11451:
The Nethinim were Temple officials of low social rank. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Joseph Jacobs for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They returned from exile in two batches. The first numbered 392, the second 220. Lists of their families stand in Ezra and Nehemiah.

They settled in Ophel, by Jerusalem's water gate. Under the Levites, they served in the Temple itself. David and the princes were said to have appointed them. Tolls could not be charged against them at all. Talmud law yet ranked them with bastards in marriage. Their children could never wed into Israel at large. Scholars guess they sprang from an older temple class.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nippur-11551:
Nippur was a great city of central Babylonia. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and J. Frederic McCurdy for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its ruins are now called Nuffar. It lay thirty-five miles southeast of Babylon. It ranks among the world's oldest named cities.

Its fame rested on the worship of Bel there. That god gathered many local Ba'als into one. By 5000 B.C. Nippur's religious lead was firm. Kings of Kish, Erech, and Ur courted its shrine. Sargon rebuilt Bel's temple about 3800 B.C. Hammurabi later shifted Bel's cult toward Babylon. Hebrew exiles settled near it beside the Chebar canal. Pennsylvania's diggers have worked there since 1888. Tens of thousands of inscriptions have come to light.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-occident-and-am:
The Occident was a Jewish journal from Philadelphia, in America. Cyrus Adler and David Sulzberger wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Isaac Leeser founded it and ran it for years. It first came out in April 1843. It ran as a monthly till March 1859. Then it ran each week for two years.

In 1861 the Occident went back to a monthly form. It went on in that form till 1869. In all, it made twenty-six volumes of print. Leeser died in 1868, just before the end. Mayer Sulzberger then brought out the last volume. In its day it led all Jewish print in the United States. Much of Leeser's own work first saw print there. It stood firm for the old faith and rites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pahlavi-literat:
Pahlavi books are the old books of Persia, in its mid tongue. Joseph Jacobs and Louis H. Gray wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Those books span from the third to the tenth century. They deal in the main with the faith of Zoroaster. That faith was the chief faith of old Persia.

In their fights with other faiths, these books name the Jews. They take shots at Judaism, the faith of Christ, and more. Some books on the past and on lands name Jews too. A few of those words count for much, the piece says. The Dinkard is the chief of those books named here. The Shikandgumanig Vijar is a second book of weight. One book calls Jews and Christians folk of a vile law. That harsh line dates, it may be, from the seventh century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pillar-of-fire-:
The pillar of fire guided Israel through the desert nights. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. By day a cloud led the camp instead. The fire gave light for the night marches.

The fire never left Israel during the night. It rose before the cloud had fully vanished. So the camp was never left without a guide. Through fire and cloud God troubled Egypt's host. A legend tells how Onkelos retold the story. His tale won the emperor's own messengers to Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollak-moriz-ri:
Moriz Pollak, later Ritter von Borkenau, was an Austrian man of finance born at Vienna in 1827. Isidore Singer and Emil Jelinek wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. At twenty-two he took charge of his father's wholesale leather trade. He soon sold goods into France and Germany as well.

Pollak joined the Vienna city council in 1857. He helped with relief and building work in the great flood of 1862. For years he watched over the city budget as auditor. In 1873 he chaired the board of the Vienna Exposition. He later led a large Vienna bank as director-general. He held bank and trade posts until late in life. He died at Vienna in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-purity-of-race-:
Purity of race asks whether today's Jews descend from Bible Jews alone. Joseph Jacobs wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The question is still open, he says at the start. No one denies one side of the matter. The Jews of Bible times were themselves of mixed blood. That much is plain from the records.

Ezra strove to stop the mixing of his day. His strife shows how wide that mixing had grown. Marriages were made most with near kin peoples. Ammonites, Moabites, and Idumeans are named as the chief sources. Those peoples were held to share one stock with Israel. Jacobs weighs blood, faith, and law in the long count.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reich-rajk-alad: Aladár Reich, also called Rajk, was a Hungarian lawyer and deputy. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Baja on June 25, 1871. He studied at Baja, Budapest, Berlin, and Paris. The article says he entered the bar at Baja. His city sent him to Parliament in 1901. In that election he defeated the Minister of Justice. Voters reelected him in 1905. A parliamentary almanac is the entry's only cited source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-riesser-gabriel:
Gabriel Riesser was a German advocate of Jewish emancipation born on April 2, 1806. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Hamburg. He died there on April 22, 1863.

The article says he studied law at Kiel and Heidelberg. Heidelberg refused him a teaching license because he was Jewish. Hamburg then refused him admission to the bar. Those refusals made him the cause's leading voice. In 1830 his essay on Mosaic believers appeared at Altona. He compared Jewish oppression with other oppressions of his age. He demanded full emancipation for Jews in Germany. He called on leaders and philanthropists to unite for it. The entry opens the story of a landmark campaign.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenfeld-samso:
Samson Wolf Rosenfeld was a German rabbi born at Markt Uhlfeld, Bavaria, on January 4, 1780. Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. At thirteen he entered the yeshibah at Fürth and studied there six years.

Rosenfeld became rabbi of Uhlfeld in 1808 and took no salary for the post. He reformed home and synagogue practice and founded a school. Unusually for Bavaria then, he preached in German. From 1826 he served as rabbi of Bamberg until his death in 1862. He also wrote pamphlets urging full civil rights for Bavarian Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-sydney-m:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Sydney Montagu Samuel. He was an English author and communal worker. Samuel was born in London on June 21, 1848. He was educated at University College, London. He died in June 1884, worn out by overwork.

For over fifteen years Samuel threw himself into Jewish communal work. In 1878 he became honorary secretary to the Board of Guardians. He wrote its annual reports for five years. In 1879 he traveled east to study Jewish life. His findings appeared in his book Jewish Life in the East. He also worked in the theater. He wrote the English libretto of Piccolino in 1879. His comedy A Quiet Pipe played at the Folly Theatre in 1880.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schreiber-moses:
Bernhard Friedberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Moses ben Samuel Schreiber, known as Moses Sofer. He was a German rabbi. Schreiber was born at Frankfort-on-the-Main on September 14, 1763. He died at Presburg on October 3, 1839. At nine he entered Nathan Adler's yeshibah. At thirteen he already lectured in public.

Schreiber headed a yeshibah at Prossnitz, then served at Dresnitz and Mattersdorf. In 1803 he took the rabbinate of Presburg. His yeshibah there drew some five hundred pupils. Many of them became famous rabbis. The wars with France troubled his work at Presburg. His wife died in 1812, and he later married a daughter of Akiba Eger. In 1819 the Reform movement rose at Hamburg. Schreiber stood as Orthodoxy's great defender against it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scorpion-hebrew:
Joseph Jacobs and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the scorpion. The creature looks like a tiny flat lobster. It carries a poisonous sting in its tail. Scorpions swarm across the Sinai desert and Palestine. Eight species live in Palestine alone. They hide in houses, wall chinks, ruins, and under stones.

In Ezekiel, scorpion stands as a figure for bitter, stinging words. In Kings it names a scourge, perhaps tipped with metal points. The place Maaleh Akrabbim means ascent of the scorpions. The Talmud says the scorpion strikes without warning. Its bite is worse than a snake's, since it repeats. Odd cures included an infant's urine and a stork's gall. Scorpion itself treated cataract in one recipe. Jerusalem counted it a standing miracle that no scorpion ever bit there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seth-hebrew-gre:
Seth was the third son of Adam, born after Cain killed Abel. Emil G. Hirsch, George A. Barton, Wilhelm Bacher, and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Genesis says Adam was 130 years old at Seth's birth. Seth lived 912 years and fathered Enosh at 105.

Through Seth, Genesis traces the line from Adam down to Noah. Later lists in Chronicles and Luke name him without adding detail. Rabbis read his name as foundation, calling him founder of the world. They also tied Eve's words at his birth to a coming messiah. The entry joins the spare Bible account with the rich tales rabbis built upon it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemaiah-samaia:
Shemaiah, also Samaias or Sameas, led the Pharisees in the first century B.C. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He presided over the Sanhedrin before and during Herod's reign. With Abtalion he ranked among the age's great teachers.

One bold act of Shemaiah's survives in the record. Herod had killed a Galilean leader on his own authority. The king let the Sanhedrin summon Herod to trial. Herod arrived dressed in royal purple, cowing the court. Only Shemaiah dared to speak against the show. He warned that the man they feared would one day hand them over. The entry honors rare courage before a rising tyrant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-richard-1:
Richard Simon was a French scholar and Orientalist born at Dieppe in 1638. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at the Sorbonne and joined the Congregation of the Oratory. In its library he read Oriental works and manuscripts. In 1670 he protested a blood charge against a Jew at Metz.

His chief work was his Critical History of the Old Testament in 1678. It treated the Bible books as ordinary writings. Bossuet and others had all 1,300 copies seized and destroyed. Simon was expelled from the Oratory for the book. Pirated editions soon appeared in Holland, and he defended his views in pamphlets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-abr:
Solomon ben Abraham ha-Kohen of Seres, called Maharshak, was an Oriental Talmudist. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived at Salonica in the late sixteenth century. His teacher was Joseph Firman. His fame rests on his large collection of responsa.

That work, She'elot u-Teshubot, appeared in three parts. The first part held 197 responsa and notes on divorce law. It was printed at Salonica in 1586. The second part held 263 responsa, printed at Venice in 1592. The third part held 122 more responsa, printed in 1594. Later editions appeared at Wilmersdorf and at Salonica.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-speyer-hebrew-1:
Speyer was a bishopric of Rhenish Bavaria with an old Jewish community. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Bishop Rüdiger first admitted Jewish refugees there about 1080. He gave them a walled quarter outside the city proper. On September 13, 1084, he granted them a special privilege.

For a yearly payment, Jews could trade in the harbor freely. They could exchange gold and silver and bury their dead. Their chief rabbi held full jurisdiction among them in law. Emperor Henry III confirmed and extended those rights in 1090. Forced baptism of Jewish children was punished by heavy fines. Yet even those charters failed to protect the Jews fully.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stiller-bertala:
Bertalan Stiller was a Hungarian physician born at Miskolez on June 23, 1837. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied medicine at Budapest and Vienna. He earned his medical degree in 1863. His whole career centered on Budapest hospitals.

In 1864 Stiller became assistant physician at the Budapest Jewish Hospital. He rose to chief of a division in 1874. He gained a lectureship in 1876 and a professorship in 1886. His main book treats nervous diseases of the stomach. A German translation carried it to wider readers. Later works cover diseases of the spleen and the peritoneum. The entry records a hospital doctor's steady climb and writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sycamore-sycomo:
The sycamore is a bushy tree of Syria and Egypt. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. It belongs to the fig family of trees. The Bible mentions it many times across books. It still grows along the coastal plain today.

Its small fig fruit fed mostly the common people. Workers slit the fruit so tart juice flows out. That step makes the fruit fit to eat. Amos worked as a dresser of sycamore fruit. Hebrews prized the wood more than the fruit. The light, lasting timber served common building needs. Egypt carved utensils and coffins from the same wood. The entry joins botany, diet, and craft in one tree.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tarragona-14251:
Tarragona is a Spanish city, the ancient Tarraco of Rome. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Edrisi called it the City of the Jews. Jewish coins from digs prove an early community. Its Jews' quarter and cemetery sites are known.

When Barcelona's count won Catalonia from the Moors, Jews gained rights. Their ghetto held ninety-five houses by 1239. They elected their own administrators there. Trade, industry, and brokerage filled their days. In 1322 the archbishop seized Jewish property. Nearly 300 Jews were killed in 1348. The 1391 riots struck the community like Barcelona's. Yet pious Jews still lived there afterward. Isaac Arama served as its rabbi for a time. The entry joins early roots with repeated blows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tisza-eszlar-af:
The Tisza-Eszlar affair was a ritual-murder charge against Jews in Hungary in 1882. Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Esther Solymosi, a Christian servant girl of fourteen, vanished on April 1. She never returned from an errand at Tisza-Eszlar.

Rumors claimed Jews killed her for Passover blood. Anti-Semitic leaders had already demanded the Jews' expulsion in parliament. Their agitation stirred bloody attacks across Hungary. The girl's mother accused local Jews before a judge. A five-year-old sexton's son was coaxed into a story. Sugar and money gifts drew the tale from him. His older brother repeated a forced confession. The accused denied any knowledge of the girl.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tychsen-olaus-g:
Olaus Gerhard Tychsen was a Christian Hebraist and Orientalist born in 1734. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Tondern in Denmark and died at Rostock in 1815. He studied rabbinics at the University of Halle. In 1759 he toured Germany seeking Jewish converts, without success.

A sermon at the Altona synagogue caused an unseemly dispute. In 1760 he became professor at the new University of Bützow. He taught Oriental languages there until the school closed in 1789. He then led Rostock's library and museum. His Bützowische Nebenstunden filled six volumes on the Old Testament. He drew heavily on Rashi and old versions. He also denied the authenticity of Maccabean coins.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-waw-14651:
Waw is the sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broydé wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name may mean nail or hook. Its shape in the Phoenician alphabet looks like a hook. The letter sounds like the English w.

Before the vowel u, waw blends into a long u sound. After an a vowel it forms the diphthong au. That sound later passed into o. At a word's start, waw rarely keeps its consonant force. As a numeral in later use, waw stands for six. The entry sums up the letter's sound, form, and value.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weissberg-isaac:
Isaac Jacob Weissberg was a Hebrew writer and teacher. Herman Rosenthal and Hillel Malachowsky wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Polonki, in Minsk province, in 1841. He died at Kiev in 1904. He trained in small schools and at Slonim's yeshibah. There he ranked among the best Talmud students.

In 1873 Weissberg settled in Kiev as a Hebrew teacher. Many of his pupils became noted Hebrew writers. From 1879 he wrote for Hebrew periodicals widely. His works critique medieval and modern literature. One book treats women's status in the Talmud. Another collects ancient proverbs in one volume. He also published letters of leading Hebrew poets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wisdom-of-solom:
The Wisdom of Solomon is an apocryphal book. Kaufmann Kohler wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. An Alexandrian Jew composed it in Greek. He wrote about the middle of the first century B.C. The book carries neither an opening verse nor a proper close. It joins three independent parts loosely.

The first six chapters address the rulers of earth. They press wisdom as a ruler's first need. They attack the ungodly who deny life after death. The righteous suffer torture in these chapters. Yet they are called sons of God there. Eternal life is promised as their reward. Wisdom herself speaks near the section's end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yahya-15051:
Yahya names a Portuguese family of the Middle Ages with wide reach. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Men of the line held rank in Portugal, Spain, Italy, and Turkey. Some bore the added name Negro with the main name.

That name came from lands won from the Moors. The first man named was Yahya ibn Yaish of Lisbon. He died about the year 1150 in that city. King Alfonso the First prized his brave deeds in war. The king gave him two homes seized from the Moors. His grandson Joseph built a synagogue at his own cost. A third man worked to curb rich show among Jews. He feared it would stir hate in their Christian neighbors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zahalon-15151:
Zahalon names a family of Spanish birth with sons in two worlds. Joseph Jacobs, Isaac Broyde, the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board, and Lazarus Grunhut wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. When Spain cast out its Jews, the kin split wide. Some went to Italy and some to the East lands.

There they won rank as rabbis and as scholars of note. The first man named is Abraham ben Isaac Zahalon. He wrote on the Jew and Muslim year counts in one book. He wrote a work on the Book of Esther as well. He wrote a mystic work on the cure of the soul. The next man is Jacob ben Isaac Zahalon of Rome. He was both a rabbi and a doctor of the body. His great work is a cure book in thirteen parts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zerubbabel-1525:
Zerubbabel was the chief of the Jews who came back from exile. Emil G. Hirsch and J. F. McLaughlin wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a son of Shealtiel and a grandson of Jehoiachin. His name may mean born in Babylon in Hebrew tongue.

It may be a Babylon form that means seed of Babylon. One hard point splits the minds of men to this day. Was he the same man as Sheshbazzar of the Book of Ezra? That man led the first band of exiles back to Zion. One side notes that both men head the returned folk. Both men stand with the high priest Jeshua in that work. Both men bear the rank of governor of Judah as well. That match points to one man with two names in use. Like Daniel, he may have borne a name of each land.
john-halifax-gentleman-pg2351:
John Halifax, Gentleman is Dinah Maria Mulock Craik's novel of a boy who becomes a gentleman by character. The narrator, Phineas, first sees John as a ragged lad in the rain at Norton Bury. John is about fourteen, with a serious, haggard face and a strong, work-browned hand. Yet no one, watching him make way politely, could call him a vagabond.

Phineas's father speaks kindly to the boy and pulls the narrator's hand-carriage under shelter. That small meeting opens a life story told across more than fifty years of memory. Craik builds her Victorian ideal in this orphan: firm lips, a resolute chin, and quiet determination. The novel became beloved for its earnest picture of self-help, honesty, and family devotion.
king-henry-iv-part-1-pg2251: Eastcheap glows in this edition: Falstaff's tavern world of sack and jest stands against the cold honor of court and rebellion. Hal moves between them, biding his time until Shrewsbury. The greatest history play, rich with England's whole life.
letter-to-friend-garrison-manuscript-185: A manuscript letter addressed to Friend Garrison is dated 1851 in its record. E. B. Kenrick is named as its writer. William Lloyd Garrison, the abolitionist editor, was its recipient. The hosted sample is unreadable handwriting in scan form. Only the address, sender, and year ground this entry. It survives as a small piece of abolition-era correspondence.
lumen-de-lumine-or-a-new-magicall-light-:
Lumen de Lumine, or A New Magicall Light, appeared in London in 1651. Its author hides behind the name Eugenius Philalethes, in fact Thomas Vaughan. The title page quotes Genesis: 'And God said, Let there be Light.' It also quotes John, that the light shines in the darkness.

Vaughan writes as a hermetic philosopher on the mystery of light. For him, light links God, nature, and the human soul. His prose mixes Scripture, alchemy, and the old Greek sages. Pythagoras is quoted: speak not of God without light. The book is a strange, rich piece of seventeenth-century mysticism. Scholars of alchemy and early science still read Vaughan.
matotechnia-medicin-praxeos-the-vanity-o: Noah Biggs wrote Mataeotechnia Medicinae Praxeos, dated 1651 in the record. Its long title calls the work the vanity of the craft of physick. The hosted sample for this entry is garbled scan text with no readable passage. Only broken letters and marks can be made out in it. This note stays with the title, the author, and the year for that reason. The book's claims cannot be described from the sample held here.
melville-moby-dick-1851:
Herman Melville published Moby Dick in 1851, in the first American edition text used here. The novel tells of Ahab, Ishmael, and the white whale Moby Dick. It sold poorly at first and sank from view for seventy years or so.

Ishmael ships on the Pequod, a whaler ruled by grim Captain Ahab. Ahab hunts one whale, the white one that took his leg at sea. Chapters mix sea craft, whale lore, and dark thought on fate and God. Queequeg, Starbuck, and Stubb fill the crew with rich contrast of souls. The last chase wrecks ship and men, and Ishmael alone survives.
michaelis-majeri-viatorivm-hoc-est-de-mo:
A later edition of Michael Maier's Viatorium appeared at Rouen in 1651. The treatise treats the seven mountains of the planets, meaning the seven metals. This printing adds an engraved title page with seven allegorical images and a portrait of Maier. Seven symbolic engravings in the text follow the 1618 edition, five of them reversed.

Maier wrote the work as a guide for lovers of truth lost among chemical errors. Its Latin text assumes readers trained in the learned language of the day. The reversed plates betray the copyist's craft behind this reissue. Together, text and images preserve alchemy's planetary scheme of metals.
notes-and-queries-number-62-january-4-18:
Old ballads upon the Winter's Tale open number sixty-two, for Saturday, January 4, 1851, through J. Payne Collier. Its paging restarts at one for a new year. Janus Dousa writes on crossing rivers on skins. Folk lore of south Northamptonshire reaches a third part. Fleet marriages sit in the minor notes.

E. Venables asks about the origin of the present penny postage. The Red Book of the Irish Exchequer draws another query. Minor queries chase Cranmer's descendants and portraits of bishops. Replies give God speed the plough as a phrase. Defender of the faith is treated by Robert Anstruther. Beatrix Lady Talbot is settled by Madden.
notes-and-queries-number-63-january-11-1:
The Breeches, or Geneva, Bible leads the notes in number sixty-three, dated Saturday, January 11, 1851. Poems found among Sir Kenelm Digby's papers follow. John Adamson treats the works of Camoens. Elizabeth Walker and Shakespeare share a note, and old English actors and musicians in Germany another.

Minor notes include the curse of Scotland and errors in the dates of printed books. Queries ask about Dousa's poem on Sidney and an old Dutch song book. Minor queries chase the invention of steam power and the sword of the Conqueror. Lynch law, an American term, also puzzles a reader of 1851.
notes-and-queries-number-64-january-18-1:
Number sixty-four, dated Saturday, January 18, 1851, sold at ninepence with the index to volume two. Samuel Hickson returns to the authorship of Henry the Eighth. The Cavalier's farewell and Gray's Elegy, through Henry Breen, follow. The Nineveh monuments are set beside Milton's Nativity Ode, lit from Lucian.

Minor notes include umbrellas and authors of anonymous works. A sonnet query by Milton, on the library at Cambridge, is raised by Kenyon. Burying in church walls draws a query of its own. Minor queries chase Darby and Joan and Sir Thomas Bullen's drinking horn. A cross between a wolf and a hound also appears.
notes-and-queries-number-65-january-25-1:
Traditional English ballads open number sixty-five, for Saturday, January 25, 1851, through Dr Rimbault. The father of Philip Massinger and Touchstone's dial follow as notes. W. Hastings Kelke catches discrepancies in Dugdale on Sir Ralph de Cobham. Henry Chettle and Coverdale's Bible get notes too.

Folk lore of Lancashire begins a run, from T. T. Wilkinson. Singer asks about the tale of the Wardstaff. Minor queries chase a book called Tartuare and William Wallace in London. Aged monks, Lady Alice Carmichael, and Dr Trusler's memoirs also puzzle readers. The price rose to sixpence for this number, per its heading.
openalex-w1842963151:
Gemma Henderson, Peter Janssen, and census collaborators ran this survey. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2015. Rumen microbes let cattle and kin digest tough plants. They also drive methane output from livestock farming. The team asked if diet, host, or place shapes them most.

Samples came from hundreds of animals across thirty-five countries. Thirty-two species of ruminants and camelids were included. Similar bacteria and archaea dominated nearly all samples, they found. Protozoal groups varied more from place to place. Diet shaped the communities most, with host second. A shared core microbiome spans the whole world range.
openalex-w1979808851:
Lilly Verhagen and co-authors studied child health in Venezuela. Their paper is dated 2013 in the catalog record. Rural children face poor growth, anemia, and parasites together. The team surveyed school-age Venezuelan children for all three. Yanomami, Warao, and Creole groups were compared directly.

Intestinal worm and protozoan infections were tested in the children. Malnutrition and anemia rates were measured at the same time. The title reports a high malnutrition rate in Yanomami children. Links among infection, nutrition, and anemia were significant. Such combined data guide joint treatment and feeding programs. Single-issue programs miss how these problems intertwine.
openalex-w2068974951:
Marcos De Donato, Sunday Peters, Sharon Mitchell and colleagues adapted a cheap genotyping method for cattle. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Fast genotyping helps study complex traits. High costs still block large animal studies. A plant method called genotyping-by-sequencing promised savings.

The team applied the method to forty-seven cattle. The animals covered seven taurine and indicine breeds. DNA was cut with enzymes and tagged with barcodes. Sequencing then read all samples together. One enzyme performed best in their tests. Tens of thousands of gene variants were found. Filtering kept the most reliable variant calls. The method offers affordable genotyping for cattle improvement.
openalex-w2112837251:
Kenneth Aamodt, Betty Abelev and colleagues in the ALICE Collaboration made the first count of particles from LHC lead collisions. Their paper appeared in Physical Review Letters in 2010. When lead nuclei collide, thousands of particles spray out. Their density tests theories of hot matter. The run was the LHC's first with lead ions.

The team focused on the most head-on collisions. They counted charged particles near the collision centre. Density per area far exceeded earlier experiments. It was roughly double the gold collision values. Per colliding pair, output rose strongly with energy. The measurement constrained models of nuclear collisions. It opened the LHC heavy-ion programme's physics harvest.
openalex-w2118415151:
Anna Rosanas-Urgell, Dania Mueller, Inoni Betuela and colleagues compared malaria diagnostic methods in Papua New Guinea. Their paper appeared in Malaria Journal in 2010. Four malaria species infect people there. Microscope diagnosis misses many light infections. Better molecular tools were needed for field studies.

The team developed a duplex real-time PCR assay. It detects and counts all four species. They compared it with three other methods. Samples came from over four hundred young children. Agreement was substantial for falciparum detection. Agreement was only moderate for the other species. No single method caught every infection. Molecular tools reveal a larger hidden reservoir.
openalex-w2761275051:
The GTEx Consortium reported this study in Nature in 2017, with François Aguet and Ayellet V. Segrè among the lead authors. It asks how inherited DNA differences change gene activity across the human body. The Genotype-Tissue Expression project collected samples from forty-four tissues, many hard to reach in living people. Hundreds of donors contributed postmortem samples for expression measurement.

Local genetic variation affects the activity of most genes, the team found. They also uncovered cross-chromosome effects for ninety-three genes, where distant DNA changes expression. The study characterizes how tissue-specific these effects are and compares local with distant control. Functional patterns in the data hint at how variants act. The resource helps researchers connect disease-linked DNA changes to the genes they actually move. That is a key step from genetic association toward biological mechanism.
openalex-w2789263551:
María Chaparro, Annelies Verreth, and Triana Lobatón lead the TEDDY study group in this 2018 paper in the American Journal of Gastroenterology. It asks whether anti-TNF drugs taken during pregnancy harm children later. These drugs control inflammatory bowel disease in many mothers-to-be. Their long-term safety for children exposed in the womb had received little attention.

The multicenter European study followed two groups of children of mothers with bowel disease. One group was exposed to anti-TNF medication before birth; the other was not. The researchers compared rates of severe infections between the groups over childhood. That outcome matters because these drugs dampen the immune system. A clear answer helps doctors and mothers weigh disease control against possible risk. The preserved sample presents the study's design and aim in detail.
openalex-w2921966151:
Daniela Parada Venegas, Marjorie De la Fuente, Glauben Landskron, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Immunology. It covers short chain fatty acids, small molecules made in the gut, and how they shape the gut lining and the immune system. The review links that science to inflammatory bowel diseases.

These fatty acids enter gut cells through dedicated transporters and switch on receptors that calm inflammation. People with inflammatory bowel disease tend to carry fewer of the bacteria that make these acids, and their acid levels run lower than in healthy people. The authors discuss ways to restore balance, including transplants of gut microbes from healthy donors, prebiotics, and fiber-rich diets.
openalex-w2994405351:
Saray Quintero-Fabián, Rodrigo Arreola, Enrique Becerril-Villanueva, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Oncology. It examines matrix metalloproteinases, a family of enzymes that cut proteins, and their role in blood vessel growth and cancer. These enzymes help tumors build supply lines and spread.

Cancer spread, or metastasis, is the leading cause of cancer illness and death. To spread, tumor cells change shape and behavior, break cell-to-cell links, and chew through the matrix that holds tissues together. The enzymes reviewed here do much of that cutting, including slicing the basement membrane under cell layers. The review explains how this activity feeds both new vessel growth and invasion of distant organs.
openalex-w3082810351:
Luciana Mendonça and Isabel Farias published this book review in the journal Educação in 2020. Written in Portuguese, it reviews a book on qualitative research, subtitled studying how things work. The book teaches readers to plan a study that explores people and settings in depth rather than counting them.

The review notes the book's audience: students, teachers, and researchers who want more than theory. Most of its worked examples use case studies from education research. Each chapter carries a study guide with questions that push readers to reflect on every step of an inquiry. The reviewer praises its push for sharp observation without stereotypes, and for weaving several sources of evidence together.
openalex-w4283324651:
Sandra López-León, Talía Wegman-Ostrosky, Norma Ayuzo del Valle, and colleagues reviewed long-COVID in children and teenagers, in Scientific Reports in 2022. Long-COVID means symptoms that linger for weeks or months after the first infection. It is less studied in the young than in adults, and estimates of its frequency vary widely. The team set out to pool the evidence and list the full range of symptoms.

They searched two large databases for studies of at least thirty patients aged up to eighteen. Studies had to match the British NICE definition, covering ongoing and post-COVID symptoms. The authors then combined results with random-effects meta-analyses to estimate pooled prevalence. A shared symptom map helps doctors recognise the condition and plan follow-up care.
openalex-w4417098251:
Takehito Yokoyama shows a deep link between an exotic superconductor type and magnetism. His paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2026. The superconductors mix two pairing parities and break a key symmetry. Such states are called nonunitary mixed parity.

Using a standard mathematical transformation, Yokoyama rewrites their model Hamiltonian. It takes exactly the form used for magnetism with spin-orbit coupling. The two systems can therefore share the same physics. He shows that several magnetic-like effects arise in these superconductors. They include magnetoelectric response and spin currents driven by supercurrent. Remarkably, all of them come from superconductivity alone. No magnetism or spin-orbit coupling is present in the material itself.
openalex-w7154973251:
Makoto Kikuchi, of Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology, led a 2026 physics study of a sheared granular gas, a loose cloud of hard spheres that lose energy when they collide. How bouncy a collision is can depend on impact speed. Using kinetic theory, the team derived how the gas's resistance to flow, its viscosity, changes as the gas is sheared faster.

The viscosity curve bends into an S shape when the restitution switches between two values with collision speed. As a result, viscosity jumps suddenly between slow-shear and fast-shear regimes, both following the classic Bagnold scaling. Unlike similar jumps in dense suspensions, this one needs no friction or jamming: it comes purely from the motion and collisions of the grains.
openalex-w7155093551:
Yuji Shimada, of Juntendo University Shizuoka Hospital in Japan, led a 2026 study tracking ten years of treatment results against Helicobacter pylori, a stomach bacterium that raises gastric cancer risk. Since 2013, Japanese insurance has covered eradication treatment for infected patients with gastritis. The team reviewed all first- and second-line treatments in their department from 2015 to 2024, covering more than twelve hundred patients.

First-line success stayed stable overall, with a modest upward trend when only patients who completed treatment were counted. Second-line success stayed high throughout. Prescribing shifted strongly toward vonoprazan-based regimens, while use of the antibiotic clarithromycin fell. The authors credit the newer regimen's spread for keeping results steady despite resistance concerns.
openalex-w7160540551:
Sana Nakamichi, of Toho University in Japan, led a 2026 physics study of a Dirac semimetal. A content whose electrons behave like particles with no mass, held under pressure near a quantum phase transition. The content, an organic crystal, shifts under pressure toward a charge-ordered insulating state. The team tracked how long electrons keep their quantum phase coherence as heat and pressure changed, using magnetic conductivity measurements.

Far from the key pressure, coherence shrank with heat in the standard way for flat, diffusive conductors, and it stayed long, spanning hundreds of nanometers. Near the key point, the heat pattern flattened in an anomalous way. The persistence of the coherence signal across the transition suggests the change of state happens without opening a full energy gap.
openalex-w7204452651:
Romulo Lacerda Dantas and Tiago Silva de Freitas released a Portuguese-language paper in Brazil in 2026 on plain language and audio accessibility in Brazil's special small-claims courts. Legal language, the famous juridiquês, can exclude people at risk from justice, and these courts lack assistive communication for the most vulnerable users. The study, using a deductive method, reviews studies, statistics, and the rules governing the courts.

The authors propose sending court communications as WhatsApp audio messages, in simplified language, alongside textual simplification. Together, they argue, plain text and listening reduce cognitive overload and help people understand procedural acts, promoting human dignity and real social inclusion in the justice system. The proposal targets a barrier that formal equality before the law leaves untouched.
openalex-w7211866551:
Ryogo Ikemura and four colleagues at Juntendo University hospitals in Japan ask which head-injury patients will suffer dangerous brain swelling after surgery. Their patients had acute subdural hematoma, bleeding between the brain and its covering, treated by opening the skull to remove the blood. The open question is when surgeons should go further and remove a bone flap, a decompressive craniectomy, to give a swelling brain room. The team reviewed seventy-four cases treated between 2017 and 2021.

Just over a quarter of the patients developed postoperative swelling. Swelling was linked, one factor at a time, to younger age, deep disturbance of consciousness, an accompanying brain bruise, and shorter time from injury to surgery. When the factors were weighed together, only the brain bruise stood as an independent predictor, and a strong one. The finding gives surgical teams a concrete signal when deciding whether to leave the bone out.
openalex-w7212127051:
Gabriela Caroline Batista dos Santos leads a team on quilombola women who guard their land in Bahia, Brazil. The work sums up a master's study of one community, Lagoa das Piranhas, in Bom Jesus da Lapa. The lake there was fouled by a state irrigation scheme, the authors say. That harm hit health, food, and the old ways of life at once. The team spoke with fifteen women and joined their talks and rounds.

The lens joins race, sex, class, and place in one frame. In that frame, the women stand at the front of the fight. They name the harm, rally the town, and keep the old skills alive. State help, the study notes, has been slow to come. The women's stand is both a shield for the land and a claim to be heard. Their fight shows how green harm is never just green.
openalex-w7212358151:
Maria Jose Ordonez, Zuleide Oliveira Feitosa, and Jackeline Santos Tigre Magalhaes review Howard Gardner's theory of many minds for the foreign tongue class. Gardner held that smarts come in at least eight kinds. They span words, sums, space, tunes, the body, ties with peers, the self, and the wild world. The team read five fresh studies, from 2023 to 2025, by the side of Gardner's own books and Brazil's school guides.

A class built on one kind of smart, they argue, shuts out the rest. Songs can carry new words for the tune-led. Maps and plays can do the same for the space-led and the body-led. Group tasks play to those strong in ties. The review sorts tools and class plans by kind. Its point for staff is wide reach: teach one tongue through all the doors a mind can use.
openalex-w7214095951:
