José Junho Rodrigues leads a large team reviewing land use change and climate intensification in Brazil. Their 2026 review follows established guidance and searches three sources for 2015 to 2025. Nine studies passed screening and formed the final synthesis.

Deforestation, mechanized farm expansion, disordered urbanization, and pressure on native ecosystems drive the account. Studies tracked surface temperature, greenhouse gas emissions, erosion, water systems, and degradation patterns. Converting native vegetation to farm or urban use cuts evaporation, raises temperature, and intensifies harmful processes, the results show. Territory change is thus no side issue in Brazil climate change. It is named one of its main vectors of intensification.
openalex-w7214194251:
Denys Willian Barbosa analyses municipal guards in Brazil's public security system, against a military police staffing crisis in São Paulo. His single-author 2026 article mixes legal analysis of a Supreme Court case and the national security system with official state police data from 2010 to 2025.

Resignation requests rose sharply across that period, he reports, and the operational shortfall in 2025 ran into the thousands. Failures in managing protective equipment logistics aggravate the picture. Strengthening municipal guards is a growing, legally supported trend to fill state model gaps, Barbosa concludes. The legal viability of guards as public security bodies is the article's central question, answered in the affirmative on the evidence presented.
oviedo-historia-general-natural-vol-1-18:
Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, the Spanish crown's official chronicler of the Indies, began his Historia general y natural de las Indias in 1535. The work ran on to 1557, and volume one here follows the Royal Academy of History edition printed at Madrid from 1851 to 1855. The text is in Spanish, as no public-domain English translation exists.

Oviedo had lived in the Americas and wrote as both historian and naturalist. His first volume opens the general history of the discoveries and the natural wonders of the New World. Plants, animals, and peoples new to Europe fill his pages. The Historia became the first natural history of the Americas, and a base source for all later study.
oviedo-historia-general-natural-vol-2-18:
Volume two of Oviedo's Historia general y natural de las Indias continues the work Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo pursued from 1535 to 1557. The Royal Academy of History edition, Madrid, 1851 to 1855, supplies the Spanish text. Oviedo wrote as the crown's own chronicler, charged with recording the lands Spain had seized across the ocean.

His history joins the story of conquest to a survey of nature in the New World. The plants, beasts, and customs he describes were marvels to his first readers in Spain. Modern scholars mine these volumes for early sightings of American life, human and wild. Volume two carries that double record forward, part chronicle and part field guide.
oviedo-historia-general-natural-vol-3-18:
The third volume of the Historia general y natural de las Indias keeps Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo's great survey moving. Oviedo, official chronicler to the Spanish crown, worked on the Historia from 1535 to 1557. This volume follows the Royal Academy of History edition of Madrid, 1851 to 1855, in the original Spanish.

By this stage the work's twin aims stand plain: tell the deeds of the conquerors, and catalogue the nature of the Indies. Oviedo describes lands and peoples from his own years in America and from reports he trusted. His pages preserve early European knowledge of American plants and animals found nowhere else. The third volume is a working part of that first natural history.
oviedo-historia-general-natural-vol-4-18:
Volume four completes the Royal Academy of History edition of Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo's Historia general y natural de las Indias. The edition ran at Madrid from 1851 to 1855, in Spanish. Oviedo's own labor on the Historia stretched from 1535 to 1557, as the Spanish crown's appointed chronicler of the New World.

The closing volume carries his record of conquest and nature to its end. Oviedo writes as a man who crossed the ocean, governed, planted, and observed for decades. His natural history gave Europe its first broad account of American species and landscapes. His chronicle, proud and partisan, remains a source no student of the conquest can skip. The set closes with its witness still speaking.
phreno-geology-the-progressive-creation-: Hosted here, the sample shows only the front matter of Phreno-Geology, the title page, copyright page, and dedication, with no chapter text visible. The full title announces the progressive creation of man, indicated by natural history and confirmed by discoveries connecting the organization and functions of the brain with the successive geological periods. The title page names J. Stanley Grimes, with James Munroe of Boston and Cambridge as publisher in 1851.
plos-pbio-0000051:
Anthony M. Giannetti, Peter M. Snow, Olga Zak, and co-workers published this study in PLOS Biology in 2003. It asks how the human transferrin receptor can bind more than one partner. That receptor sits on cell surfaces and pulls iron into cells by catching transferrin, the blood protein that carries iron.

A receptor that must catch iron-loaded transferrin, let go at the right time, and still deal with other binders needs a neat trick. The authors work out the shape and contact points that let one receptor handle these jobs. The result helps explain how cells control iron intake. That process matters for blood health. It also matters in diseases where iron builds up or runs short.
plos-pbio-0020351:
Richard W. R. Retallick, Hamish McCallum, and Rick Speare surveyed a frog disease in Australia in PLOS Biology in 2004. A fungus called chytrid has driven sharp frog declines worldwide. The team checked a frog community after its decline, to see whether the fungus was still present.

It was: the fungus persisted at low levels in the surviving frogs, a state called endemic infection. That finding changes the recovery picture. Frogs that remain are not free of the threat; they live with it. Some species may have gained tolerance, while others stay rare. For conservation, the message is that saving such communities means managing a lasting disease, not waiting for it to pass.
plos-pone-0000051:
Yoshitake Sano, Tadashi Nakaya, Steve Pedrini, and co-authors tested a suspected cause of Alzheimer's disease chemistry in a 2006 paper. The amyloid precursor protein, APP, is cut to make the A-beta fragments that pile up in Alzheimer's brains. Adding a phosphate at one site on APP, threonine-668, was thought to drive that cutting in the living brain.

Measuring normal mouse brains, the team found physiological A-beta levels are not related to that phosphorylation state. A negative result can be as useful as a positive one. It steers drug hunters away from a target that does not govern A-beta under normal conditions. It also sharpens the search for what does.
plos-pone-0000151:
Claudia Hetzer, Dwayne Bisgrove, Michael S. Cohen, and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines how the viral protein Tat recruits and switches on RSK2, an enzyme inside human cells. Tat is the protein HIV uses to drive production of more virus from an infected cell.

By tracing Tat's grip on RSK2, the authors map one step in HIV's takeover of cell machinery. Each such step is a possible place for a drug to intervene. The paper adds detail to the picture of how the virus borrows host enzymes, knowledge that antiviral design depends on.
plos-pone-0000251:
Dario L. Ringach published this theoretical neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks where the functional architecture of the cortex comes from. These are the orderly maps in the brain's outer layer, where neighboring neurons respond to similar features of the world. The author proposes an account of how that organization originates.

Cortical maps are among the most striking patterns in the brain, and their origin has been debated for decades. The paper argues for a developmental explanation rooted in the statistics of input and wiring. It is a theory piece, meant to organize data and provoke tests, rather than report a new experiment.
plos-pone-0000351:
Jules B. Panksepp, Kimberly A. Jochman, Joseph U. Kim, and colleagues published this mouse behavior paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Adolescent mice vary genetically in how social they are. The authors report that affiliative behavior, ultrasonic communication, and social reward are all influenced by genetic variation in these young mice.

Mice talk ultrasonically and find company rewarding, much as social mammals do. Showing genes sway those traits makes the mouse a model for the biology of sociability. The work is relevant to research on conditions marked by social differences, where genetic effects are strong but hard to study in people.
plos-pone-0000451:
Sukanya Narasimhan and colleagues vaccinated against tick saliva itself, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The black-legged tick Ixodes scapularis spreads Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia bacteria. The team targeted salivary proteins the tick injects within 24 hours of attachment, aiming to build immunity against those early proteins.

The title states the strategy worked: immunity thwarted tick feeding and impaired Borrelia transmission. A vaccine that stops the tick from feeding could block several tick-borne diseases at once, not just one germ. The study supports anti-tick vaccines as a different line of defense, aimed at the carrier rather than the disease.
plos-pone-0000551:
Scott R. Evans and colleagues tested a drug for HIV-related nerve pain with the help of an electronic diary, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. HIV-associated sensory neuropathies cause burning pain in the feet and hands. Their randomized trial evaluated Prosaptide for this condition, while patients recorded neuropathic pain in an electronic diary rather than from memory at clinic visits.

Pain is subjective and fades in recall, so real-time diaries measure a drug's effect more honestly. A randomized trial built on such records sets a higher standard for pain claims. Even the measurement method here is part of the contribution to a difficult field.
plos-pone-0000651:
Pengyuan Liu, Haris Vikis, Yan Lu and co-authors mapped complex traits in mice by computer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Understanding the genetics of common diseases and their measurable traits should aid diagnostics and treatments. Mice offer rich genome and trait data gathered in many separate resources. Bringing those resources together quickly could speed gene discovery.

Their approach is in silico mapping at large scale, meaning computation across inbred mouse strains rather than new breeding. Inbred strains differ in known ways, so trait differences can be matched to genome differences. A validated shortcut like this saves years, and its hits point biologists to candidate genes for lab testing.
plos-pone-0000751:
Tara G. Martin, Iadine Chadès, Peter Arcese and colleagues asked how to spend conservation money on animals that will not stay put. Migratory species make up a significant portion of the world's biodiversity, and annual conservation investment in them exceeds several billion dollars. Designing effective plans is enormously challenging, because migrants are influenced by events across whole routes and seasons.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study seeks the optimal conservation of migratory species. Optimal means deciding where protection buys the most survival: breeding grounds, wintering grounds, or the stops between. A species can be guarded carefully in one country and lost in another. This work frames that allocation as a solvable problem.
plos-pone-0000851:
Komla Sobo, Isabelle Le Blanc, Pierre-Philippe Luyet and co-authors showed how cholesterol stuck inside cell compartments jams the cell's internal traffic. In Niemann-Pick type C, a storage disease that harms the brain, cholesterol builds up in late endosomes. Endosomes are small sacs that sort and move material a cell takes in. The team studied sick cells, and healthy cells dosed with a drug that copies the defect.

They tracked how the buildup changes the endosome membrane and slows traffic within it. Their title states the result plainly: the buildup leads to impaired intra-endosomal trafficking. If sorting stalls, the cell starves amid plenty. That jam helps explain the wide cell damage seen in this disease.
plos-pone-0001051:
Peter Mohler, Jane Healy, Hui Xue and colleagues described a heart gene variant set with a balanced trade off, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The gene ANK2 makes ankyrin-B, a scaffold that organizes heart cell proteins. Certain variants are common: about two percent in Europeans and up to eight percent in West African groups, by the authors' figures.

The team call the pattern ankyrin-B syndrome. The variants enhance cardiac function yet carry a risk of cardiac death and early senescence, cell aging. A variant kept common by an advantage while carrying a late cost is a classic evolutionary balance. The report reframes these carriers from patients to a trade off case.
plos-pone-0001151:
A piece of tissue mixes many cell types, so measuring its gene activity gives an average that can hide what any one type is doing. Konstantin Khodosevich, Dragos Inta, and Peter Seeburg addressed that problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They worked with cells made fluorescent inside living animals, so the cells of interest glow and can be picked out.

The authors describe gene expression analysis of these labeled cells, comparing approaches such as laser microdissection for isolating a cell type. Their method gives cleaner profiles of single cell populations. That precision helps researchers connect genes to the specific cells that use them.
plos-pone-0001251:
Bevirimat is a drug that blocks HIV at an unusual step: maturation, the final assembly step that makes new virus particles infectious. Cheryl Stoddart and colleagues tested it in mice carrying human thymus and liver tissue, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The compound, also called PA-457, showed activity at very low concentrations against many wild-type and drug-resistant HIV-1 isolates.

The authors report potent activity of bevirimat against HIV-1 in these SCID-hu Thy/Liv mice, a standard preclinical model. A drug with a novel mechanism is valuable because it can work where existing drugs fail. The mouse results supported moving the compound toward human study.
plos-pone-0001351:
Aging is accompanied by a low-grade rise in inflammatory signals throughout the body. Magnus Bäck and colleagues asked whether the mouth is one site of that chronic inflammation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. A variety of locally released mediators and inflammatory cells had been reported in the human oral cavity.

The authors investigated the presence of inflammatory mediators in the oral cavity across ages. The mouth is an accessible window on systemic inflammation, and it is also where gum disease develops. Their findings bear on whether oral inflammation is part of aging itself or a separate, treatable process.
plos-pone-0001451:
Kuo Ching Chao and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a new source of insulin making cells. People with type 1 diabetes lack such cells, and donor supply is short. The team took stem cells from the jelly of human umbilical cords. These cells are easy to get and to process, unlike embryo cells.

They guided the cord cells to form clusters much like the islets of the pancreas. Such clusters are the body's insulin factories. If they work after transplant, they could help control blood sugar. The work is an early step, but it names a rich and low cost cell source to test further.
plos-pone-0001551:
Teruaki Nakatsuji and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a shot aimed at acne. Acne hits more than fifty million people in the United States alone. Its weight tracks the immune reply to a skin germ that lives in pores. Standard care uses germ drugs or skin peels. The team aimed a vaccine at a surface enzyme of that germ.

Blocking that enzyme could blunt the germ's harm without broad germ drugs. A shot for acne would be a new class of care for a very common ill. The work is a first step, testing the aim in lab models. It opens a path worth a close watch.
plos-pone-0001651:
Maria Teresa Landi and co-authors searched smokers' lung tissue for a gene activity pattern tied to cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Smoking causes more than 90 percent of lung cancers, yet the exact gene changes it drives, and how they shape survival, were still unclear. The team focused on lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of the disease.

They measured gene activity with Affymetrix chips in samples from 135 people and looked for a signature that marks smoking's effect. The full text gives the gene lists, how the pattern tracked with cancer growth, and how it related to patient survival. A clear signature could one day help doctors judge risk or pick treatments for smokers who develop lung tumors.
plos-pone-0001751:
Daniel J. Kelley, Terrence R. Oakes, Larry L. Greischar, and their co-authors built software to clean brain scan noise in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Resting-state functional MRI studies look at slow neural fluctuations. Breathing and heartbeat create fluctuations in the same low frequency range, muddying the signal. Labs lacked automated tools to process the physiological signals recorded at high rates during scans.

Their software processes those waveforms automatically for noise correction and analysis. The full text gives the pipeline, the test scans, and how much cleaner the brain signals became. Routine cleanup of heart and lung noise makes resting-state studies more reliable across labs, which matters as such scans enter clinical research.
plos-pone-0001851:
Julie Lozier, Brent McCright, and Thomas Gridley studied bile duct formation in mice in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Alagille syndrome is a developmental disorder caused predominantly by mutations in Jagged1, a gene encoding a ligand for Notch family receptors. A characteristic feature is intrahepatic bile duct paucity: too few bile ducts inside the liver.

Building on their earlier work with mutant mice, the team shows Notch signaling regulates bile duct morphogenesis, the shaping of the duct network. The full text gives the mouse genetics and liver images. Children with Alagille syndrome can need liver transplants, so knowing the pathway that builds ducts guides both diagnosis and any future regenerative approach.
plos-pone-0001951:
Gurinder Atwal and co-authors used information theory to sort cancer risk factors, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Inherited genes, sex, and hormone signals all shape the risk of cancer and how it grows. How these factors interact in one patient was hard to weigh, yet the mix may decide who gets ill and how fast.

The team applied tools from information theory, which measure how much one fact tells about another, to data from cancer patients. Their aim was to weigh genes, gender, and age side by side. A clear ranking of these forces could sharpen prevention and help aim treatment at the risks that count most.
plos-pone-0002051:
Mark Humphries and Kevin Gurney gave network science a stricter ruler, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many networks, in technology, biology, society, and information, are called small-world. Their nodes form tight clusters, yet the average path between nodes is as short as in a random graph with the same counts.

Loose use of the label made unlike networks sound the same. The pair offer a quantitative method, small-world-ness, that scores how small-world a network truly is against the random match. A number, rather than a slogan, lets fields as far apart as brain science and the web compare networks fairly.
plos-pone-0002151:
Melissa Thomas and Leigh Simmons tested a prediction from sperm competition theory in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. When females mate with many males, each male faces rivals whose sperm compete to fertilize eggs. Theory says males should adjust how much they invest in each mating based on how strong that rivalry is.

One version of the theory says that whether rival males are close kin should change that choice. Thomas and Simmons report that relatedness among rivals did not shift ejaculate allocation as predicted. A clear negative result like this one helps refine what males actually respond to when they adjust their effort.
plos-pone-0002251:
Endre Majorovits, Mohamed Nejmeddine, Yuetsu Tanaka, and co-authors took close-up pictures of a virus passing from cell to cell, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Human T-lymphotropic virus 1 spreads by direct contact between cells, across an organized junction called a virological synapse. Light microscopy had shown the synapse exists, but its fine structure stayed hidden.

Using electron tomography, which builds a 3D view from many electron microscope images, the team visualized the virus at the synapse in detail. Seeing the handed-over particles up close may reveal weak points where drugs or antibodies could block this hidden route of infection.
plos-pone-0002351:
Adam Fisher and Matthew DeLisa evolved a faster-folding version of the green fluorescent protein, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. GFP glows green and is one of the most used proteins in cell biology, letting researchers tag and watch molecules in living cells. It is sturdy, but slow folding can dim its glow when cells make it in large amounts.

The team ran laboratory evolution, selecting improved variants over generations, and used the secretory pathway's quality control to screen them. Their fast-folding GFP should light up more reliably in hard cases. Better folding reporters sharpen one of the basic tools of modern biology.
plos-pone-0002451:
Hatori joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Megumi Hatori, Hiep Le, Christopher Vollmers, among others. Its subject is inducible Ablation of Melanopsin-Expressing Retinal Ganglion Cells Reveals Their Central Role in Non-Image Forming Visual Responses.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002551:
Yu led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Kai Yu, Zhaoming Wang, Qizhai Li, among others. Its subject is population Substructure and Control Selection in Genome-Wide Association Studies. Determination of the relevance of both demanding classical epidemiologic criteria for control selection.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002651:
Leonardo de Oliveira Martins and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was phylogenetic detection of recombination with a bayesian prior on the distance between trees. Authorship is credited in the record to Leonardo de Oliveira Martins and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Genomic regions participating in recombination events may support distinct topologies, and phylogenetic analyses should incorporate this heterogeneity. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002751:
Caroline M. Nieberding and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was the male sex pheromone of the butterfly bicyclus anynana : towards an evolutionary analysis. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Caroline M. Nieberding, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Female sex pheromones attracting mating partners over long distances are a major determinant of reproductive isolation and speciation in Lepidoptera. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002851:
Oluwarantimi Atijosan and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a national survey of musculoskeletal impairment in rwanda: prevalence, causes and service implications. The catalog record names Oluwarantimi Atijosan first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Accurate information on the prevalence and causes of musculoskeletal impairment (MSI) is lacking in low income countries. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002951:
Johann Pötzl, Catherine Botteron, Eugen Tausch and co-authors tracked a marked set of helper T cells after vaccination in 2008. Where T cells travel shapes what they can do, and the receptor CCR6 marks tissue-homing effector cells. Th17 cells are a helper type tied to defense at body surfaces.

The team traced functional, antigen-specific CCR6-positive Th17 cells following vaccination. Tracing means they could find cells aimed at the vaccine target, not just any Th17 cell. Published in PLOS ONE, the method helps vaccine scientists check whether a shot truly creates the cell type they intend.
plos-pone-0003051:
Ida Damgaard, Tina Jensen, Jørgen Petersen and co-authors ran a birth cohort study of undescended testis in Denmark and Finland from 1997 to 2001. In total, 2,496 boys were examined for congenital cryptorchidism at birth and again at three months. At birth, 128 boys had the condition against 2,368 healthy boys.

Risk factors were investigated prospectively, meaning data were gathered forward from pregnancy and birth. At three months, 33 cases remained among those checked. Published in PLOS ONE, a two-country cohort with exams at two ages gives unusually solid ground for judging which early factors matter. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003151:
Sara N. Vallerie, Masato Furuhashi, Raquel Fucho and colleagues ask where a key enzyme acts in insulin resistance in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme JNK1 is known to be essential to the development of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. JNK also affects inflammatory signals, but it was unclear whether its action in macrophages drives fat tissue problems.

The title reports a predominant role for parenchymal JNK, the enzyme in the tissue cells themselves, in control of whole-body insulin sensitivity. Readers learn which cell types matter most for this pathway. That focus can sharpen where future diabetes drugs should aim.
plos-pone-0003251:
Jeanne Farrell, Lavoisier Ramos, Martin Tresguerres and colleagues resolve a puzzle about a knockout mouse in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mammalian soluble adenylyl cyclase, or sAC, is a source of the second messenger cAMP distinct from the widely studied transmembrane cyclases regulated by G proteins. Genetic deletion of exons two to four in the Sacy tm1Lex mouse was expected to remove the enzyme.

The title reports that somatic soluble adenylyl cyclase isoforms are unaffected in these knockout mice. Readers learn that alternative forms can survive a targeted deletion. That warning matters for anyone who interprets knockout results as total loss of a gene's products.
plos-pone-0003351:
M-J. S. Milloy, Thomas Kerr, Mark Tyndall and colleagues estimate lives saved by a supervised injection site in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Illicit drug overdose remains a leading cause of premature mortality in urban settings worldwide. The team sought to estimate number of deaths potentially averted by implementation of a medically supervised safer injection facility in Vancouver, Canada.

Readers get a modelled count of estimated drug overdose deaths averted by North America's first such facility. The study cannot count people who did not die directly, so modelling assumptions matter. Still, it gave policy debate a numeric estimate instead of anecdote alone.
plos-pone-0003451:
Jochen Maurer and co-authors compared mouse and human stem cells in this 2008 paper. Both kinds of embryonic stem cells are workhorses of lab research. Gene data hinted they differ in keratins, proteins that form inner cell scaffolds. The team checked those hints at the RNA and protein level.

The contrast held up in the cells themselves. Human and mouse stem cells switched on different keratin sets. That gap may mark a basic difference between the two cell types. It warns against assuming mouse stem cell results apply directly to humans.
plos-pone-0003551:
Yu-Fang Pei and co-authors compared ways to fill gaps in gene data in this 2008 paper. Missing genotypes weaken genetic association studies. Researchers can impute, or infer, untyped markers from typed neighbors. Known linkage patterns between markers make that inference possible.

The team analyzed the accuracy of different imputation methods. Each method was tested on how well it recovered hidden variants. Accuracy gaps matter for replication studies done on computers. Their comparison guides gene hunters toward methods that hold up. Inferred data now fill most large gene banks used by labs worldwide.
plos-pone-0003651:
Elena M. Lucchetta, Meghan E. Vincent, and Rustem F. Ismagilov published this embryo study in PLOS ONE in 2008. In fruit fly embryos, a protein called Bicoid forms a gradient that helps set the head-to-tail pattern. Textbooks treat that gradient as a precise map the embryo reads.

The team tested whether the map must be exact during division cycles 11 to 13. Patterning still came out precise even when the gradient was not exact at those steps. Their result suggests the embryo can tolerate loose input at this stage. Final body precision, it seems, does not require precision at every earlier step.
plos-pone-0003751:
Yelda A. Leal, Laura L. Flores, Laura B. García-Cortés, and colleagues published this meta-analysis in PLOS ONE in 2008. Helicobacter pylori is a stomach bacterium that infects many children. Antibody blood tests can detect it, and designs such as ELISA and Western blot compete. Poorer countries need the cheaper option to work.

The authors pooled studies of antibody-based tests for infection in children. Their combined verdict weighs how well each test design performs. The result guides which test clinics should trust when young patients need a diagnosis and lab resources are thin.
plos-pone-0003851:
Chuancheng Ren, Xuwen Gao, Gang Niu, and colleagues published this stroke study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Briefly interrupting blood flow just after it returns, called postconditioning, can shrink stroke damage in rats. The catch is timing: protection seemed to demand action within seconds or minutes of reperfusion.

The team tested delayed postconditioning against focal ischemic brain injury in rats. Even with the delay, the treatment protected the brain. Extending the window matters, because a therapy that only works in the first minute can rarely reach patients in real hospitals. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008.
plos-pone-0003951:
De-Hua Yu, James Macdonald, Guohong Liu, and co-authors revisited an old worm drug as a cancer agent in 2008. Pyrvinium pamoate has long treated intestinal worms in people. The team found it blocks free-floating cancer cell growth far more than anchored growth. Others had reported anti-tumor effects in living animals too.

Their PLOS ONE article links pyrvinium to the unfolded protein response under low sugar. Stressed cancer cells lean on that response to survive. Pairing pyrvinium with other therapy raised its anti-tumor activity. An approved old drug with a new use could reach trials faster.
plos-pone-0004051:
Marta Mendiola, Jorge Barriuso, Andrés Redondo, and co-authors profiled vessel genes in ovarian cancer in 2008. Ovarian carcinoma is the top gynecological cancer killer in Western societies. Standard chemotherapy pairs paclitaxel with carboplatin. Most advanced cases still relapse after treatment.

Their PLOS ONE article measured genes tied to angiogenesis, the growth of blood vessels. A gene profile carried prognostic value independent of other factors. Tumors feed themselves by growing vessels, so the profile tracks aggression. Such a profile could help sort patients by likely outcome. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004151:
Wei Hu and colleagues published this drug delivery study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Minocycline is an antibiotic pill that reaches the brain well. It also blocks MMP-9, an enzyme tied to inflammation, and it eases disease in an animal model of multiple sclerosis called EAE.

The team packaged minocycline inside liposomes, tiny fat bubbles coated with PEG to help them circulate longer. They tested whether this packaged form calms autoimmune disease in the central nervous system better than the plain drug. The work explores a delivery trick that could make an old drug work harder against brain inflammation.
plos-pone-0004251:
Stefano Tiziani and colleagues published this leukaemia study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two drugs, bezafibrate and medroxyprogesterone acetate, show unexpected activity against acute myeloid leukaemia when combined. That activity is tied to the generation of reactive oxygen species inside the tumour cells.

The team used metabolomic profiling, a broad survey of small molecules in the cells, to map how leukaemia cell lines respond to the drugs. Charting the chemistry of the response helps explain why the drug pair works. It may also reveal which patients' cells are most likely to answer.
plos-pone-0004351:
Derryck Klarkowski and colleagues published this HIV testing study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Concerns about false-positive HIV results led to a review of testing procedures. The review covered a Médecins Sans Frontières HIV programme in Bukavu, in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The programme used the WHO two-test rapid diagnostic algorithm, where two positive rapid tests alone diagnose HIV.

The team evaluated a rapid in situ HIV confirmation test in this programme, which had a high failure rate under the standard algorithm. Confirming positives on the spot protects patients from a wrong, life-changing diagnosis.
plos-pone-0004451:
Tiny parts that build themselves into boxes follow a simple rule, report Anum Azam, Timothy Leong, Aasiyeh Zarafshar, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Nature builds structures by self-assembly at every scale, from atoms to whole bodies. Engineers hope to copy that trick to make complex three-dimensional objects in bulk, cheaply and all at once.

The team tested small flat parts designed to fold and join into cubes and octahedrons, a shape with eight faces. Some part designs worked and some failed, and the pattern came down to compactness, how tightly a part packs its shape. Parts that were more compact assembled with more success. That rule of thumb can guide future designs for tiny machines, drug carriers, and materials that build themselves.
plos-pone-0004551:
Thirteen years of the same malaria treatment on Thailand's northwestern border are reviewed by Verena Carrara, Julien Zwang, Elizabeth Ashley, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Artemisinin combination treatments are the recommended first-line therapy for falciparum malaria worldwide. The regimen here paired mefloquine with artesunate for three days.

The team reviewed how well that regimen worked over thirteen years of continuous deployment. Watching one treatment in one place for that long shows how drug resistance grows in real conditions. Malaria parasites have defeated drug after drug in this region. A long record helps planners judge when a trusted regimen is starting to slip, and what to put in its place before failures mount.
plos-pone-0004651:
Attention boosts nerve cell responses through a balancing act called normalization, model Joonyeol Lee and John Maunsell in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many studies have shown that attending to a stimulus enhances the responses of individual cortical sensory neurons. Little is known about how attention accomplishes this change in response.

The authors propose a normalization model of attentional modulation of single unit responses. In normalization, a neuron's response is scaled by the pooled activity of its neighbors. Attention, on this model, changes the balance of that scaling. A concrete model makes predictions that experiments can test, neuron by neuron. It also connects attention research to a general computation the cortex seems to use everywhere.
plos-pone-0004751:
Eileen Knorr and colleagues showed that matrix cutting enzymes guide both growth and immunity in a beetle model, in PLOS ONE in 2009. These enzymes are kept across many species and do many jobs in growth and body balance. Much past work used cells in dishes, so their full roles in living animals stayed unclear.

The team used the red flour beetle, a handy lab insect, to test the enzymes in vivo. They found roles in both body building and defense against germs. One enzyme family thus links two systems often studied apart. The beetle offers a cheap model for that link.
plos-pone-0004851:
Meian He and colleagues reported that functional variants in the HSPA1A gene predict risk of coronary heart disease, in PLOS ONE in 2009. HSP70 plays crucial roles in endothelial cell apoptosis involved in early phase and progress of coronary heart disease. Association between polymorphisms of HSP70 genes and risk still remained unclear, prompting a genetic study in patients and controls to test specific functional sites.

Variants altering heat shock protection tracked with risk. Stress defense capacity may be inherited in part. Genetic screening could refine prevention. Endothelial survival is a disease bottleneck. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings.
plos-pone-0004951:
Fibroblast growth factor, or FGF, is a key developmental signal. It helps specify and pattern the mesoderm layer. It also supports the self-renewal of human embryonic stem cells. Peter Branney and colleagues catalogued its reach in PLOS ONE in 2009. They set out to list the full transcriptome that depends on FGF. The focus was early development.

The catalogue lists genes that answer to FGF signaling. Together they map one signal's influence across the embryo's first decisions. Mouse stem cells also need FGF to specialize properly. The list is a reference for developmental biology. Anyone studying how embryos take shape can mine it.
plos-pone-0005051:
The BIO14.6 hamster inherits a deadly muscle disease. A spontaneous deletion breaks its delta-sarcoglycan gene. The disease hits the heart and skeletal muscle. Average lifespan is about eleven months. Carmen Vitiello and colleagues tested gene therapy on it. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The treatments used AAV viruses carrying repair genes.

Combined AAV treatments rescued the disease. They also increased the hamsters' lifespan. One treatment alone was not enough. The pairing matters for inherited cardiomyopathy and muscular dystrophy. The study shows gene therapy can beat a lethal inherited disease in a faithful model. It gives hope for human forms of the same conditions.
plos-pone-0005151:
Neanderthals lived across Europe, western Asia and the Middle East. Since the 1950s, bone studies suggested regional variety among them. Virginie Fabre, Silvana Condemi and Anna Degioanni tested that idea genetically. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They analyzed Neanderthal mitochondrial DNA from different areas. The population covered a vast range in the Middle Pleistocene.

The genetic evidence supports geographical groups among Neanderthals. The ancient population was not one uniform crowd. Regional lineages carried distinct signatures. Bones and genes now tell a shared story. The finding sharpens the picture of our closest extinct relatives. It may also bear on how they met modern humans. Structured populations interact differently than uniform ones.
plos-pone-0005251:
The connections between neurons end in dense protein scaffolds called post-synaptic densities. Studying them in human brain tissue could clarify mental illness, but postmortem tissue is hard to work with. Hahn and colleagues set out a study approach for that tissue in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Recent gene studies point to processes across the synapse in psychiatric disease. A workable method for examining pre- and post-synaptic scaffolds in patients' brains opens that biology to direct tests. The paradigm gives researchers a route from gene hints to the actual protein machinery of human synapses.
plos-pone-0005351:
A single-letter mutation in the small heat shock protein HSPB5 causes desmin-related cardiomyopathy, a heart and muscle disease with protein clumps in cells. Sanbe and colleagues tested a protective drug in that disease model in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The drug, geranylgeranylacetone, is known to raise heat shock defenses. Its protective effect worked through stronger induction of HSPB8, a related small heat shock protein. Turning up a sibling bodyguard protein is an appealing strategy for a disease with no specific treatment yet. Heat shock proteins are the cell's own repair crew, called out when proteins fold wrong. So a drug that calls out more of them works with the body, not against it.
plos-pone-0005451:
Shannon DeVaney and colleagues modelled where four Asian carp could spread, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Fish brought from other places can harm local waters once they get loose. Once such fish are settled, they are very hard to remove.

The team used maps of climate and habitat to judge which waters suit each carp. Their models flag the places most at risk before the fish arrive. Acting early on those warnings is far cheaper than fighting the fish later. The maps give managers a head start on keeping the carp out.
plos-pone-0005551:
Patricio Retamal, Mario Castillo-Ruiz, and Guido Mora studied a virulence factor of typhoid bacteria in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A protein called MgtC helps Salmonella bacteria grow when magnesium is scarce and survive inside immune cells. The gene sits in a known disease island of the Salmonella genome.

The team characterised MgtC in the strain that causes typhoid fever in people. They checked where the gene sits and what the protein does there. Knowing shared virulence tools across Salmonella types helps in the search for drugs or vaccines that cover more than one disease.
plos-pone-0005651:
Arnaud Ahier and co-authors reported a new family of receptors in insects and other invertebrates in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Receptor tyrosine kinases are surface switches that control cell growth and behaviour across animals. The team had earlier found an odd one in a parasitic worm.

The new family carries a trap-like binding part known from other receptors and is switched on by amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Finding such switches in invertebrates widens the known reach of this signalling system. It may offer targets for pest control.
plos-pone-0005751:
Marte Swart, Rudie Kortekaas, and André Aleman examined alexithymia in 2009, a trait marked by having no words for feelings. People high in this trait struggle to name and manage their emotions. Whether the core problem lies in feeling, sensing, or thinking about emotions was unclear.

The team characterized how the trait shapes emotion regulation strategies and mental processing of feelings. Pinpointing the weak step matters for therapy: training can target the right skill. Their profile of the trait helps explain why some people seem cut off from their own inner life. It also informs care for conditions where alexithymia is common.
plos-pone-0005851:
Edmond Byrnes and co-authors reported in 2009 the first known case of Cryptococcus gattii infection in the southeastern United States. This fungus, kin to a common AIDS-related pathogen, usually lives in warmer regions and can sicken healthy people. The patient was an HIV-negative man in North Carolina.

He developed a large fungal mass in his thigh in 2007, which surgeons removed before long drug treatment. A case far from the fungus's known range raises the travel question: did he catch it abroad or at home? The answer shapes how doctors in the region should watch for it.
plos-pone-0005951:
A growth gene called c-Myc also helps start the copying of DNA before a cell divides. Kristin Robinson, Nichaya Asawachaicharn, Denise Galloway and colleagues asked in 2009 what that extra role costs the cell. Their PLOS ONE paper studies cells with too much c-Myc as they rush through the copying phase of the cycle.

Speed has a price: the rushed copying strains the DNA, a hazard known as replication stress. A helper protein, WRN, turns out to be required to keep that strain in check. The work links a famous cancer gene to the daily work of copying DNA, and it names a partner that fast-growing cells may depend on to survive.
plos-pone-0006051:
Flu is often dismissed in the tropics, yet it can kill there as surely as anywhere. Wanna Hanshaoworakul, James Simmerman, Ubolrat Narueponjirakul and colleagues studied severe influenza in Thailand in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses national records to ask how much oseltamivir, the main flu drug, guards against a fatal outcome, and which factors raise the risk of death.

Thailand's health system had the records to answer at national scale. Knowing whether the drug protects the sickest patients shapes how scarce stockpiles are used. The risk factors named can help clinics spot, early, the patients who need the drug and close care the most.
plos-pone-0006151:
Atlantic bluefin tuna cross whole oceans, and their routes were long a matter of guesswork. Andreas Walli, Steven Teo, Andre Boustany and colleagues let the fish draw their own maps in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses implantable archival tags on five hundred sixty-one bluefin to reveal seasonal movements, aggregations and diving behavior in the Atlantic.

Tags that record depth and place show where the giants gather and how deep they dive, season by season. That knowledge is the base for protecting a fish hunted hard for its price. Knowing the oceanic habitat a tuna truly uses lets managers place limits where the fish are, not where charts assume.
plos-pone-0006251:
Cancer cells under stress sometimes eat parts of themselves to stay alive, a process called autophagy. Alejandro Vazquez-Martin, Cristina Oliveras-Ferraros, and Javier Menendez asked whether that trick also shields breast cancer from trastuzumab, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Trastuzumab, or Herceptin, targets tumors that overproduce the HER2 growth switch.

Autophagy helps tumor cells survive the drug, the authors report, building resistance to its effect. Blocking the self-eating pathway could therefore restore sensitivity. The finding names a partner target for a widely used breast cancer drug. It also warns that stress defences inside tumors deserve as much attention as growth signals.
plos-pone-0006351:
Shots of germ parts that block anthrax can guard animals against the disease. Ronit Rosenfeld and her team set out to find and improve one such blocker in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Their target was the part of the anthrax toxin that helps it enter cells, called protective antigen.

The team found a strong blocker and rebuilt part of it with human parts, a step called chimerization. The aim is a drug that can guard people after they have been exposed. A ready drug of this kind would add a key tool against a feared germ. Tests in animals showed the guard can hold against a lethal dose.
plos-pone-0006451:
Bo Xing and Xue-Bo Yin built a new light-based sensor, described in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their device uses electrochemiluminescence, light given off by a chemical reaction driven by electricity. A ruthenium compound provides the glow. The hard part is fixing the sensing layer firmly to the electrode surface.

For the first time, they used dopamine as the adhesive for such a sensor. A film of halloysite nanotubes, tiny clay tubes, was cast on a glassy carbon electrode and dried. Dopamine solution then glued the active layer in place. A simple, sticky coating could make these sensors easier and cheaper to build.
plos-pone-0006551:
Jing Jin, Timothy Sturgeon, Ora Weisz, and colleagues studied how HIV builds its shell in PLOS ONE in 2009. Retroviral Gag polyproteins are necessary and sufficient for virus budding. Productive HIV-1 Gag assembly takes place at the plasma membrane. However, little was known about how Gag reaches that membrane.

The team reports that matrix-dependent membrane targeting is regulated by Gag mRNA trafficking. The RNA that codes for Gag also helps direct where Gag goes. That dual role is an elegant piece of viral economy. Blocking the trafficking step could become an antiviral strategy.
plos-pone-0006651:
Angela Keuling and co-authors combined two treatments against melanoma cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malignant melanoma is resistant to almost all conventional forms of chemotherapy. Recent evidence suggests anti-apoptotic proteins of the Bcl-2 family are overexpressed in melanoma. The drug ABT-737 targets some of those proteins, but the protein Mcl-1 can shield cells from it.

Their title reports RNA silencing of Mcl-1 enhances ABT-737-mediated apoptosis in melanoma, via a caspase-8-dependent pathway. Removing the shield lets the drug kill. Combination logic like this is how resistant cancers are often beaten. The study maps the death pathway involved.
plos-pone-0006751:
Matthias Albrecht and co-authors tracked pollen movement in a wildflower over two years in PLOS ONE in 2009. The plant is Centaurea jacea, a knapweed of farmed landscapes. Agri-environment schemes aim to protect rare plants in such landscapes. Their effects on gene flow between plant populations were poorly known. Pollen dispersal is the main route of that gene flow.

The experiment measured how far pollen effectively travels. Long-distance dispersal proved real and meaningful for this species. Distant pollen can connect isolated patches genetically. Connection keeps small populations healthier and more diverse. The findings help scheme designers judge how far apart protected patches can sit.
plos-pone-0006851:
Yuan-Ping Pang and his team built bug sprays meant just for mosquitoes in PLOS ONE in 2009. New sprays are a dire need. Old sprays fail as mosquitoes grow proof against them, and fears for man's health grow too. Their target is an enzyme that nerve signals need in order to stop. That enzyme is acetylcholinesterase.

The mosquito form of the enzyme holds a free cysteine part. The team used that part to build sprays that bind for good and strike just mosquitoes. A spray that spares man and beasts while it kills mosquitoes is the aim. Such sprays could help curb malaria and the other ills that mosquitoes carry.
plos-pone-0006951:
Cristin Davidson, Nafeeza Ali, Matthew Micsenyi, and colleagues tested a treatment for a fatal brain disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. Niemann-Pick type C disease is a deadly disorder of nerve degeneration. A fault in the NPC1 protein causes most cases. Cholesterol and fatty glycosphingolipids build up inside cells across the body.

The team gave cyclodextrin to diseased mice over a long course. Treatment eased the cholesterol and lipid storage in neurons. It also slowed the progress of the disease. At a time with few options, the study offered real hope for a therapy worth testing further.
plos-pone-0007051:
Lawrence Sirovich, Mark Stoeckle, and Yu Zhang presented a DNA display method in PLOS ONE in 2009. Comparing DNA sequences reveals evolution and builds the tree of life. Databases now hold sequences from ever more organisms, gathered from every habitat on Earth. Tree-building tools strain under that growth, and ladder-like classifications fit the flood of new data poorly.

Their method analyzes and displays sequences at large scale. It is designed to stay workable as datasets keep growing year by year. A scalable view of sequence data helps biologists classify new species. It also helps them spot where the standard tree picture breaks down.
plos-pone-0007151:
Chengkang Zhang, Kimberly Truong, and Qun-Yong Zhou mapped clock output wiring in the mouse brain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The suprachiasmatic nucleus, in the hypothalamus, is the body's master circadian clock. Its timing signal must reach many brain regions to set the daily rhythm. Prokineticin 2 is one candidate messenger carrying that signal out.

The team traced where neurons that make prokineticin 2 send their projections. Those outgoing paths show which brain areas hear the clock directly. Mapping them is basic wiring knowledge for sleep and rhythm science. It also frames where clock disorders might be treated.
plos-pone-0007251:
Smita Jaiswal, Todd Pearson, Heather Friberg, and colleagues built a humanized mouse model for dengue fever research in 2009. Dengue virus causes major illness in tropical regions. A lack of suitable animal models had slowed study of the virus and of human immune responses to it for years.

The authors use mice with human immune components and a weakened mouse immune system. They study dengue infection and virus-specific responses restricted by the HLA-A2 molecule. Their PLOS ONE paper tests whether this model reproduces human dengue immunity. A working model could speed vaccine and treatment testing.
plos-pone-0007351:
David W. Sims, Nuno Queiroz, Nicolas E. Humphries, and colleagues tracked ocean sunfish with GPS in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Satellite tracking reveals the behavior and population structure of large ocean fish. Until then, fish were tracked mainly by Argos satellite positioning or by light-based geolocation from archival tags.

Ocean sunfish, or Mola mola, are huge and poorly understood. The authors report long-term GPS tracking of these fish. They argue the method offers a new direction in fish monitoring. Precise GPS tracks can show feeding migrations and habitat use in far finer detail.
plos-pone-0007451:
Dong Hoon Shin and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how tumor cells gain the ability to move. Spreading cancer must crawl through tissue, and an enzyme called MLCK drives much of that motion. MLCK is seen as a promising drug target for blocking invasion. The team studied a protein, Arrest Defective-1, that interacts with the enzyme.

They found that Arrest Defective-1 attaches an acetyl tag to MLCK. That chemical modification changes how tumor cells behave, including how they move. Controlling the tagging step could therefore slow cancer cell wandering. Slower wandering means less invasion and fewer metastases. The study points to a regulatory step that future drugs might exploit.
plos-pone-0007551:
Krisztina Johansen and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on blood chemistry in Parkinson's disease. Mutations in the LRRK2 gene are the most common known genetic cause of the disease. The team used metabolomic profiling, a broad scan of small molecules in blood plasma. They compared patients whose Parkinson's came from the LRRK2 G2019S mutation with patients whose disease had no known genetic cause.

The profiles revealed chemical signatures tied to each form of the disease. Shared patterns could serve both groups, while distinct ones mark the genetic form apart. Such biomarkers might aid diagnosis and help track how the disease progresses. They could also show whether treatments hit their targets. The study treats blood chemistry as a fingerprint of what is going wrong in the brain.
plos-pone-0007651:
Jennifer Taylor and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how skin builds its outer barrier. The epidermis renews itself constantly and faces a hostile environment. Its principal cell, the keratinocyte, matures as it moves outward, producing the proteins of the barrier. Those proteins protect against microbes and water loss. The team tracked gene expression as keratinocytes differentiate and form the barrier.

Genes switched on in coordinated clusters during the construction. The clustering is physical as well as dynamic: related genes sit together on the chromosomes. An organized program, not a scattered list, builds the front line of defense. Knowing the program helps explain barrier diseases like eczema. It also guides efforts to grow skin in the laboratory. The study reads the construction schedule of our most exposed organ.
plos-pone-0007751:
Eneour Puill-Stephan and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It looks for chimerism in a reef coral on the Great Barrier Reef. A chimera is a single body made of cells from two or more distinct individuals. The coral, Acropora millepora, spawns by broadcasting eggs and sperm into the sea.

Chimeras are known in at least nine major animal and plant groups. They seem common among sea creatures without backbones. The authors measured how much chimerism occurs in wild adult coral colonies. The answer affects how scientists think about coral growth, survival and reef recovery.
plos-pone-0007851:
Gordon King and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests how the plate a protein sits in can change crystal-growing trials. To read a protein's structure, labs first need good crystals of it. Screening means testing many conditions in parallel to find a promising start.

Screens usually run in ninety-six-well plates. The authors ask whether the plate's material itself interacts with the protein. Such an interaction could bias which conditions seem to work. Their results warn crystallographers that the plate is not a neutral bystander. Choosing plates with care may improve screening success.
plos-pone-0007951:
Laura Hughes and colleagues asked whether hunger early in life shapes bowel cancer risk, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dutch records let them track people who lived through famine as children or teens. Past work had linked lean early years to lower risk of this cancer in later life.

The team probed epigenetic marks, chemical tags on DNA that can last for years, as the likely bridge. Hard years during growth may set those tags in ways that change cancer risk decades on. The study joins a growing case that the body's early diet writes long-term notes on its genes.
plos-pone-0008051:
Heling Zhou and colleagues watched brain tumors in living mice drink in sugar, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Cancer cells burn far more sugar than healthy cells. The team tagged a sugar look-alike with a dye that glows in near-infrared light, which passes through tissue fairly well.

Cameras tracked the glow as gliomas grown in the mouse brain took the sugar up in real time. Maps of that uptake could show surgeons where tumor ends and healthy brain begins. They could also show within days whether a drug is starving the tumor as hoped.
plos-pone-0008151:
Guy Madison built a sound illusion of a beat that speeds up forever in PLOS ONE in 2009. People are rare among animals in keeping time together by predicting beats rather than reacting to them. Music and dance rest on that forward-looking timing.

By stacking rhythms at several levels, the illusion makes tempo seem to rise without end, like a barber pole for the ears. No trick recording is speeding up; the brain's own prediction does it. Such illusions expose the rules the timing system follows, and where those rules can be fooled.
plos-pone-0008251:
Sigrid Marie Blom, Nicole Schmitt, and Henrik Sindal Jensen studied a drug-like compound in PLOS ONE in 2009. Kv7 potassium channels calm cells by reducing their excitability. They are attractive drug targets for epilepsy, migraine, and nerve pain. Those diseases involve cells that fire too easily. The compound studied here is an acrylamide known as (S)-2.

The team tested it on Kv7 channels expressed in frog eggs, a common lab setup. The compound acted as both a positive and a negative modulator, depending on the channel. Mixed effects matter when designing drugs for precise action. The study refines how this channel family can be targeted.
plos-pone-0008351:
M. Ruby Siddiqui and colleagues described leprosy program changes in Orissa, India, in PLOS ONE in 2009. India eliminated leprosy as a public health problem by December 2005. Elimination meant fewer than one case per ten thousand people. With that target reached, a separate vertical program seemed less needed. The national program therefore entered a second phase of decentralization.

Leprosy services were integrated into primary health care in Orissa. General health staff took over work once done by specialists. Integration keeps services available while cutting parallel structures. The experience shows how programs adapt after success.
plos-pone-0008451:
Jianbing Yan and co-authors mapped maize genes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They used a new chip with many SNP markers, which are small changes in DNA code. Their sample held hundreds of inbred maize lines from around the world. Lines came from mild, tropical, and warm zones. Public breeding programs had supplied them.

The team found more than a thousand useful markers across the genome. They used them to sort lines by kinship and shared descent. They also measured how fast marker links fade with distance. Those measures help breeders pick parents and find genes for traits. The work gives a global view of maize diversity.
plos-pone-0008551:
Stacy Zamudio and co-authors study pregnancy at high altitude in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Living high up is known to reduce fetal growth. Babies born above a high threshold weigh less on average. Low oxygen to the placenta is thought to underlie this effect. Like problems occur in growth restriction and preeclampsia at any altitude. The team ask if low blood sugar also plays a role.

They propose hypoglycemia, or low glucose, helps cause the reduced growth. At altitude, mothers and fetuses handle sugar and oxygen in changed ways. Their data link low glucose to the origin of the growth drop. The work adds a metabolic piece to an oxygen story.
plos-pone-0008651:
Ivanka Savic and co-authors test a body odor in women in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Whether pheromone signaling exists in humans is still a matter of intense discussion. Androstenol is a steroid produced by the human body. It has been reported to affect human behavior. The team test if smelling androstenol elicits cerebral activation in women. They scan brains while subjects smell the compound and control odors.

They find androstenol activates the hypothalamus in women. The hypothalamus controls hormones, appetite, and sexual behavior. Activation there, rather than in smell areas alone, supports a pheromone-like effect. The work adds brain evidence to a long debate on human pheromones.
plos-pone-0008751:
Marcelo Golemba, Federico Di Lello, Fernando Bessone, and colleagues investigated a hepatitis C hotspot in Argentina. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Across Argentina, roughly two in a hundred people carry the virus. Certain small rural towns, though, show far higher rates. One such town stood out for genotype 1b, a viral subtype.

The team combined blood surveys with family-tree style analysis of the virus. Comparing viral sequences can show when an outbreak began. Their timeline points to how the infection spread locally. Such tracing helps health officials target screening where it counts most.
plos-pone-0008851:
Mojdeh Mohtashemi and L. Masae Kawamura looked for linked timing between TB and HIV among homeless people in San Francisco. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tuberculosis surged again in the mid-1980s in many countries. The rise is often blamed on the spread of HIV and AIDS. Among homeless people, the two diseases meet in crowded, hard conditions. Proof of true synchrony, though, needs data rather than assumption.

The authors compared the timing of TB cases with patterns among HIV-positive contacts. Waves of the two rose and fell together in their data. Synced timing supports a coupled epidemic on the streets. Outreach can plan for both diseases at once.
plos-pone-0008951:
Fredros Okumu and colleagues built and field-tested a fake human scent that draws mosquitoes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mosquitoes find people by smell, reading odours from breath, sweat, and skin. A lure that smells more human than a person could pull them into traps instead. The study ran outdoors where malaria-carrying mosquitoes hunt at night.

The team blended scent chemicals into a synthetic lure and set it against real human bait. Traps with the blend caught more mosquitoes than traps near actual people. A lure that beats the real thing can protect whole areas without using human volunteers. It also gives malaria control programmes a safer, standard tool for catching and counting mosquitoes.
plos-pone-0009051:
Basirudeen Kabeer and co-authors weighed three ways to diagnose active tuberculosis, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Blood tests like QuantiFERON-TB Gold measure interferon gamma released by immune cells. A related marker, IP-10, rises on the same signal. The old tuberculin skin test is the third method compared.

Latent TB tests were already known; active disease in high-burden settings was the question. The team checked how each test performed where TB is common. Combinations might catch cases that single tests miss. Better diagnosis matters because active TB spreads while it goes unrecognised.
plos-pone-0009151:
Jean-Baptiste Rioux and co-authors found a second skeleton protein serving a bacterium's internal compass, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Magnetotactic bacteria swim along the lines of Earth's magnetic field. They build magnetosomes, small pockets that hold magnetic crystals inside the cell. The crystals line up along actin-like filaments to form a working compass needle.

MamK is the actin-like protein that threads those crystals into a line. The team found a second MamK-like protein in the species Magnetospirillum magneticum. Oddly, its gene sits outside the island of magnetosome genes. A spare compass builder hints at backup for the system, or a second job.
plos-pone-0009251:
Stefanie Beck and co-authors published this brain and motivation study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Working memory, holding facts in mind while using them, responds to motivation. But different kinds of reward may not act the same way. The study separated primary rewards, like food or money's basic pleasures, from secondary ones.

The team measured brain activity while people did working memory tasks under each incentive type. Primary and secondary rewards changed the dynamics of neural activity in different ways. Those dynamics track how control rises and falls across a task. Untangling reward types helps explain why motivation sharpens thinking on some days and not others.
plos-pone-0009351:
Nan Gao and co-authors published this eye defense study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flagellin, the protein of bacterial tails, is a loud alarm for surfaces like the cornea. It stirs strong protection against germs, chemicals, and even radiation. The team traced which signals carry that alarm in the eye.

Flagellin made the cornea produce antimicrobial peptides, small proteins that kill germs. It also sped wound repair there. The route they found is unusual: it needs the growth receptor EGFR but not the classic alarm switch NF-kappaB. A new pathway to protection could be harnessed to guard eyes after injury or surgery.
plos-pone-0009451:
Sebastien Deregnaucourt used hybrid quail to study bird song in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bird song helps set species apart, yet how much of it is inborn is hard to tell. Quail of the genus Coturnix have clear, distinct crows. By crossing two species, he could see which parts of the crow come from each parent.

The hybrid crows mixed traits from both parent species in telling ways. That pattern shows a strong inborn base for the call. The work uses song to study how species split apart. Voice changes may be one of the first steps when one bird group becomes two.
plos-pone-0009551:
James Cooper and co-authors studied fish feeding shapes across African lakes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cichlid fishes in the rift lakes have split into hundreds of species. Much of that split turns on how they feed. Some graze near the bottom, and others hunt in open water. The team compared feeding structures in fish from several lake radiations.

The shift between bottom and open water feeding was large. It also arose again and again, in lake after lake, in a like pattern. That repeat performance shows evolution finding the same solution many times. Few cases let us watch adaptive change replay itself so clearly.
plos-pone-0009651:
Graham Poage and co-authors compared two kinds of change in head and neck tumors in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tumors carry genetic changes, meaning altered DNA letters. They also carry epigenetic changes, meaning chemical tags that switch genes off. The team measured both kinds across many tumors of the head and neck. They asked whether the two kinds of change line up at the same spots.

The changes were coordinated across the genome as a whole. They were not, though, targeted together at the same local sites. So the tumor rewrites its control system broadly rather than gene by gene. That whole system view may change how these cancers are classified and treated.
plos-pone-0009751:
Nikolaus B. M. Császár and co-authors published a reef study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study asks how well corals can adapt, in a genetic sense, to warming seas. Warm water breaks the bond between corals and their algae partners, a harm called bleaching. The team worked on a common reef coral and its two kinds of algae.

Traits of the algae, such as light use and shield pigments, showed strong genetic shares, the team found. The coral host's own stress genes showed no such share. Colony growth did run in families. The authors worry that the slow-breeding host may not adapt in time.
plos-pone-0009851:
Estrogen protects brain cells, but not all of that protection flows through the cell nucleus. Li-cai Yang and colleagues traced the outside-the-nucleus route in the rat hippocampus. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The hippocampus handles memory and is sensitive to hormones.

Extranuclear estrogen receptors sit outside the nucleus, on or near the cell surface. The team showed these receptors mediate estrogen's neuroprotective effects in this memory region. Fast, surface-level signals can guard neurons without changing gene activity first. The finding refines how scientists picture hormone protection in the brain.
plos-pone-0009951:
Muscle fibers come in fast and slow types, and a single gene helps choose between them. Mary Lou Beermann and colleagues studied that gene switch in bird muscle grown in the lab. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The gene is Prdm1, also called Blimp-1. The team tracked its link to the fast and slow forms of myosin heavy chain. Isoforms are variant forms of the same protein. Watching the switch during avian myogenesis, muscle building in birds, clarifies how fiber types form. Muscle type decides speed and stamina.
plos-pone-0010051:
Nishit Doshi and Samir Mitragotri asked a simple question in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Macrophages are immune cells that swallow invading germs and debris. Most work on how they spot targets focused on surface receptors. The pair wondered whether sheer size and shape also guide recognition.

Using plastic particles of different shapes and sizes, they tested what macrophages take up. Their title gives the answer: these cells do recognize size and shape. That finding matters for designing drug-carrying particles that either avoid macrophages or seek them out on purpose.
plos-pone-0010151:
The authors were Christina Ting, Tarek Rajji, Zahinoor Ismail, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study compared thinking profiles in older clinic patients. Patients came to a hospital memory clinic at a center for addiction and mental health. The team compared older people with schizophrenia against those with Alzheimer's disease or depression in late life.

Using demographic, clinical, and test data, they mapped how each group's cognition differed. Telling these profiles apart helps doctors avoid mixing up very different conditions. Clearer profiles can guide care and spare families the wrong diagnosis at a difficult stage of life.
plos-pone-0010251:
The authors were Tale Sliedrecht, Chao Zhang, Kevan Shokat, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used a chemical trick to switch off a mitosis protein. Correct cell division needs chromosomes attached firmly to spindle fibers. A checkpoint delays division until every chromosome is stably attached, guarding against cells with wrong chromosome counts.

The team built stable human cell lines where the kinase Mps1 could be blocked chemically. Turning Mps1 off at chosen moments revealed new aspects of its job in mitosis. A timed off-switch gives finer answers than removing a protein for good.
plos-pone-0010351:
Bethany Cool, Guy Chan, Lin Lee and others described a mouse brain gene variant in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, Gprc5b, makes a receptor whose exact job is still unknown. It switches on in response to retinoic acid, a vitamin A relative. Many receptor genes come in several spliced forms, each slightly different. This study began with a puzzle about a neighboring gene.

Chasing that puzzle led the team to a new spliced form of Gprc5b. The form shows up mainly in the brain of one common lab mouse strain. It also appears as neurons mature. A strain-specific form can confuse studies that assume all lab mice match. More broadly, it shows how hidden gene versions shape brain biology.
plos-pone-0010451:
Zahra Faghiri and co-workers recast the skin of a parasitic worm as a waste organ in PLOS ONE in 2010. Schistosoma mansoni lives in human blood vessels and feeds on glucose. It ferments much of that sugar, making large amounts of lactic acid. How the worm dumps that acid was unknown at the molecular level. The team studied a channel protein in the worm's outer surface, called SmAQP.

When they silenced the channel's gene, the worms' acid handling suffered. The surface channel appears to export lactate, the acid's form in solution. A parasite's waste route can be a drug target: block it and the worm poisons itself. Schistosomiasis affects millions, and drug options are few. This study names a fresh target on the worm's skin.
plos-pone-0010551:
Jian Jiao and co-workers found a tiny RNA that sets the level of a brain protein tied to dementia in PLOS ONE in 2010. Too little progranulin, a brain protein, is blamed for some cases of frontotemporal dementia. That disease strikes earlier than most dementias and erodes personality and language. How progranulin levels are controlled was largely unknown. The team searched for microRNAs that bind its gene's message.

One, miR-29b, bound a site preserved across species and lowered the protein's level. A small RNA thus acts as a dimmer on a dementia-linked protein. Raising progranulin by blocking that dimmer is a conceivable therapy. The finding also explains part of the protein's normal regulation. It connects two hot fields: microRNAs and neurodegeneration.
plos-pone-0010651:
Ana Traven and colleagues found a second job for a yeast RNA-binding protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, Puf5, normally helps destroy selected messages and slow protein building. It usually works by recruiting a partner complex led by Pop2.

When DNA copying came under stress, Puf5 still protected the cells. That protection did not need the Pop2 partner at all. So Puf5 runs two separate programs, one for routine message control and one for stress. Moonlighting proteins like this complicate simple gene charts, but they also reveal backup systems cells rely on in trouble.
plos-pone-0010751:
Rebecca Koehler and colleagues built a fast, detailed HLA typing method for East Africa, in PLOS ONE in 2010. HLA genes shape how the immune system presents germs to T cells. They are the most varied genes in the human genome. East Africa faces HIV, malaria, and tuberculosis, yet local HLA data were thin.

Their high-throughput method read class I HLA genes at high resolution in large sample sets. The data give vaccine and disease studies a proper local baseline. Typing built elsewhere can miss African variants entirely. A method tuned for the region helps ensure that vaccines are tested against the immune types people there actually carry.
plos-pone-0010851:
Aamir Aslam and Colin Logie published this yeast genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. DNA is wound around proteins called histones, and small chemical marks on those proteins help control when genes are read and how damage is repaired. The authors examined two marks on the same histone that sit close together and may influence each other.

They built yeast carrying fake versions of each mark, locked always on or always off, in every pairing. A switched-on mark at one spot softened the harm caused by a switched-on mark at its neighbor when cells faced drugs that stall DNA copying or gene reading. Yet the same pairing worsened harm in other settings. Aslam and Logie show these neighboring marks do not act alone. Their interplay helps cells recover from the stress of copying DNA.
plos-pone-0010951:
Yasutaka Mizoro, Yoshiaki Yamaguchi, Rena Kitazawa and co-authors published this body clock study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The brain's master clock, a cluster called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, resets daily using light signals carried by the chemical glutamate. One glutamate receptor type was well studied in this resetting; the authors focused on the other, the AMPA receptor.

They found two AMPA receptor parts are plentiful in the clock region that receives signals from the eye. Injecting the activator into the clock area early in the night delayed the mice's activity rhythms. Applied to clock tissue in a dish, it also shifted the rhythm of clock genes, in a way that depended on timing. Mizoro and colleagues establish AMPA receptors as genuine clock-setting levers, refining the circuit diagram of how light entrains sleep and waking.
plos-pone-0011051:
Ju Hye Lee, Mutsumi Kishikawa, Motofumi Kumazoe and co-authors published this cancer nutrition study in PLOS ONE in 2010. EGCG, the main active compound in green tea, kills cancer cells in dishes but only at doses far above what drinking tea delivers to the blood. The authors searched food ingredients that could amplify its effect at realistic levels, landing on vitamin A.

A vitamin A derivative raised the amount of the molecule that senses EGCG on melanoma cells, a receptor on their surface. With more sensors, EGCG inhibited the cancer cells' growth more strongly, and the combination was tested against tumors growing in mice. Lee and colleagues show a nutrient pairing that could make a dietary compound behave like a drug. The strategy matters because it works at concentrations a tea drinker might actually reach.
plos-pone-0011151:
King, Keim, Teo and colleagues hunted drug response genes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lithium is a main treatment for bipolar illness, yet it helps some patients far more than others.
