Some lack those faults, hinting at other routes. Studying small bowel growths, the team found repeated deletions in a gene called COPA, often together with truncating faults in another gene, USP9X.

Lab-grown mini-guts from patients and gene-edited cells with the COPA deletion grew without a growth factor called R-spondin, the team reports. The mutation stabilized a partner protein in the Wnt pathway, keeping the pathway on under lean conditions. Loss of USP9X strengthened the effect. COPA normally helps move cargo inside cells, a fresh link to gut cancer.
pmc-13263351:
Zahra Batool and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on new lab-made compounds against colorectal cancer, cancer of the large bowel. They built a series of 21 hybrid molecules joining indole and dihydrothiazole parts, then checked their structures with standard instruments. The compounds were tested on HCT-116 colon cancer cells and on normal skin cells for safety.

Several compounds killed cancer cells more strongly than the reference drug sorafenib. The lead compound, called 5d, stood out, halving cancer cell growth at a low dose while sparing normal cells about twelve times over. Computer docking and simulations showed 5d binding stably to four cancer-related protein targets. Drug-likeness predictions also looked favorable.
pmc-13263751:
Yves Renaudineau and others report on a December twenty twenty-five Toulouse symposium on two body-wide autoimmune diseases. The fourth meeting of a French immune referral lab tackled systemic sclerosis and lupus together. Their 2026 update spans genes, cells, biomarkers, and therapy.

Talks opened on a spot on the X chromosome, the TLR7 and TLR8 locus, and interferon signals shared by both diseases. T cells that calm or tire out, macrophages, and vessel cells filled the cell sessions. Efforts to make biomarker tests uniform, plus hopeful urine and blood markers, came next. The treatment frontier held CAR T cells that erase B cells and cell treatments that restore tolerance, with care tailored to each patient as the closing theme.
pmc-13263951:
Frederic Hilkenmeier and two colleagues present a 2026 proof-of-concept study on using large language models to screen papers for systematic reviews. Screening titles and short summaries by hand is slow as the number of papers grows. Their idea is to trust a machine label only when three models agree.

The team tested ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude on six data sets. About four in five summaries got the same label from all three models and could be sorted without a person. On that agreed group, scores beat earlier single-model methods on all set measures. Cases where models disagreed still went to human review. The authors say wider testing is still needed.
pmc-13264551:
Ellen Lutnick led a 2026 case series on humeral shaft nonunion, where a broken upper arm bone fails to heal. The team reviewed adults treated at one major trauma center over two decades. They looked for traits that slowed healing or forced repeat surgery.

The series held 59 patients, with a mean age near 60. Most first had non-surgical care, and many had risks like smoking or thyroid disease. Of those with surgery, most healed after one revision, but 12 needed more than one. Patients whose revision samples grew bacteria healed far more slowly, taking about 451 days against 198. Bone graft use did not speed healing in this group. The authors flag hidden infection as a key drag.
pmc-13264651:
Ugwu Okechukwu Paul-Chima led a 2026 systematic review of nanotechnology that steers reactive oxygen species, unstable molecules that can help or harm cells. Too much of them drives cancer growth and long-term inflammation. Tiny materials can raise or lower their levels, but clinical use lags behind lab promise.

The review searched three databases for work from 2013 to 2023 and checked bias with a standard animal study tool. In cancer, excess reactive oxygen aids tumor change and drug resistance. In inflammation, steady signals switch on pathways that scar tissue. Trials that sorted patients by biomarkers did better than unsorted ones, and combined nano therapies killed more cancer cells than single ones. The authors demand safer profiles, standard tests, and precise targeting before clinic use.
pmc-13264951:
Antoine Benichou and colleagues published a 2026 study on how fast chest aortic aneurysms grow when the aorta wall is inflamed. Most such swellings come from wear, but aortitis, inflammation of the aorta, is a less understood cause. The team compared growth in proven aortitis cases against matched patients with wear-based swellings.

The study held 23 aortitis patients and 42 matched controls. Swellings in the aortitis group grew about four and a half times faster, at 2.12 millimetres a year against 0.47. Isolated aortitis, confined to the aorta, grew fastest at about four millimetres a year, roughly double the rate in giant cell arteritis. Most aortitis tissue showed a granulomatous pattern, a specific kind of inflammation. The authors call for planned studies to confirm the rates and guide watch schedules.
pmc-13266051:
Renjie Hu and colleagues present a 2026 physics study on sending chiral signals, spin-linked messages tied to twisted molecular structures, over far longer distances than before. Such signals usually die within tens of nanometres, limiting chiral spintronics. The team induced chirality in a semiconductor polymer and built it into a transistor device.

In darkness with a magnetic field, the chiral signal traveled up to ten micrometres, already far beyond the norm. Under light, spin-selective effects switched the signal into another form and stretched its range to the millimetre scale, a leap of orders of magnitude. Gate voltage, temperature, and polarized light each tuned the signal, giving detailed control. The authors expect the long range and light switching to advance chiral spintronics theory and devices.
pmc-13267351:
Lauren Angel and colleagues describe a 2026 workshop that let patients help design a vulvar cancer trial. Standard care removes lymph nodes in the groin, which can cause lasting swelling and harm. The planned ANVU trial, across several countries, will test whether ultrasound checks can safely replace that surgery for some women.

Patients with lived experience of the disease joined the research team for a structured session. Short-term, they prized full cancer removal and accepted some side effects. Later, quality of life, fear of the cancer returning, and avoiding chronic swelling mattered most. These views set the trial's main outcome, survival after node spread at 30 months, and added patient-centered measures such as return to daily life.
pmc-13267551:
Saleck Choumad and colleagues present a 2026 case report on brain inflammation in a child after a viral illness. Their patient was seven years old and developed behavior changes two weeks after a flu-like illness, along with vomiting and tiredness. Spinal fluid tests were normal, so imaging carried the diagnosis.

Brain MRI showed bright patches on both sides of the deep gray nuclei, the basal ganglia, on water-sensitive sequences. Blood tests suggested a recent herpes-family infection, though no direct virus test was done. The child got supportive and anti-inflammatory care and slowly improved. At three months the child had no lasting problems, and a repeat MRI showed the patches fully gone. The authors stress MRI's central role in such cases.
pmc-13268051:
C R Horsburgh and colleagues wrote a 2026 scoping review of community-wide tuberculosis screening. TB still kills more people than any other single infection. Many infectious people have no symptoms, so waiting for clinic visits misses them. The team gathered studies since 1945 where whole communities were actively screened, keeping those that measured TB rates before and after or against an unscreened community.

Eight studies qualified, spanning nine countries from China to Zimbabwe. Starting TB rates varied widely. Five studies cut TB prevalence by 44 percent to over 80 percent. The winners shared a trait: over several years they found well over the number of cases first estimated to exist. Two studies failed to cut rates and found far fewer. The authors conclude that repeated full rounds of screening can break transmission.
pmc-13269151:
Daniele Napolitano and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on family carers of adults with inflammatory bowel disease in Italy. Carers help with daily self-care for a long-term gut illness. The study asked whether giving more of that help goes with better or worse quality of life for the carer.

Surveys from 275 carers at nine centers were analyzed. Help with upkeep, watching, and managing care showed no clear link with physical quality of life. Only upkeep help showed a link with mental quality of life, and the link was curved rather than straight. Carers in the upper middle of upkeep help scored 6.58 points higher on mental health than those lower down.
pmc-13269251:
Vitor Heidrich and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on how microbe strains pass between the mouth and gut, and between people living together. A strain is a close variant of a germ species. The team compared mouth and stool samples taken in pairs.

Across 1,644 paired samples, housemates shared far more strains than strangers, in both mouth and gut. Romantic partners shared the most mouth strains, even more than their gut sharing. Within one person, 74.5 percent of species found at both sites were the same strain, pointing to saliva as the route. One gut species was an exception, never matching between sites. Some highly shared gut species linked to poorer heart and metabolic health.
pmc-13269651:
Sarah Aljefri and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a 59-year-old woman treated with topiramate for pressure inside the skull. Eight days after starting the drug at 25 milligrams twice daily, she developed painless blurred vision and faded colors in both eyes. Eye exams found fluid lifting the retina, the light-sensing layer, in several spots.

Tests for infection and inflammation found nothing. The drug was stopped, and over three months the fluid cleared fully and vision improved to 20/30 in both eyes. Detachment of this fluid type is a rare side effect of topiramate, which is used for seizures and migraine. The authors stress fast drug withdrawal when it is suspected.
pmc-13269751:
Noa Scholz-Murcia and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on a web tool that calculates where places sat on Earth in deep past time. Plate models describe how continents drifted, but using them often needs coding skills. Their tool, PACA, lets users upload located data and pick a model.

Reconstructions appear in three dimensions, layered on classic world maps of past eras. Checks against desktop software showed near-perfect agreement, with median position errors under 17 meters. Statistical tests found no systematic bias across models. The authors say the tool widens access to these reconstructions and makes Earth science work easier to repeat and check.
pmc-13269951:
Yan Xu, Jing Ye, and Shuaiqing Chen published a journal article in 2026 on remnant cholesterol, a lesser-known blood fat, and gout in United States adults. National survey data from 2007 to 2018 covered 11,685 adults aged 20 and over. Statistical models adjusted for age, lifestyle, and health factors, and tested the shape of the link.

Higher remnant cholesterol went with more gout, in a straight rising line. Each small unit increase raised gout odds by a factor of 1.01. People in the top quarter of levels had 65 percent greater odds than those in the bottom quarter. Body weight explained 23 percent of the link, and uric acid, the chemical that builds up in gout, explained 40 percent.
pmc-13270251:
Akino Inagaki and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on wild boars responding to a dead female of their own species in Nikko City, Japan. Camera traps watched the carcass from October 1 to November 11, 2023, through its full decay. Three boars visited, and animal responses to dead group members are rarely documented in this way.

One adult male mounted the carcass, a necrophilic act counted as only the 11th documented case in mammals. His interest lasted about 17 days after the first visit, including stepping on the carcass and resting beside it. No visitor ate soft tissue, so feeding did not drive the visits. The authors argue that watching carcasses reveals behavior shifts across decay stages.
pmc-13271151:
Andrea Brandstetter is lead author of a 2026 journal article mapping the human bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, a small deep brain structure involved in stress responses and anxiety. The structure has distinct parts, but routine MRI cannot show them because it is tiny and low in contrast, making it hard to locate in living brains.

The team mapped the nucleus across its full extent in stained tissue slices from ten human brains, making 1,130 annotations and identifying four subdivisions: central, dorsal, medial, and posterior. They produced probability maps in a standard brain space, plus ultra-detailed maps in a high-resolution model brain. Both sets are openly available as references for imaging studies.
pmc-13271751:
Bridget O'Sullivan is lead author of a 2026 methods article on co-designing technology-supported integrated care with the people who will use it. Integrated care pathways and new technology both fail often when built without deep knowledge of local users and settings, and reviewers have called for earlier, more continuous stakeholder involvement, reported in detail.

The study develops and tests a method combining participatory rapid appraisal with focus groups, applied in the GERONTE project on older people's care. It was designed to engage many end-users in different places, allow quick feedback between users and designers, and flex around users' time. The article reports the process, the application, and the core steps so other teams can adopt or adapt it.
pmc-13272651:
Yutaka Akikusa leads a 2026 study of why fission yeast stops growing well at high heat, focusing on how cells make proteins. Earlier work found two proteins that hinder heat growth. Here the team shows they form a pair and work with a larger complex that controls RNA fate.

The pair normally holds down genes needed to build ribosomes, the cell's protein-making machines. When the pair is lost, those genes become more active, protein making improves, and heat growth recovers. The authors argue that the heat sensitivity of protein making itself may set the upper temperature limit for this yeast. Gene activity data support that view.
pmc-13272951:
Xiaoli Li leads a 2026 genetics study seeking treatment targets for two blood disorders marked by excess blood cell production. In essential thrombocythemia, platelets run high; in polycythemia vera, red cells run high. The team used a post-GWAS framework that joins gene data with causal inference methods to rank molecular drivers.

Higher predicted levels of five proteins linked to risk of both disorders, while one gene, MYB, linked only to the platelet disorder. Several markers also changed platelet, red cell, and white cell counts in distinct patterns. Two DNA marks lowered one key protein and raised risk for both disorders, pointing to shared and separate pathways for therapy.
pmc-13273151:
Gustavo Rey Alvira-Arill leads a 2026 cross-sectional survey of antimicrobial stewardship programs in children's hospitals in the United States. Such programs promote optimal antibiotic use in children. The survey, run in late 2024, asked about structure, staffing, activities, and after-hours on-call coverage.

Twenty-two programs replied, most from academic centers. Physician staffing rose with hospital size, from 0.1 full-time equivalents in the smallest to 0.8 in the largest, while pharmacist staffing rose to 2.25 in the largest. Nearly all programs did audit and feedback during work hours. Only six programs, 27.4 percent, offered on-call coverage, mainly for urgent approvals and inquiries on evenings, weekends, and holidays.
pmc-13274551:
Reina Murasawa and a large team report a 2026 case report of a newborn's abdominal tumor that masqueraded as a different cancer. A fast-growing mass above the right adrenal gland was spotted late in pregnancy and first read as neuroblastoma, the commonest malignant tumor of this age. Its mixed cystic and solid look, plus nonspecific blood tests, fit that guess.

After birth the mass kept growing, yet scans showed no abnormal tracer uptake and hormone byproducts stayed normal. Repeat imaging over time revealed new calcium deposits and fatty parts, classic teratoma clues that were missing at first. Surgery removed the mass completely, and testing confirmed an immature retroperitoneal teratoma with no adrenal involvement. The authors stress watching such masses evolve over time.
pmc-13275151:
Daniele Sciuto, Madeline C MacKechnie, and Michael J Terry report a 2026 case series on limb-saving flap surgery in Samburu County, Kenya, performed by an orthopedic surgeon rather than a plastic surgeon. Severe leg wounds need prompt soft-tissue cover to prevent bone infection and amputation, but reconstructive specialists are scarce in low-resource regions. The surgeon had taken a short-term training course in flap techniques.

The series covers fifteen procedures in thirteen patients between 2018 and 2024, most for severe open shin fractures with exposed bone. The reverse sural artery flap was used most often. Overall flap success reached 86.7 percent. The authors present short, hands-on orthoplastic training as a scalable way to close the reconstructive care gap in austere settings.
pmc-13275551:
Yasuharu Suga and co-authors present a 2026 case report of eye ulcers in two kittens traced to their own vaccine strain. The two-month-old littermates received a core feline herpesvirus vaccine at six weeks old, then developed sneezing and eye discharge within days. Another clinic misread it as allergy and gave steroid eye drops for a week, which can worsen herpes eye disease.

On presentation, each kitten had branching dendritic ulcers in one eye and a shallow ulcer in the other. Genetic testing matched the virus to the vaccine's F2 strain, with no wild strain present, though a second virus, calicivirus, shared the shallow ulcers. Branching ulcers healed in six days on antiviral treatment. The shallow ones later grew crystal deposits and deep blood vessels, ending in scarring complications in both cats.
pmc-13276051:
Dieta Hanson and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on counting visitors to public lands in the United States. Land managers need visitor numbers for planning, but counters are costly at remote sites with many entrances. The team tested whether phone and online data could stand in for on-site counting.

They gathered counts from seventy Bureau of Land Management sites, totaling over thirteen hundred site-months of data. Three computer models combined site features with mobile phone locations, geotagged social media, and nature observation records. Models using site features beat models using digital traces alone. Accuracy on new sites varied, depending on whether similar sites were in the training data. The authors advise blending many data sources rather than trusting phone data by itself.
pmc-13276251:
Karen Kai-Lin Hwang and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a flexible way to watch cell health in real time. Reporter proteins that glow can track acidity, stress chemicals, and energy levels inside cells. But hard-to-grow primary cells resist the usual DNA delivery, and making stable reporter lines for each use is impractical.

Instead, the team delivered the reporter instructions as messenger RNA, the short-lived molecule cells read to build proteins. Uptake was high in primary skin cells, cancer cells, and stem cells grown from adult tissue. Three ratio-based reporters worked as intended, sensing acidity, hydrogen peroxide, and ATP, the cell's energy currency, in specific cell compartments. The authors say the approach frees metabolic studies from commercial kits and suits patient-derived cells.
pmc-13276451:
Shuaikang Hao and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on measuring light-activated drug levels inside tissue more precisely. Photosensitizers gather in tumors and glow under light, guiding surgery and powering light-based therapy. Tissue bends and dims that glow, so raw brightness misstates the true drug amount.

Their deep learning system, called HS-QFNet, learns from both the glow's full spectrum and reflected light images. It was trained on lab phantoms, fake tissue blocks with known drug levels and varied optical traits. An attention mechanism helps it model how distortion depends on tissue properties. In phantoms it cut measurement error by about two thirds versus traditional correction. In mouse tumors its estimates stayed close and tracked true levels tightly. The authors see uses in drawing tumor margins and personalizing light therapy doses.
pmc-13278051:
Medha Sridhar Rao wrote a 2026 reflective essay on a student medical elective at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, Australia. The essay, chosen among the best submissions from Queen's University Belfast students for 2025, contrasts past and present children's bone and joint care. In Victorian London, conditions such as clubfoot and scoliosis drew stigma and care was mostly non-surgical.

Modern practice centers on function and quality of life, though resources and place still shape what children receive. Cases during the elective included a thirteen-year-old with severe cerebral palsy who had never walked despite custom supports. The reflections weigh what the specialty offers beyond the bones themselves, in the author's phrase.
pmc-13278451:
Moemen Khalifa leads a 2026 study of thyroid harm after breast radiotherapy given in fewer, larger doses. Radiation to the breast area can expose part of the thyroid gland, causing underactivity months or years later. The team followed 109 women with normal thyroid function who received regional breast radiotherapy and retested them six months after treatment.

About eight percent developed radiation-induced hypothyroidism, an underactive thyroid, by that check. Risk rose with higher maximum and mean thyroid doses and with smaller thyroid lobe size on the treated side. A key dose measure, the share of thyroid receiving forty gray, passed clear thresholds tied to higher risk. The authors propose planning limits to spare the thyroid and call for larger, longer studies.
pmc-13278851:
Yangha Kim reports 2026 surveillance figures on seat belt non-use among adolescents in Korea, drawn from the twenty-first Korea Youth Risk Behavior Survey of 2025. Non-use means riding while wearing a belt seldom or never. The note tracks three settings: front seats, rear seats, and express buses, over the period from 2016 to 2025.

In 2025, non-use stood at thirteen percent for the front seat, about forty-three percent for the rear seat, and twenty-seven percent for express buses. Rear seat non-use has fallen substantially over the past ten years, the report notes, yet it remains by far the highest of the three. The figures are published in both English and Korean by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency.
pmc-13279751:
Bruna Mezzomo Bejes and colleagues report a 2026 study of drug resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa from hospitals in south Brazil. The germ is a major hospital threat that shrugs off many drugs. Carbapenem drugs, a last line class, fail when germs make carbapenemase enzymes that break them. The team read the genomes of clinical isolates from Parana and Santa Catarina states. They matched gene finds with drug test results.

Eight isolates, eighty percent of the set, ranked as extensively drug resistant. They beat back beta lactam drugs, carbapenems and paired inhibitor drugs alike. Type reads showed a mixed clone scene, with ST1560 the top type at thirty percent. Many beta lactamase genes showed up, held both on chromosomes and on plasmids, small DNA rings that can jump between germs. Gene spread by plasmids raises the stakes for hospital control.
pmc-13280351:
Shuling Wu and colleagues report a 2026 case of long survival in a rare chest cancer after immune and vessel therapy. Mediastinal sarcomatoid carcinoma arises in the chest centre and often ends poorly. No past work tested immunotherapy plus anti angiogenic therapy, which starves tumour vessels, for it. Their patient was a seventy four year old woman. Tumour tests showed high PD-L1 expression, an immune brake protein, with a score of eighty.

She first got two cycles of chemotherapy and one cycle of radiotherapy with anlotinib, a vessel blocker, for stable disease. Two cycles of durvalumab immunotherapy with anlotinib then gave a partial response. Immunotherapy stopped due to severe side effects, while anlotinib went on. She stays alive with no disease progression past forty two months. The pair of therapies may suit PD-L1 high cases of this rare cancer.
pmc-13280451:
Linda G. Franken and colleagues report a 2026 study of guanabenz dosing in children with vanishing white matter disease. Vanishing white matter is a leukodystrophy, a white matter decay illness, that causes neurological decline and early death. No treatment exists for it. Guanabenz, a blood pressure drug that acts in the brain, eases the disease in mouse models. The team built a translational dosing model from rodent and adult data for a phase one two trial in children.

The estimated target dose was two milligrams per kilogram per day. The minimum effective dose was one, and the maximum was ten, in the same units. Pharmacokinetic modelling used thirty two trial participants aged about two to thirteen years. The study also explored links between drug levels and side effects, and estimated brain levels via a biological effect marker. Model based dosing can spare children trial and error in rare disease trials.
pmc-13280651:
Luiz E T Avelar and colleagues shared a 2026 case series on face care after weight loss from GLP-1 drugs. These drugs treat diabetes and obesity, but fast weight loss can hollow the face and deepen lines. The series followed fifteen women, aged thirty to fifty, in four Latin American countries. Each woman got two kinds of filler shots to restore the face.

Photos taken about ninety days later showed less loose skin and softer wrinkles. All fifteen women said their looks had improved, and most said they were pleased. No one had a serious side effect. Mild bruising and swelling cleared on their own within three days. The authors say the paired fillers may help patients who lose weight on these drugs.
pmc-13281351:
Laurence Cobbaert wrote a 2026 letter on harm caused by eating disorder care itself. Talk therapy can ease eating disorders, but gain is not proof of safety. Harms from care are poorly defined and rarely tracked, the author argues. So no one can say how often harm and gain occur side by side. When patients report harm, staff may brush it off as resistance or poor insight. That dismissal can deepen the wound and block learning.

Harm also falls unevenly, the letter says. Care that ignores culture, body diversity, or social barriers can hurt marginalized patients in distinct ways. Cobbaert calls for tracking harms from the start in every study. Patient reports and open-ended checks should count as core data. People who lived the harm should help design care and define what repair means. Claims of proof, the author warns, must cover safety too.
pmc-13281951:
Yingchao Ma and colleagues built a dosing model for a last-resort antibiotic in a 2026 study. The drug revives old power against germs that resist modern standbys. Its safe band is narrow, and levels swing widely between patients. The team enrolled fifty-one very ill patients with drug-proof infections at a Hebei hospital. Care ran from 2021 to 2023. Blood readings, one hundred twenty-three in all, fed the model. Computer runs then tested doses across kidney strength and germ toughness.

About six in ten patients improved in care, and about half cleared their germs. Kidney harm was rare, in two patients. A one-room model fit the drug's path, with kidney strength as the key dial. Standard doses hit the target zone reliably only for the most sensitive germs in normal kidneys. Tougher germs or weaker kidneys broke the target. The authors offer it as a dosing guide.
pmc-13282151:
Sana M Salih and co-authors wrote a 2026 case report and literature review on fertility during long-term treatment with a targeted lung cancer drug. The drug, osimertinib, blocks a faulty growth signal in some lung cancers. Older chemotherapy is well known to harm the ovaries, but newer targeted drugs are far less studied. Their patient was a thirty-year-old woman with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, an inherited condition that raises cancer risk, plus lung cancer.

Over thirty-six months of therapy, her ovarian reserve stayed normal. Blood hormone tests and repeated ultrasound counts of small follicles, the sacs that hold eggs, remained stable. Still, hard choices remain. Pregnancy is not allowed during the drug treatment. Gene testing of embryos may be used to avoid passing on the cancer-risk mutation, and a surrogate carrier may be considered. A preserved reserve lets patients delay fertility treatment until a better time.
pmc-13282251:
Emily R Shertzer and co-authors report a 2026 field study on how nestling traits shape death risk after young songbirds leave the nest. Early conditions can carry over into later life stages. The team tracked three sagebrush songbird species in the post-fledging period, the weeks after leaving the nest. They recorded causes of death and tested which nestling body traits predicted each cause.

Carryover effects differed by species and by cause of death. Leg length, unexpectedly, had an outsized effect on predation risk in the two sparrow species. Most deaths fell in the first five days, when young birds could not yet fly. At that stage they likely escaped by running or scrambling, so leg traits mattered more than wing traits. The authors say growing birds face trade-offs, since body investment that helps against one risk may not help against another at a different stage.
pmc-13282351:

Earlier results favoured the combined treatment for survival and quality of life.

Three hundred twenty-eight patients were included across three treatment arms. Both combined arms improved overall quality of life scores against chemotherapy alone. Breathing difficulty improved in both, while chest pain improved in only one combination. In one arm, improvement in chest pain and cough each linked to about a third lower risk of death. The authors used a joint statistical model to connect symptom change, symptom flare events, and survival. They argue that how patients feel carries information about how long they may live.
pmc-13282851:
Adeline Rosenberg and co-authors present a 2026 paper proposing a matrix model to help teams choose the right level of patient involvement and patient expertise for medicines and medical technology projects. Separately, patient expertise ranges from lived experience alone to recognised key opinion leaders.

The authors, drawn from academia, industry, and patient advocacy, built the model through three consensus workshops and illustrated it with case examples. The matrix crosses the two spectra, so a project can match its involvement level to suitable expertise. Patterns emerged along the axes: lower involvement levels typically engage larger, more diverse patient groups, while deeper involvement involves fewer, more expert partners over longer projects. The authors aim to help involvement professionals plan fairer, more effective, and better patient partnerships.
pmc-13282951:
West Java's largest hospital supplied the records for a 2026 cohort look at labor induction after fetal death, led by Vania Flowerina. The study was done at Dr Hasan Sadikin General Hospital in Bandung, the largest hospital in the region. It tests vaginal misoprostol for pregnancies at 20 weeks or more.

Records from 2021 to 2023 covered 155 cases, and 71 used misoprostol alone. Time to contractions and to birth fell as pregnancy age rose. Total dose also fell, from a median of 200 micrograms early to 50 micrograms at term. Maternal age and prior births did not differ by group. The authors call for larger prospective studies across centers.
pmc-13283151:
Leaf-nosed bats in a Brazilian city forest fragment carry flies, mites, and blood microbes, Nicolas Colacio's group found in 2026. The bats lived in a forest patch inside an urban area in the southeast. Bats can host many germs, but blood parasites in this group were little studied.

A total of 74 bats were checked for outer parasites and blood germs. About a third carried bat flies, mites, or both on their bodies. Blood smears showed no visible parasites under the microscope. Gene tests found Ehrlichia in one bat and Leishmania in one bat. About a fifth carried blood Mycoplasma types linked to bats. Findings show these agents move through city forest patches.
pmc-13283751:
A mushroom stuck in a narrow gut passage revealed a birth defect in a 2026 case described by Koki Higashi and colleagues. The boy, aged three, had Down syndrome, a group where this gut narrowing occurs more often. Most cases surface in newborns, so late discovery is tricky.

Vomiting at a local hospital first looked like a stomach infection flare. Contrast scans hinted at blocked passage in the duodenum and raised suspicion. Closer image review showed a mushroom shape wedged at that same spot. A scope confirmed both the stuck food and the underlying narrowing below it. Late signs can mislead, so blocked passage deserves care in such children.
pmc-13283951:
Double-shell sulfur hosts that move electrolyte on their own anchor a 2026 battery study by Ziqing Yao and colleagues. Lithium-sulfur cells promise very high energy storage but suffer sulfur shuttling and slow reactions. The host design aims to stop sulfur compounds pooling near catalysts.

Hosts were built from Prussian blue relatives through ion exchange with careful ratios. The shell layout drives fluid movement during charge and discharge cycles. That motion spreads reactants and steadies the sulfur reaction zone. Cycling stability improved for practical cells built with the hosts. A pouch cell at ampere-hour scale reached a high energy density value. Steps toward real-world use are the focus.
pmc-13285651:
A self-feeding loop locks liver cancer growth on, Chunxun Liu and co-authors map in a 2026 study. The protein STRAP runs high in many cancers, yet its liver role was fuzzy. Database, cell, and patient sample checks confirmed high STRAP in liver tumors and a link to poor outlook.

STRAP grabs a brake protein, DKK1, sparing a growth messenger from breakdown and letting it enter the nucleus to switch genes on with a partner. That same partner then binds the STRAP gene switch, making yet more STRAP. Hitting both STRAP and the Wnt path at once crushed tumor growth in tests. The authors back paired targeting as a liver cancer plan.
pmc-13286351:
Pablo González-Suárez and co-authors revisit the gene switches that build leaf breathing pores in a 2026 plant study. Twisting target genes out of their proper timing warped pore shape and function. The revised picture replaces a relay race with two partners whose shifting ratio steers the last steps of pore building.
pmc-13287151:
Feng Qiu and co-authors examined a growth-related gene called RHEBL1 in mouth cancer during 2026, asking whether two stem-cell factors switch it on. Tissue staining compared healthy, precancerous, and cancer samples, while altered cell lines and mouse work tested what changing the gene does.

The paired factors Oct4 and Sox2 attached at two places in the gene control region and boosted its activity. The authors link that control route to early tumour growth.
pmc-13287351:
Haitham Jahrami and colleagues translated a six-question scale on problem YouTube use into Arabic in 2026 and checked it with 1,134 young adults from Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Tunisia. The short scale was rendered through forward and back translation, then tested for structure and stability over time.

Answers fitted a single underlying trait well. Scores were steady on repeat testing and lined up with related measures of social media overuse, distress, food addiction scores, and poor sleep. The scale behaved the same across sex and viewing habits. The authors offer it as a screening aid for clinics and surveys in Arabic-speaking settings.
pmc-13287651:
Urszula Hohmann and co-authors filmed living glioblastoma cells in 2026 to see how crowding changes the way this aggressive brain tumour spreads through tissue. Established and patient-derived cell lines were watched at varied densities, and cell division events were tracked against nearby movement.

A division briefly sped up cells up to three cell lengths away. Under a density slope, some lines kept crawling on their own while others moved mainly by growth pressure. Cells that lined up into liquid-crystal-like order kept moving well even when packed tight. The authors suggest that self-ordering may help the tumour keep invading under confinement, a trait that makes it hard to contain.
pmc-13287751:

Lab work on patient cells and mice came first. Then 64 patients at nine Chinese centres joined a first-in-human dose study run from late 2018 to late 2020.

Patients had primary disease or disease that grew out of related blood disorders, at medium or high risk. The letter format outlines dose steps and expansion groups rather than full outcome tables. Existing drugs of one family shrink spleens but often fade; the dual blocker aims for deeper control with one pill.
pmc-13288551:
Afeefa Tahira and co-authors survey diabetes app users in Pakistan in 2026. The survey drew 397 patients with type 2 diabetes. Hospitals in four provinces took part. Both public and private sites joined. Models tested what turns trial use into steady use.

Acceptance strongly foretold steady use. Doctor advice fed acceptance a lot. Social image and confidence also fed it. Day to day, satisfaction mattered most. Better sugar reads also helped. Easy access to trusted facts helped too. Fast internet and good clinics aided use. They worked in part through confidence. Local context should shape app design, they say.
pmc-13288951:
Javeria Mansoor and colleagues map active learning in public health schools. Their 2026 scoping review covers case, problem, and team methods. These methods are well studied in clinics. Their use in public health is less clear. Public health work deals with whole groups.

The search found 22 studies in all. Problem-based work led the set. Team work came next. Topics ranged from global health to job health. Six themes ran through the reports. Skill growth and real-world fit stood out. Each method had its own snags. Problem work could overload students. Team work ate student time. Case work needed more staff and funds.
pmc-13289251:

Most trainees were women, and just over half were aged 18 to 29 at training. Basic life support scores jumped from a median of 9.0 to 22.0 right after training in the data. Repeat testing then tracked how much skill faded over time, a key test for rural readiness.
pmc-13289551:

Three activity classes emerged: Active Movers, Balanced Movers, and Sedentary Movers, based on steps, sitting bouts, and activity levels. Stronger pain tied to the sedentary class versus the active class in the full sample. Links clustered in women and in those aged 80 or older.
pmc-13289651:

Differences in cell subtypes, tissue residence, and disease stage decide the net effect. The authors map drug ideas that tune rather than erase these cells.
pmc-13289851:

She had six months of belly pain, vomiting, weight loss, and inability to keep food down before care. Scoping showed hair filling about 90 percent of the stomach and blocking its outlet, while scans showed stomach stretching that mimicked an artery squeeze syndrome. Open surgery removed the mass whole, recovery went smoothly, and psychiatric review confirmed hair pulling and eating.
pmc-13290151:
Outcomes of a radical operation for advanced pancreatic cancer are reported by Carsten Hansen and co-authors in 2026 from a high-volume center. The procedure removes part or all of the pancreas together with the celiac artery axis, territory once considered untouchable because of ischemia risk.

Data collected prospectively covered 58 patients operated on between 2014 and mid-2025, most after chemotherapy or similar treatment first. Median overall survival reached 28.0 months for patients treated before surgery, yet recurrence-free survival had a median of just 6.0 months, showing how early the cancer tends to return. Leak and ischemia rates were in line with standard pancreas removals. Hansen and colleagues conclude the operation is feasible but demands careful patient selection.
pmc-13290551:
Something in cow's milk calms human immune cells in a dish, and Lili Flad and colleagues name a suspect protein in a 2026 study. Milk's beta-casein comes in A1 and A2 variants, long debated for health effects, and both kinds were already known to slow the growth of stimulated blood immune cells.

The team split each milk type by molecule size and found the heavy fraction did the inhibiting. Protein screening of the cell supernatants singled out TOM1, the only protein markedly raised after exposure to both milks' heavy fractions. Added on its own, TOM1 also curbed the stimulated cells, and marker analysis tied it to interleukin-1β signaling. Flad and colleagues propose TOM1 as an anti-inflammatory mediator hiding in milk.
pmc-13290851:
Childhood emotional neglect may deepen adult depression partly through body-wide inflammation, Yongqi Ding and colleagues report in a study from 2026. They tested whether a combined blood marker sits on the path between early neglect and how bad depression gets in major depressive disorder.

The study enrolled 236 patients who filled in trauma and mood surveys and gave routine blood tests. Patients with childhood trauma histories showed higher inflammation and worse depression. Among trauma types, neglect predicted depression scores most strongly, and among blood markers the combined index predicted best of all. A mediation analysis assigned about 28% of the neglect-to-severity link to that index. Ding and colleagues stress the design cannot prove cause, but flag inflammation-lowering add-on treatments as worth testing in future trials.
pmc-13291251:
Dogs and owners act much alike across the world. Juliane Bräuer leads a 2026 study testing hunting dogs in five rural societies. Most past work used dogs from rich western homes. That bias left a big gap in knowledge.

Teams worked in Vanuatu, Mongolia, Madagascar, Peru, and Germany. Owners and dogs did six shared social tests. A survey also probed the bond in daily life. Bonds looked strikingly alike across all sites. Small gaps traced back to hunting style. A few gaps split rich and poor settings. Shared roots may matter more than local custom. The bond seems a deep, world-wide human trait.
pmc-13291351:
One kinase does far more than start DNA copying. Lorenzo Galanti and Boris Pfander review this enzyme in a 2026 article. The kinase, called DDK, pairs two protein parts. Its classic job is firing DNA copying starts.

The review views the enzyme from three angles. Timing shows when it acts across the cell cycle. Placement shows where it sits on chromosomes. Targets show what proteins it switches on. New targets guard chromosome splitting and DNA repair. Damage response work also sits on its list. Cancer drugs may exploit this wider role. Genome care, not just copying, is its true brief.
pmc-13291551:
An antibody can turn killer immune cells on pancreas tumors. Ruoxi Xiao leads a 2026 study of KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer. Such tumors shrug off growth signal blockers. The mutant gene keeps growth switched on below the blocker.

Antibodies of one class can still flag tumor cells. Killer cells then destroy the flagged cells directly. The team paired nimotuzumab with added killer cells. Dish, ball culture, and mouse models all showed strong killing. Killer cells woke fully and homed to tumors. Tumor EGFR levels predicted how well it worked. KRAS status did not block the effect. Flag-based killing thus bypasses the mutant switch.
pmc-13292051:
Julia Banaszkiewicz and co-authors review a 2026 topic in cancer therapy: using Clostridiaceae bacteria, which thrive without oxygen, to attack solid tumors. Tumor interiors hold low-oxygen and dead zones that resist standard drugs, yet suit these anaerobic microbes perfectly. The review surveys strains, engineered variants, and combinations with chemotherapy, radiation, and immunotherapy.

Clostridium spores germinate inside tumor tissue while sparing healthy tissue, and their toxins and enzymes can burst cancer cells and wake up immune responses. The strain Clostridium novyi-NT, stripped of virulence factors, produced strong tumor cell killing in studies. Engineered strains can also carry enzymes that switch on prodrugs only at the tumor, cutting body-wide toxicity. The authors see real promise, especially in combined regimens.
pmc-13292551:
Gabriel Caetano de Jesus, Victor Ary Câmara, and Arthur Menino Castilho audit a 2026 twelve-year record of newborn hearing screening across Brazil's states. Federal law has required screening in every maternity hospital since 2010, with national guidance from 2012 targeting coverage above 95 percent in a baby's first month. The study traces how actual coverage evolved as the program matured.

Coverage fell to 26.39 percent nationally in 2023, far below target in the reported figures. The South region led the states at 62.52 percent, and the Federal District reached 83.19 percent that year. Brainstem response testing has grown in both number and share since 2018, suggesting a shift toward the method reserved for at-risk newborns. The authors frame the state-by-state gaps as the central policy problem.
pmc-13292651:
Paula Gerlero, Silvia Vanessa Lourenço, and Marcello Menta Simonsen Nico report a 2026 letter on an unlikely pairing: white sponge nevus inside the mouths of two patients with ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-cleft syndrome. The syndrome, usually driven by TP63 mutations, deforms limbs, skin, and the lip, while the nevus thickens oral mucosa into white, velvety plaques. Fewer than a handful of combined cases exist.

Both patients, treated at the University of São Paulo dermatology service, showed diffuse mucosal thickening reaching tongue and palate, with biopsy features matching the nevus. Symptomatic lesions received liquid nitrogen cryotherapy. Results were excellent in both, and one patient's lesions had not returned after ten years. The authors suspect the overlap is no coincidence, pointing to shared keratin biology, and offer freezing as a practical fix for painful lesions.
pmc-13292851:
Songping Yi and co-authors set out a trial plan, published in 2026, testing mindfulness training for women having frozen embryo transfer. Many patients feel anxiety, low mood, poor sleep, or strain during fertility care, which the trial aims to ease.

Women aged 18 to 45 with mild to moderate distress will be split evenly between mindfulness sessions and basic counseling without mindfulness. The main outcome is the clinical pregnancy rate, with mood, sleep, and stress tracked as well. Enrollment will reach 434 participants across the single center. The team will also test whether calmer minds explain any link to pregnancy.
pmc-13292951:
Akihiro Kojima and colleagues report, in 2026, two cases of hernia through a surgery port hole after robot-assisted prostate removal, plus a new way to prevent them. Such hernias are rare yet serious and need repair surgery.

Both cases arose in 2024 among 73 robot prostate operations at their center, where a 12-mm port had sat. Their fix applies an anti-stick agent at the port site and sews the tough wall layer closed without the inner lining. One later patient treated with the new method stayed hernia-free. The team calls the step simple and safe for all patients.
pmc-13293451:
Donghao Zhang and co-authors build, in a 2026 finance study, a network map of extreme loss risk among Chinese financial firms. Gauging how shocks spread between firms matters for guarding the whole system, yet older models miss joint tail events.

Their method blends factor and pairing models to estimate expected shortfall shared across firms, then checks the model with backtests. The new model cut test rejection rates clearly versus three rival models, with gaps the authors report as large for two of them. The risk network's shape matched real market stress events. Firm and market traits shaped how strongly risk spilled across the network.
pmc-13293651:
Whether a plant compound called morin can block a key energy enzyme in Cryptosporidium parvum is what Mengge Chen and colleagues tested in a 2026 study. The gut parasite causes severe diarrhea in children and people with weak immunity, and good drugs are lacking.

The parasite leans on sugar breakdown for energy, so its aldolase enzyme is a tempting target. The team mapped the enzyme, found it in parasite cells and secretions, and showed morin docks onto it. Morin or immune serum cut sugar uptake, energy levels, and parasite counts in dishes. In infected young mice, morin cut egg shedding by 61.8% and eased gut harm, a drop the authors report.
pmc-13294051:
Md Jashim Uddin and colleagues probe a protective immune pathway in mouse COVID in a 2026 study. Lung RNA data showed sharp rises in CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11 after infection with mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2, along with their shared receptor CXCR3. Flow checks linked stronger arrival of CXCR3-bearing T cells and other immune cells to milder illness.

Blocking CXCR3 worsened disease, cut T cell entry, and let neutrophils flood in. Removing neutrophils eased that harm, and mice lacking adaptive immunity lost the protection. Transfer of normal CD4 T cells, but not CXCR3-deficient ones, restored defense. The axis appears to guard lungs by holding neutrophil damage in check.
pmc-13294151:
Jehad A. Aldali leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of central line bloodstream infections in Saudi Arabian intensive care units. Lines save lives but can seed severe infections, and local pooled data were scarce. Four databases were searched for studies from January 2015 to November 2025 that reported rates, microbes, or outcomes.

From 2,788 records, 11 studies entered the review and 7 entered the pooling. The combined rate was 3.05 infections per 1,000 line-days, with wide variation by unit type, region, and design. Mixed units ran highest at 3.41 per 1,000 line-days in the reported subgroup. High statistical heterogeneity warns against treating one national figure as uniform.
pmc-13294651:
Andrew Dickman leads a 2026 consensus study on giving intravenous medicines safely in critical care and cancer care. Open questions include which tubing materials to use, when filters are needed, and when light protection matters during storage and infusion. Poor choices can degrade drugs, block access devices, or harm patients.

Eight expert pharmacists rated statements over three Delphi rounds, starting from 181 medicines and finishing with 174 medicines. In all, 1044 storage and administration requirements were judged, and agreement was reached for 697 of them. The resulting guidance gives pharmacists and nurses shared, evidence-informed rules for tubing, filtration, and light protection in routine practice.
pmc-13294851:
Jon García-Ormaza and colleagues study suicidal thoughts and self-injury in early adolescence in a 2026 survey from Spain. Both problems are common at this age and carry serious health risks. Attention difficulties, mood, and trouble managing emotions were examined together rather than separately.

The sample held 1,079 pupils aged about 13 in their first year of secondary school. Roughly one in ten reported suicidal thoughts and about one in six reported self-injury without suicidal intent. Young people with either problem showed more attention difficulties, more negative mood, and far greater trouble regulating emotions, which emerged as the strongest single predictor in the models.
pmc-13295851:
Sofia Rouot and co-authors introduce ProbeST in 2026, free software for designing probes that map gene activity in tissue slices. Commercial probe sets cover only humans and mice, which blocks studies of infection where both host and germ matter.

The team tested their pipeline on preserved mouse gut cells infected with Salmonella, pairing custom germ probes with a standard mouse panel. Both host and bacterial signals were picked up cleanly in place, and host response genes sat near bacterial ones. The authors argue the workflow opens spatial mapping to non-model species and host-pathogen work.
pmc-13297051:
Xuele Xu and co-authors engineer, in 2026, a zirconium-based solid electrolyte for all-solid-state lithium batteries. The base material is cheap but conducts ions sluggishly and reacts at interfaces, so the team dose it with extra lithium, aluminium, oxygen and fluorine together.

Oxygen loosened the structure into a glassy state easing ion flow, aluminium raised lithium content, and fluorine hardened the cathode boundary against side reactions. The tuned material conducted well at room conditions. Cells built with a high-nickel cathode kept most capacity after five hundred cycles. The authors credit the combined doping recipe.
pmc-13298851:
For women living with daily urinary leakage, mood may shape sexual wellbeing more than the leakage itself, find Nancy Yang and colleagues in a 2026 analysis of trial data. They studied 240 women aged 45 and older enrolled in a pelvic floor yoga versus conditioning trial, tracking sexual function scores over thirty-six weeks.

Among the 54.7% who were sexually active, more frequent leakage modestly worsened condition-specific sexual scores, as did depression and anxiety symptoms. Among inactive women, depression and weaker physical function tracked with poorer ratings. After adjustment, the type of incontinence, urge or stress, made no difference. The authors argue care should address psychological and physical health alongside bladder symptoms.
pmc-13301751:
Pulling a child's central line early can be the difference between life and death, Coskun Ekemen and colleagues show in an eighteen-year candidemia cohort from western Turkey. The 2026 study covers 465 bloodstream infection episodes in hospitalized children between 2008 and 2025. Candida parapsilosis caused the largest share of cases, and nearly nine in ten episodes involved a central catheter.

Thirty-day mortality ran at 10.8 percent overall. Among line-linked infections, death claimed 4.8 percent of children whose catheters came out within seventy-two hours, against 13.1 percent without early removal. Keeping the catheter was the strongest independent death predictor in adjusted models, ahead of low platelets, severe neutropenia, and immune suppression.
pmc-13302851:
Teaching a computer model how water moves in cement pores speeds durability work a thousandfold, Chunlong Liu and colleagues report in a 2026 study. Atom-level simulations first traced how pore water spreads through calcium silicate hydrate, the glue of concrete. A graph neural network then learned to link each atom's surroundings to that movement.

The model's guesses matched the slow simulations while running about a thousand times faster. It also handled rougher, many-particle pore shapes it had never seen. The authors sketch a future where these fast pore-level guesses feed bigger models of salt attack, guiding tougher concrete design.
pmc-13303451:
Rukiye Burucu and Tuba Korkmaz Aslan report a 2026 descriptive study of body esteem and sexual life in 103 cancer patients in Turkey. Treatment can change weight, cause swelling, and require catheters, all of which may affect how patients feel about their bodies.

Patients treated in a university oncology unit between November 2022 and January 2023 completed a body esteem scale and a sexual experiences scale. Body esteem scores fell below the scale midpoint, and sexual problem scores sat well above the clinical cut point. Weight loss, swelling, and catheter use shaped body esteem, while sex, body mass index, and cancer stage shaped sexual function.
pmc-13303951:
Francesc Cabré and Marta Cascante survey drug treatment options for cardiovascular disease in a 2026 narrative review. Heart and vessel diseases remain the top global cause of illness and death, and many patients juggle several conditions at once.

Established drugs for high blood pressure, heart failure, rhythm problems, and thickened heart muscle are covered by how they act, proof of benefit, harms, and guideline place. Newer options include gene-silencing drugs for hormone pathways, SGLT2 blockers, vessel-relaxing stimulators, and heart muscle inhibitors. Shared pathways with lung vessel disease receive special attention throughout.
pmc-13307151:
Chinmaya Mutalik tested dye films that both catch and read breath aerosol parts in a 2026 study. Methylcellulose films carrying phenol red were exposed to model aerosols mixing sulfate salt, serum protein and plastic beads across acid to alkaline settings.

Infrared spectra moved in opposite directions for sulfate and protein bands as acidity changed. Their ratio climbed from 0.86 ± 0.01 at pH 4 to 3.56 ± 0.32 at pH 10 in reported values, separating ion and protein shares. Colour shifts from 432 to 556 nm confirmed the dye still answered after capture. The cheap films could suit field kits where breath tests must stay fast and light to carry.
pmc-13307351:
Lei Wang and co-authors propose in 2026 a self repair plan for sensor networks that float on the sea surface and drift with currents and wind. Drift breaks links and bends the backbone of such networks, so fixed round based upkeep often reacts too late.

Their plan fixes faults close to where they occur, through cluster head handover, backbone repair, and member rejoining, and it rebuilds the whole network only when quality stays poor. In tests fed with Taiwan Strait flow and wind data, the full method cut the cluster head break rate to 5.15 percent, well below the rate for the DARCR method.
pmc-13308351:
Gabriele Rigano, Daniela Billi, and Yannick Lara compare in 2026 the genomes of three desert cyanobacteria strains that have flown in space and faced Mars like tests. These Chroococcidiopsis strains dry out for long spans and shrug off harsh rays, which makes them models for life at its limits.

Fresh gap free genome builds let the team spot shared and strain only genes for drying defence, DNA guard work, and repair after harm. Every strain held the gene set for a sun screen pigment called scytonemin, and one strain added a second shield. Such shared tools may explain how the cells revive after wetting, and they hint at survival odds off Earth.
pmc-13308751: Chinasa Odo and co-authors issue a 2026 correction to their protocol paper. That protocol covers a qualitative case study of a symptom based risk tool for suspected head and neck cancer. The item itself is only a brief publishing notice, so it adds no new data or findings. It records that Multimedia Appendix 1, a topic guide for case study interviews, has been swapped for a fresh file. The fixed version has been sent again to the main repositories that hold the work.
pmc-13308851:
Katrina Himpson and co-authors track in 2026 healed sea turtles set free in the Indian Ocean, using satellite tags to learn how they fare and roam. Olive ridley, green, and hawksbill turtles all took part, with young turtles a focus since past tracking work has skipped them most.

Freed turtles lived long past release and moved in ways that matched wild kin of the same kind and age. Monsoon driven currents pushed open sea paths, yet turtles swam hard to hold place or to ride shelf and ridge lines. Rehab thus aids both welfare and science, and wide ranging turtles need joint guard work across sea borders to stay safe.
pmc-13309551:
Jan Maier and co-authors trace carbon movement along the whole Danube River in a 2026 study. Rivers carry carbon from land to air and sea, yet basin-wide seasonal control data stay scarce. Dissolved inorganic carbon, its isotope mix, and water carbon dioxide levels were the core measures.

Five sampling trips covered the main river and its large side streams across seasons. Dissolved carbon made up over 90 percent of total carbon and stayed fairly steady along the river, fed by groundwater and rock weathering upstream. Isotope shifts downstream pointed to steady carbon dioxide loss to the air. The authors confirm the Danube acts as a lasting source of that gas and map where inputs enter.
pmc-13309651:
Abigail Tisler and co-authors describe a newborn with two rare conditions in a 2026 case report. The baby girl had an enlarged clitoris at birth, a sign of excess male-type hormones before birth. Adrenal hormone disease is the usual cause and can threaten life, so hormone treatment began at once while tests ran.

Chromosome testing showed a mosaic pattern matching Turner syndrome, a condition that does not usually cause such genital change. A search for Y chromosome material came back negative, and the newborn adrenal screen was also negative. A later hormone panel showed a raised marker more in line with adrenal disease. The authors present the case as a diagnostic puzzle where both conditions may coexist.
pmc-13310051:
Ming Yang and co-authors screen inflammation proteins in eye fluid from people with severe nearsightedness in a 2026 study. High myopia stretches the eye and raises the risk of sight loss, yet its inflammation signals were little mapped. Fluid taken during cataract surgery offers a direct sample from inside the eye.

Twenty surgical patients were split into a high myopia group of twelve and a control group of eight. A panel measured 92 inflammation proteins in the fluid, and nine proteins ran higher in the high myopia group under strict cutoffs in the analysis. The strongest signals included HGF, CST5, and CCL19. The authors flag these proteins as candidate markers for study in larger groups.
pmc-13311151:
Dorothy Armstrong and colleagues explore safety risks felt by optometrists in Scotland in a 2026 focus group study. Proof on risk in eye care practice is sparse next to other primary care fields, and pandemic era change reshaped roles. Safety was picked as the theme for required national training, so views were gathered first.

Sixteen optometrists from nine health boards joined three online groups in 2021. Six themes covered current risk views, skill gaps, conduct, work setting, future tech risks, and fixes. Peers felt clinical risk is rising with new tech and wider roles. More role training and incident support were urged.
pmc-13311251:
Katarzyna Pogoda and co-authors analyze the 2026 cohort on how HER2 status shifts in breast cancer after drug treatment given before surgery. Such shifts can change which follow-up drugs make sense.

The team compared tumor samples before and after treatment in 736 patients treated from 2019 to 2024. HER2 class changed in 34.2 percent of patients, and drops in HER2 level were more common than rises. New HER2-positive status after treatment was rare. Knowing how often the marker moves helps doctors decide when retesting the leftover tumor is worth doing. That timing question matters for drug choice after surgery.
pmc-13311951:
Shivana Neeta Modi and co-authors present their 2026 London cohort study on what counts as a successful move from child to adult epilepsy services, and whether success improves seizure outcomes.

The study followed patients aged 20 to 24 who had moved from a pediatric service between 2009 and 2023. Success needed four marks: timely start, full preparation, a joint clinic visit, and adult follow-up within six months. Of 59 eligible patients, 72.9 percent met all four in this cohort. Successful movers had over fourfold adjusted odds of better seizure control or staying seizure-free by age twenty.
pmc-13312051:
Juan Yang and co-authors follow, in a 2026 longitudinal study, how symptom groups and quality of life change around surgery in women with cervical cancer. They tracked 183 patients at a hospital in northwestern China from admission through the days after their operations.

Using symptom and quality-of-life questionnaires at three time points, the team found five symptom clusters, covering pain and fatigue, mood, hot flashes and nerve symptoms, digestion, and low energy. Most clusters peaked one to three days after surgery and then eased, while quality of life dipped and only partly recovered. Worse cluster scores went with worse quality of life, which supports watching symptoms as shifting groups rather than one by one.
pmc-13312151:
Caio César Gonçalves Silva and co-authors report a 2026 three-dimensional study of how Le Fort I osteotomy changes the nose and sinus region. Comparing scans from before and after surgery, the team found that breaks in the continuity of the sinus walls, nasal cavity, and septum were common after the operation. The lining of the maxillary sinuses thickened more in the postoperative period, while the air volume of both the sinuses and the nasal cavity shrank. The authors suggest watching factors that could upset sinus balance after surgery, since lasting swelling raises the risk of sinusitis.
pmc-13312251:
Jay Olivet and colleagues present a 2026 program evaluation of rapid molecular testing for bloodstream infections caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. This severe infection does best on targeted beta-lactam drugs such as cefazolin. Many patients sit on vancomycin while conventional cultures crawl, and late switches are tied to slower clearance, more failures, and kidney harm.

The study compares care before and after the hospital adopted a blood culture identification panel, run on an automated platform, that names the organism directly from a positive culture. Patients are then ranked by a combined desirability score weighing treatment success, kidney injury, and survival, with secondary measures such as time to optimal therapy and length of stay. The authors set out to learn whether faster identification leads to earlier targeted treatment and better overall outcomes for these patients.
pmc-13312551:
Mohamed Mahmoud Shalaby and Fatma Aboalsoud Taha follow, in a 2026 prospective study, the hearts of newborns born with a left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia around the time of surgical repair. Babies with this defect face lung and circulation trouble, and a small, strained left ventricle often decides how they fare, yet serial heart measurements across the operation were scarce.

Thirty term newborns at a tertiary center had detailed ultrasound heart scans within a day before repair, again two to three days after, and once more at one month. Significant pulmonary hypertension was present before surgery in 70 percent of the babies. After repair, left ventricular dimensions, both raw and size-adjusted, grew significantly at the early and one-month checks, while several measures of pumping function dipped significantly in the early period. The authors chart a heart reshaping itself as circulation normalizes.
pmc-13315451:
Jinmei Gao and colleagues studied in 2026 how high homocysteine in mother mice affects the fertility of their daughters. Mothers fed a high-methionine diet developed the condition, defined by blood homocysteine above 15 micromoles per liter, and the team then checked the ovaries and eggs of female offspring.

Resting follicles switched on too early, driven by stronger signals through proteins including mTOR, AKT, FOXO3a, and RPS6. Mature eggs held fewer mitochondria that worked less well, with more reactive oxygen, more DNA damage, and more spindle faults. Together those changes lowered egg quality and help explain reduced fertility in the offspring.
pmc-13316651:
Yang Zhang and colleagues report 2026 lab work on Staphylococcus aureus, a germ that switches between free floating growth and sticky biofilm life on skin and inside cells. Acid stress is common in those niches, and the team asked how a secretion machine part called EssC shapes the switch.

Deleting the essC gene made biofilms grow thicker and heavier at acid levels near skin, even though fewer bacteria inside stayed alive. The mutant stuck faster, clumped more, and leaked more DNA from self-digested cells, all changes that cement a biofilm. Gene control circuits shifted in step, turning down a biofilm brake and turning up glue making paths. EssC emerges as a quiet governor of survival strategy.
pmc-13316751:
Maureen Norah Nabulime and colleagues offer a 2026 protocol for sorting and testing city solid waste from many sources, so towns can judge energy recovery options on solid data. Waste differs by source, and sloppy sampling ruins the math for digestion or gasification projects.

Called MSW-CAP, the framework standardizes collection, sorting, and lab checks, building on an existing ASTM method. Trials ran on home, grocery, restaurant, and school waste across five United States states. Samples split by moisture level, sending wet waste toward digestion and dry waste toward gasification paths. The shared recipe lets cities compare results fairly and pick recovery routes with fewer surprises.
pmc-13318051:
Mathieu Hénault and co-authors build, in a 2026 yeast study, a unified model of how wrong chromosome counts arise, persist, and sometimes fix themselves. Extra or missing chromosomes cause many birth and tissue disorders, and oddly, a second sorting error can restore balance.

The team measured gain and loss rates for each chromosome in budding yeast, weighed the fitness of each state, and fed the numbers into population models. True back-errors proved too rare to matter for most chromosomes. A few chromosomes that seemed to revert fast instead passed through a brief unstable state, with stuck-together chromosomes breaking and being repaired across divisions, as sequencing and live imaging confirmed. Chromosome-specific routes, they conclude, shape genome change.
pmc-13318251:
Giovanna Spina leads a 2026 retrospective study of total elbow replacement for older patients whose lower arm bone fractures near the elbow could not be rebuilt with plates and screws. Records covered operations done between January 2017 and December 2024.

Thirty-seven patients, averaging 80.4 years old, were followed for a mean of 107 months and assessed for movement, pain, function scores, imaging findings, and complications. Final results showed good elbow motion and function, with a revision rate of 11 percent and implant survival of 94.2 percent at five years in this group. Other health problems did not clearly change outcomes, supporting replacement as a primary option for selected older patients.
pmc-13318551:
Adriano José Pereira and a large team set out a 2026 protocol for TELESCOPE 2, a trial testing whether telemedicine support can shorten stays in intensive care units in Brazil. Earlier work showed remote intensive care is safe and workable, but its effect on patient outcomes is unproven.

The package combines daily remote rounds led by intensive care doctors, coordinated input from nurses, physiotherapists, and pharmacists, and a quality and safety programme. Length of intensive care stay is the main measure, backed by death rates, ventilator-free days, readmission, and tube accidents.
pmc-13319651:
Şeyba Sara Mansuroğlu and co-authors compare rinse methods for killing germs deep in tooth roots in a 2026 lab study. Germs that hide in tiny tubes in root walls are a main cause of lasting tooth infection. Five ways to stir rinse fluid were tested for how deep their kill reached into those tubes.

Sixty pulled human teeth with one root canal each were filled with a hardy germ type, then rinsed by needle, soft tip, sound, or pulse methods. Slices at three depths were viewed under a strong scope to measure the kill zone. Pulse rinsing reached deepest at both top and tip ends, while plain needle rinsing reached least. No method cleared germs in full.
pmc-13320351:
Wanyue Li and co-authors study sleep habits and spine curve risk in a 2026 long follow up study from a British health bank. A five part sleep score joined bed time type, sleep length, sleeplessness, snoring, and day sleepiness into one habit grade.

Among 408870 adults free of the curve at the start, 2976 new cases arose over a mean span near sixteen years. Each added healthy sleep trait cut risk by about a tenth in the adjusted counts, and those with all five traits faced far lower risk than those with almost none. The link held across most subgroups, which hints sleep care may aid spine health.
pmc-13320451:
Kamran Dousti and co-authors survey public knowledge of invasive mosquitoes in Saarland, Germany in a 2026 study. The region has no settled tiger mosquito yet but faces rising invasion risk as the insect spreads in Europe and can carry tropical fevers. A public form ran from February to June 2024 through digital and paper routes to gauge awareness, habits, and knowledge.

Of 1064 replies, 623 met the study rules for a close look in the counts reported. More than half knew that clearing still water blocks breeding, yet fewer than one in five did it on a regular basis. Most had heard of the tiger mosquito, but fewer than half tied it to one fever it can carry. Seasonal teaching drives may slow the insect foothold, the team argues.
pmc-13321251:
Ernestina Melicoff, David Moreno McNeill, and Christian Benden look ahead for children's lung transplantation in a 2026 review. The piece opens a special issue on paediatric chest transplantation and covers donor access, graft failure, and how fitness shapes outcomes. Lung transplant is a settled option for a small group of children with severe lung disease.

In the United States, 1511 paediatric lung transplants were reported from 1988 to 2024, and 46.8 percent were for cystic fibrosis, long the leading reason. New cystic fibrosis drugs are reshaping who needs a transplant. The authors argue that donor supply, long term graft health, and frailty checks will decide the field's next gains.
pmc-13322751:

Direct laser writing was used to arrange the particles in stacked tiers inside a composite material.

By adjusting particle size, particle type, loading, and laser settings, the team widened the reflected colour range across the visible spectrum. Electron microscopy showed the neat, non-packed order survived the writing process, with features below a micron made reliably. pmc-13322951:

pmc-13337451:
