When the enzyme was reduced in human cells, three specific messages lasted longer and produced more of their proteins. Those messages reach the recycling compartment through a transporter in its membrane. Two of the three proteins had not been linked to fat stress before. Testing their roles showed they protect cells against fat damage, so destroying their messages removes a shield.
pmc-13383051:
Kawakami and colleagues provide the first test of whether a spontaneous chemical change in a protein can trigger amyloid disease, in 2026 protein research. The protein, beta2-microglobulin, builds up in long-term dialysis patients and forms amyloid fibrils that damage joints, a condition called dialysis-related amyloidosis. An age-related change, isoaspartate formation, was suspected but untestable because chemists could not build the modified protein. The team built variants carrying the change at the two hotspots, positions 17 and 42.

The isoaspartate-17 variant formed fibrils even more readily than the known pathogenic truncated variant. Microscopy and spectroscopy confirmed amyloid fibrils. The position-42 variant did not share that potency, localizing the effect to one specific aging site on the protein. Kawakami argues it is a general driver of pathological protein aggregation, and casts the disease as one of accumulated damage that healthy kidneys would normally clear.
pmc-13386951:
Xu Wang and colleagues propose microbe-based wastewater recycling for long-term space habitats in a 2026 perspective. Closed-loop water recovery is essential off Earth, and microbe systems promise lower energy use than chemical systems. Habitat wastewater, though, brings high ammonium, a low carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, and stacked stresses that break standard setups.

Their answer joins synthetic microbiology with single-cell Raman spectroscopy, a light method that fingerprints single cells. Paired with isotope tracing, it can pick out hardy working microbes without long enrichment cultures. The same tool could watch the system live, giving early warnings and smarter control for resilient space water loops.
pmc-13387751:
Anshuman Panda and colleagues report urine leaking into the chest in a man with blocked kidney drainage in a 2026 case report. A 30-year-old man arrived breathless and needed intensive care for the fluid around his right lung. Scans showed ureter stones with kidney swelling and fluid tracks running from the kidney area up to the chest space.

Chest fluid carried very high urea and creatinine, confirming urine as its source, a condition called urinothorax. Both urine and chest fluid grew the same drug-resistant E. coli, treated with meropenem. Stents placed in both ureters addressed the blockage at the root of the problem.
pmc-13390551:
Mahmoud Issam Salameh, Amani Anwar Khalil, and Majed Alamri assess, in 2026, genomic skills among nurses through a genetics and genomics nursing practice survey. In intensive care, genetic information can clarify diagnoses, tailor drug choices, and trigger referral to specialist genetics services.

Critically ill patients often show complex multi-system illness or unexplained features with a possible inherited basis. The authors argue that nurses need not only basic genomic knowledge but also positive attitudes, confidence, and sound judgement to take family histories, spot genetic risk, and teach patients. Nursing educators gain a competency snapshot that shows where intensive care nurses feel equipped and where training should focus.
pmc-13390851:
Rui Wang leads a 2026 analysis sorting younger Chinese patients with high blood pressure into distinct medication literacy profiles. Knowing how to use medicines safely varies widely among patients, and averages hide the groups most at risk of misuse.

Using latent profile analysis, a method that groups people by shared response patterns, the team identified separate literacy profiles among young and middle-aged patients. They also examined which personal and clinical factors predict profile membership. Hypertension clinicians gain a segmentation they can act on: education efforts can target the profile that struggles most. That may mean help with dosing schedules or side-effect judgement. It beats giving every patient the same leaflet.
pmc-13391051:
Hiroshi Shimizu reports, in 2026, a stitch-free method for re-fixing a dislocated man-made lens together with its capsular bag, years after cataract surgery. Late dislocation of this lens-bag complex is a key delayed problem that leaves patients with blurred, decentered vision.

A 75-year-old man developed a shifted lens with symptoms about two years after cataract surgery. He had also had a laser cut to the lens bag since then. Through small corneal openings, and after limited removal of vitreous gel, the surgeon anchored the complex using a standard shop-bought iris hook with a flanged end, avoiding stitches. Eye surgeons gain a single-case method note with shop gear. It may help where special fixation tools are not at hand. One case shows the move can be done, though more cases must show it lasts.
pmc-13392151:
Sevil Yasar leads a fifteen-year look, in 2026, at whether blood markers of the renin-angiotensin system predict later cognitive decline. This hormone system, best known for blood pressure control, is implicated in Alzheimer's disease processes, but long-term human evidence has been thin.

In a secondary analysis of 310 community-dwelling adults who began cognitively healthy in a randomised trial cohort, the team measured angiotensin compounds and converting enzymes. They then followed new decline and impairment over time. Geriatric and dementia researchers gain long-horizon evidence on whether a blood pressure pathway doubles as an early dementia risk signal, which could connect two common prevention agendas.
pmc-13393151:
Charbel Saad, Thadeu Rangel, Juan Pablo Menendez, and Gregory Nicolas reviewed how surgeons rebuild the face in the same operation that removes the parotid gland and sacrifices the facial nerve to cancer. Waiting months for repair leaves patients with drooping, an unprotected eye, and trouble eating and speaking. The review gathered studies of immediate or single-stage reconstruction reporting function, patient views, complications, or later revisions.

Nineteen studies covering two hundred seventy-seven patients described nerve grafts, transfers from a chewing nerve, muscle flaps that move, and combinations. Immediate work generally restored resting symmetry, eye closure, and mouth control, while moving reconstructions more often returned a smile. Graft results settled around the middle of the standard facial function scale. Complication rates were modest, and later radiotherapy did not always block recovery.
pmc-13394651:
Srikrishna Sulgodu Ramachandra leads a 2026 study of skin illness among metal casting workers in Goa, India. Casting exposes staff to heat, fumes, dust, and harsh chemicals. At a yearly health check, 345 workers at one factory answered questions and had skin exams by a skin doctor. The team linked illness to age, work area, years on the job, and glove or mask use.

About one third of workers had a job-linked skin problem. Contact rash and prickly heat led the list, ahead of ringworm and burn scars. Core-making staff carried the heaviest load, with about two thirds affected. Reported gear use and long service both tracked with illness. The authors urge better guards by work area.
pmc-13394851:
Elsa Zhang and co-authors track, in 2026, how paid AI software spread through private health plans in the United States. Using national claims data from 2018 to 2023, they counted bills for AI tools in eye scans, heart imaging, lung checks, and more. Use grew fast over those years. It also spread unevenly across patients, plans, and regions.

The team sorts who got these tools by age, sex, illness load, town or country home, and plan type. Gaps in use raise fair-access worries, they argue. Rules and payment choices shape which tools reach which patients. The authors call for study and policy that spread gains more evenly.
pmc-13395251:
Srishti Chauhan, Khurshid Parveen, and Ashutosh Kumar survey, in 2026, gender gaps in food and schooling for children in rural India. Their team visited homes in Jasra block, Prayagraj, and enrolled 486 children aged seven to twelve. Mothers answered questions, and staff measured height and weight. Equal counts of boys and girls took part.

Girls were twice as likely as boys to have never entered school. Stunting, a sign of long-term underfeeding, was also more common in girls at both moderate and severe levels. Thinness ran higher in girls, though that gap did not reach firm proof. The authors call for fairer shares of food and school chances at home.
pmc-13395351:
Winifred Maduko and colleagues listen, in 2026, to communities in Enugu, Nigeria, about antibiotic use and drug resistance. Many people buy antibiotics without prescriptions from chemist shops. The team surveyed 1,281 people and added interviews and group talks. Well over half had used antibiotics in six months, often for malaria, cough, or fever.

Nearly half of users dosed themselves, and few had heard of resistance. Many mistook it for fake drugs or allergy. New habits surfaced, such as use to end pregnancy or as a cleanse. Poverty, poor access, and loose rules drove the pattern. Locals suggested radio jingles, faith leader teaching, and tighter shop rules.
pmc-13395451:
Xiao Yang and Liangzhu Feng track, in 2026, how running demands in World Cup football changed across four tournaments. Tracking data covered 225 matches from 2010 to 2022, across five world regions. The team measured total distance, top speed, sprints, and low and high effort running. Match state and team strength were weighed in the maths.

Top speed, sprint, and easy running rose everywhere over the span. Total distance rose in some regions but not in South America. Hard running fell in Asia, South America, and Europe, with little change in Africa. The authors read a global shift toward speed over sheer volume. Training plans may need region-wise tuning.
pmc-13395551:
Mary Arden G. Guillory and co-authors run, in 2026, a hands-on surgery workshop for junior medical students and measure its effect. Fifty-one students at a Texas medical school rotated through eight skill stations. Stations covered stitching, tube placement, sterile dress, scopes, and more, taught by residents and senior doctors. Surveys before and after scored confidence in each skill.

Confidence rose sharply for nearly every skill. The biggest jumps came in tasks new to classroom students, such as sterile gowning and tube work. Interest in a surgery career did not shift, since it started high. The authors say early practice cements interest without overselling. Comfort in a lab may ease the move to wards.
pmc-13396451:
Gopal and colleagues report, in 2026, the rapid development and field evaluation of a portable CRISPR-based test for mpox. The work unfolded during Sierra Leone's 2025 clade IIb outbreak, which passed 4,000 confirmed cases by July. Their assay, Mpox SHINE, uses the Cas13 enzyme with freeze-dried reagents and room-temperature sample lysis, read by a portable fluorescence device called DxHub, reaching clinics without laboratory infrastructure.

Analytical sensitivity reached 10 viral copies per microliter of sample in laboratory testing. In field validation on 56 clinical specimens in Sierra Leone, the assay matched the reference qPCR test completely, with 100 percent sensitivity and 100 percent specificity in the sample set. It worked directly on unextracted lesion swabs with the same perfect scores, averaging 27.9 minutes to a result against 11.4 minutes for extracted samples. The whole path from genome sequence to validated field testing took under three months.
pmc-13396551:
The editor of the journal and Sage Publications issued an expression of concern in 2026 for a 2020 study of breast cancer cells. The study had claimed that a mix of melatonin, estrogen, and progesterone fights cancer in two cell lines. The notice alerts readers that parts of the evidence are in dispute and should be read with care.

Readers on the PubPeer site flagged that Western blot images for two proteins looked highly similar across different experiments in two tables. The publisher obtained the raw, uncropped images and the authors' explanation, which the editor found plausible but not enough to uphold the claims. The raw images were published as a supplement, and the warning stays in place unless stronger evidence settles the matter.
pmc-13396851:
Rodrigo Torres-Castro writes a 2026 letter to the editor about a study by Groningen and colleagues that sought simple physical tests to estimate peak oxygen uptake in people on hemodialysis. His point is a distinction he calls necessary: physical capacity and physical function are not the same thing, though clinics often swap the words.

A cardiopulmonary exercise test, he notes, measures capacity, the body's ceiling under full effort, and its target value is that peak. Most bedside tests measure function instead: the sit-to-stand test chiefly reads leg strength and power, and even the six-minute walk stays below maximum for most patients. Mixing the two, he argues, can mislabel what a test result means.
pmc-13397451:
Nicolas Jahn and co-authors studied what happens to a light-switching molecule when it is anchored to gold, a pairing of interest for catalysts driven by light. Their 2026 study examines azobenzene thiols, sulfur-tipped molecules that flip shape under light, bound to gold surfaces.

Quantum calculations at two levels of detail, read through a tool called transition density matrix analysis, mapped the molecules' excited states. The bright state that normally absorbs ultraviolet light sits very close in energy to gold's own excitations. The two mix, splitting the state, shifting its color toward the red, and boosting absorption around it, a coupling designers of light-driven surface chemistry must reckon with.
pmc-13400651:
Chun-juan Zhang and Ling Zeng build, in 2026, a combined health index to predict cardiometabolic multimorbidity, the presence of several heart and metabolic conditions together, in middle-aged and older Chinese adults. Their index merges inflammation, blood fat and sugar markers with a frailty score, aiming to capture risk that single measures miss.

Data came from a national aging cohort covering 4,438 people. Higher index values at the start, and higher accumulated exposure over time, both tied to greater risk of developing multiple conditions, rising in a clear dose pattern. People whose index stayed high or climbed faced about five times the risk of the stable-low group. Adding the accumulated measure improved an existing national risk model.
pmc-13400751:
Xuming Zeng, Mengdong Zhang, Xuanxuan Liu, Xionglei He and Li Liu show, in 2026, that selection acting during meiosis itself can swiftly reshape the gene pool of a yeast population. Evolution is usually credited to differences in survival and reproduction. But biased inheritance during spore formation can skew gene frequencies directly.

Tracking a hybrid yeast group over six meiotic generations, and checking single gametes, the team saw fast shifts at many DNA sites. A chromosome swap from one parent formed four-way structures that favored one sorting pattern. That made more unbalanced gametes and shifted nearby gene frequencies. Because such swaps are common, the authors argue this meiotic selection is a broader force than appreciated.
pmc-13401651:
Ngan Thi Tran and co-authors describe a 2026 study developing a machine learning model to flag episodes at risk of drug-induced liver injury using ordinary hospital data. The injury is hard to spot early because no single biomarker defines it, and many existing computer tools focus on the drug rather than the patient.

At Hai Phong International Hospital, linked health record, laboratory, and pharmacy data supplied drug-exposure episodes with baseline liver tests. Cases were defined by the RUCAM causality method. The cohort split by calendar time at the patient level: a development set from 2019 to 2023 and a later prospective validation set from 2024 to 2025. Building and then testing the model on genuinely future data gives a fairer read on whether routine records can stratify liver injury risk before damage shows.
pmc-13402251:
Isabella Pereira Pesenato and a large team report frogs in Bahia, Brazil, carrying two kinds of parasites at once: soft ticks and chigger mites. The hosts were Bokermannohyla frogs caught in Chapada Diamantina National Park, a genus spread across Brazilian habitats with several endangered species. Parasites can weigh on frog survival, and some tick and mite families specialize on this frog group.

Using body shape alone, the team named the ticks as Ornithodoros saraivai, the first record of that species in Bahia State. The mites proved new to science and are described as Hannemania diamantinensis, raising the known Brazilian Hannemania count to eight. Finding both parasites on the same frogs, a pattern called co-parasitism, adds a data point for tracking the health of threatened frog populations.
pmc-13402651:
Takuya Takami and colleagues compare two ways of joining the bowel during keyhole colon surgery: stitching inside the body, or pulling the bowel out through a small cut to join it outside. Their COMMIT analysis drew on a Kyoto multicenter database covering 3213 patients operated between 2018 and 2025, then matched 650 pairs by propensity scores to level the comparison.

Heavy bleeding of 200 milliliters or more struck 2.5 percent of the inside-join group against 4.9 percent of the outside-join group, a gap the authors call significant. Total blood loss, lymph node harvest, and complication rates otherwise ran close, and inside joins tended to take longer, though the time gap flipped by surgical approach in subgroup checks. Margin quality leaned toward the inside method without reaching significance. The authors present inside joining as a way to cut heavier bleeding events.
pmc-13402951:
Daniel M Ripley and Ashleigh Donaldson report, in a commentary, on catch-and-release stress in Greenland sharks, drawing on fieldwork by Yuuki Watanabe and colleagues. Twelve sharks were caught, blood-sampled, fitted with GPS trackers, and released. The question matters because these ancient, slow Arctic sharks increasingly meet fishing gear, and nobody knew how badly capture harms them.

During capture their blood lactate and glucose, markers of exhaustion and stress, ran lower than in many other sharks. Released sharks swam hard for a while, then settled back to normal behavior within about 10 hours, and at least 90 percent survived the 30 days when capture deaths usually strike. Longer hooking did not raise lactate, supporting the idea that a calm, slow life blunts the ordeal. Cool Arctic surface water, near 3 degrees, may help too.
pmc-13403051:
Md Mohiuddin and Md Al Mamun Ahsan write a perspective on autophagy, the cell recycling system, as a double-edged target in cancer therapy. Early in cancer, recycling suppresses tumors. In established tumors it keeps stressed cells alive and blunts chemotherapy. That feeds the resistance that defeats treatment. The balance shifts with tumor stage, which cell groups are present, and the surroundings, which is why simple on-off strategies disappoint.

First-generation blockers such as hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine sensitize some tumors in the lab and have reached trials, but they lack specificity and bring off-target toxicity. The authors spotlight narrower pathways, mitophagy and ER-phagy among them. They argue for precision approaches: selective blockers, markers that warn ahead, and nanoparticle delivery that controls where and when autophagy is touched. Their verdict is promise with discipline.
pmc-13403151:
Stem Cells International retracts a 2021 article that claimed lithium and copper drive bone-forming and vessel-forming coupling in bone marrow stem cells through Wnt and HIF-1 alpha signaling. The retraction was agreed between editor-in-chief Renke Li and publisher John Wiley and Sons. It followed an investigation into image concerns. The probe began when the authors themselves asked to correct figures after repeating experiments.

A PubPeer commenter flagged a staining panel in Figure 6a that closely matched a panel in another group article. The journal probe found more. Corners of Figure 1a echoed Figure 6a. Two Figure 2c panels looked alike, one seemingly a magnification of the other. Near-duplicate staining panels sat within Figure 6a itself. GAPDH blot bands in Figure 4d reappeared flipped in Figure 6c under different stated conditions. With core images compromised, the findings could no longer stand.
pmc-13403551:
Juliana Pineda-Ortega, María Juliana Soto-Chavez, and Ana María Gómez told in 2026 of a young man with type 1 diabetes who grew brain damage usually tied to salt shifts. His blood sugar swung wildly, across a very wide range, and his sodium stayed steady. He also had heart and kidney failure that needed dialysis.

Brain scans showed the pattern of osmotic demyelination, where protective nerve coating breaks down. Other causes were ruled out by the team. They blame sharp sugar swings and unstable body-fluid balance, made worse by dialysis. The case widens the list of triggers doctors should watch for.
pmc-13404251:
Jose Antonio Sanchez Salas and co-authors looked back in 2026 at what shapes bleeding control when people with haemophilia face procedures. Such patients bleed easily around any invasive step, so prep matters a great deal. Their center's records covered 158 procedures in 61 men from 2010 to 2025.

Bleeding response rated good or excellent in about 95.6 percent of procedures overall. Poor or fair response clustered in the heaviest patients, hitting about 27 percent of procedures in men over 100 kilograms. That rate far topped lighter weight bands. Major procedures also trended worse, though less firmly. Weight care before procedures may lift safety, the team suggests.
pmc-13404851:
Theresa Ms Burkard leads a 2026 network study of autoimmune and inflammatory illness after COVID-19 across nine countries. Records come from primary care, hospitals, registries and claims in Europe, the United States and Korea. Follow-up starts on day 91 after infection or a negative test, placing the focus on the post-acute period.

Conditions tracked include POTS, chronic fatigue syndrome conditions, multi-inflammatory syndrome and diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. Patients are followed for up to a year, until an outcome, death or a new infection ends their record. A separate reinfection group shows whether a second infection changes risk. The design uses shared definitions so results can be compared across databases.
pmc-13405451:
Yuan-Lang Brian Chan and colleagues survey glioblastoma care with an Asian focus, in a 2026 review of challenges and future directions. Glioblastoma is among the most feared brain cancers, with high illness and death rates despite rarity. Brain tumour incidence across Asia has risen since 1990 and is expected to keep climbing.

Care quality varies sharply across the region in their account. Centres in Singapore, Japan, South Korea and other wealthy settings offer advanced imaging, awake surgery and combined drug-radiation treatment. Many lower-income countries lack enough trained specialists to match that standard. The review sets out current obstacles and research horizons, framed around closing that regional gap.
pmc-13406951:
Meiqing Yang and co-authors review, in 2026, electrochemical sensors built to find antibiotic leftovers in fish and other aquatic animal foods. Leftover drug traces threaten food safety, so quick, cheap, small-scale tests carry real value for producers and inspectors.

The review covers eight antibiotic families, from fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines to beta-lactams, and sorts sensors into four kinds: direct devices, antibody-based sensors, aptamer-based sensors, and molecularly imprinted versions. Attention goes to how each target behaves electrically, how sensing surfaces are built, how signals get amplified, and how samples are prepared before testing. Stubborn problems remain, notably messy real-world samples and uneven preparation methods, and the authors sketch where development should head next.
pmc-13407951:
Chady Ghnatios and Kazem Fayazbakhsh model, in 2026, why composite tape warps while a robot prints it. Continuous-fibre thermoplastic printing promises strong light parts, yet feedstock deformation during deposition seeds defects and defeats path planning. The team therefore combined experiments with physics-based and learning-based modelling to pin down the drivers.

Residual stress relief, drying, crystallisation, and thermal stress were separated using thermal and mechanical test data. A viscoelastic physics model handled the prepreg mechanics while a stabilised neural differential-equation model captured drying and ordering behaviour. Fitted together, the hybrid reproduced tape conduct well beyond the temperatures it was trained on, a strong sign of validity. Robotic printing trials then validated the model in real printing settings.
pmc-13408051:
Cahit Ucar and co-authors probe, in 2026, a stress-defence protein as an early warning of heart trouble in lupus. People with systemic lupus erythematosus suffer cardiovascular damage long before symptoms. Sestrin-1, an antioxidant guardian protein, was measured in 60 patients and 60 matched healthy controls. It was read alongside heart tracings, heart ultrasound, and neck-artery thickness scans.

Patients carried far less Sestrin-1, about 10 against 17.8 nanograms per millilitre, and their corrected QT interval, an electrical timing measure, ran significantly longer. In adjusted modelling, lower Sestrin-1, a wider left atrium, and longer QT each independently accompanied lupus status, with every unit of Sestrin-1 lowering the odds substantially. The authors propose the protein as a marker of the subclinical cardiovascular alterations accumulating silently in lupus.
pmc-13408151:
Li Wang and co-authors report, in 2026, a phase II trial of a two-in-one immune antibody plus chemotherapy. It targets the hardest-to-treat lung cancer subgroup: advanced non-small-cell tumours with no PD-L1 expression, where immunotherapy usually falters. Cadonilimab blocks PD-1 and CTLA-4 in a single bispecific molecule, and fifty patients received it first-line with chemotherapy.

The headline endpoint was met: 42.1 percent of patients remained progression-free at twelve months, median progression-free survival reached 9.7 months, two-thirds responded, and every patient's disease was at least controlled. Median overall survival had not been reached. Severe treatment side effects hit 52 percent. Blood DNA methylation patterns predicted real responses about five treatment cycles before scans did, and a baseline methylation risk score separated longer from shorter benefit. Controlled trials are warranted.
pmc-13408351:
Andrea Di Pietro and a large Australian team profiled melanoma lymph node samples in 2026 to learn what responding tumours contain that resistant ones lack. T cells that take up residence inside tumours are known guardians against melanoma, yet their part in checkpoint immunotherapy success had not been mapped in full.

Thirty-two samples from untreated, responding, and resistant patients were profiled cell by cell and in place. Responding tumours were rich in resident CD8 and CD4 T cells that had multiplied and switched on killing programmes, while resistant tumours showed exhausted cells stuck in chronic interferon signalling. Only responders held an organised trio of the two resident T-cell types plus a particular dendritic cell. That spatial pattern could become a biomarker for predicting who benefits from treatment.
pmc-13409551:
Jiali Yu and colleagues ask in 2026 whether a trip to the dentist changes what patients do at home afterwards, surveying two hundred forty-six patients at a Guangzhou hospital. Brushing, interdental cleaning, diet, and follow-up attendance were each recorded for the period before and after treatment, and statistical models hunted for what predicts actually adopting prevention.

Twice-daily brushing rose modestly but significantly after treatment. Daily interdental cleaning stayed low at under a quarter of patients, while about three fifths reported changing their diet and just over half kept follow-up appointments. Most demographic traits predicted nothing. The consistent lever was comprehension: patients who understood the preventive advice flossed more, returned more, and followed recommendations more, while merely receiving advice, in whatever format, showed no independent effect. Men brushed adequately less often than women. The message for clinics is to teach until understood, not just to advise.
pmc-13410551:
Sarah Jasat and co-authors update in 2026 a review of what helps or blocks physical activity for people on dialysis. Exercise improves health for these patients, yet few stay active and clinics offer it unevenly. The review uses behavior theory to turn scattered views into a plan for lasting change.

Five databases yielded 17 papers with views from patients and staff. Barriers and supports were mapped onto a standard framework of behavior domains. Patient and staff views lined up closely, and every broad driver of behavior played a part. Training, reshaping clinic settings, teaching, showing examples, and practical support came out as the most workable levers for routine care.
pmc-13410851:
Stephen Olaide Aremu and colleagues survey in 2026 hepatitis B vaccination among adults at a hospital in Nasarawa State, Nigeria. The virus remains a major health threat in sub-Saharan Africa despite a safe vaccine. Adult uptake inside hospital populations was poorly documented, so 1,200 attendees answered a structured questionnaire.

Awareness ran high, and about 94 percent reported at least one vaccine dose. Finishing the full three-dose course was another story: only about 22 percent had done so. Most people said they were willing to complete the course. Cost, poor access to facilities, and fear of side effects topped the barriers named. Knowledge and attitudes scored well overall, which suggests access, not awareness, is the binding problem.
pmc-13410951:
Verena Petzer and co-workers search in 2026 for a simple clue that flags men carrying mutations behind VEXAS, an inflammatory illness described only in 2020. The mutation hides in blood-forming cells and can mimic many diseases, so picking who to test is hard. Oversized red blood cells are a near-constant sign of the syndrome.

The team traced men who had both a blood protein disorder and available marrow samples, narrowing over a thousand cases to 160 for gene testing. They compared mutation rates in men with and without those enlarged red cells. Pairing the size clue with the protein disorder may preselect patients far better than either sign alone, sparing many men an unneeded gene hunt.
pmc-13411151:
Di Zhang and Jing Zhou mine in 2026 a United States side-effect database for safety signals of three drugs used to trigger ovulation in polycystic ovary syndrome. The condition is common, and each drug carries its own risk profile. Knowing those profiles apart can guide personal prescribing.

Of 21,730 reports tied to the condition, letrozole accounted for the vast majority, then tamoxifen, with clomiphene rarely reported. Fatigue surfaced as a shared signal, and tumor progression plus joint pain appeared across all three drugs. Tamoxifen and letrozole reports clustered around tumor-related terms, while clomiphene leaned toward psychiatric and gut events. The authors stress matching drug choice to each patient's risk profile.
pmc-13413451:
Zlatko Kirovakov, Angel Yordanov, and Vasilena Dimitrova gather in 2026 what is known about pregnancy in women with myasthenia gravis. The disease weakens muscles when nerve signals fail at the muscle door. Pregnancy can stir it up or calm it down, with little warning. Their review searched four large databases for group studies, case sets, and strong case reports. The mixed designs ruled out pooled sums, so the team wove the finds into a story form.

Birth results were most often good when care teams watched closely and tuned treatment to each woman. Flares bunched in pregnancy and just after birth, most in wide-spread disease or weak breathing. Past thymus surgery may lower flare rates and brief weakness in newborns, though data stay thin. Joint care by nerve, birth, sleep-drug, and newborn staff is the core advice.
pmc-13415151:
Irene Zapata-Martínez leads a 2026 systematic review of physical activity in people with celiac disease. Gluten triggers immune damage in this condition, and a gluten free diet is the only proven treatment. The reviewers searched five databases for studies linking activity levels or exercise programs to health outcomes.

Fourteen studies qualified, most of them one-time surveys rather than trials. Higher activity sometimes matched better body composition, calmer inflammation, and stronger quality of life. Findings for metabolism and bone density conflicted across studies, often tied to diet differences. The authors call those findings preliminary and ask for long term trials, especially in children.
pmc-13415551:
Abdulhusein and co-authors test, in 2026, whether curcumin, the compound in turmeric, helps broiler chickens withstand coccidiosis, a gut parasite disease, and whether the oil source matters. Their 42-day trial placed 660 one-day-old male Ross 308 chicks into five treatments with six replicates of 22 birds each, crossing soybean or canola oil diets with curcumin at 0.02 percent, and challenged the birds with mixed Eimeria parasites on day 14.

Among challenged birds, curcumin improved weight gain and feed efficiency, trimmed abdominal fat and relative liver and spleen weights, and raised post-challenge antibody levels. It shifted gene expression protectively, suppressing the inflammatory switch NF-kappaB and interleukin-6 while boosting interleukin-10 and the antioxidant master gene NRF2 in the factorial analysis. Gut counts moved the right way too, with more Lactobacillus and less ileal E. coli. The canola oil plus curcumin group showed the clearest recovery, while canola oil alone gave endpoint-specific effects.
pmc-13415751:
Laure Inçaby and co-authors publish the first complete mitochondrial genome of the Pacific spiny dogfish, in 2026. This small North Pacific shark is taken in commercial and bycatch fisheries. Long read sequencing assembled a circular genome of 16,738 bases holding the standard thirty-seven mitochondrial genes.

Thirteen protein coding genes, twenty-two transfer RNAs, two ribosomal RNAs, and a control region make up the set. Adenine and thymine together form about 61 percent of the sequence. Family tree analysis placed this shark as sister to the Atlantic spiny dogfish with maximum support. Gene change ratios suggest strong purifying selection since the pair split.
pmc-13415851:
Roman Jerala and Duško Lainšček comment in 2026 on a molecular velcro trick for precise genome repair, discussing work by Mu and colleagues. Base editors rewrite single DNA letters without cutting both strands, yet the editors are too large for the adeno-associated virus carriers used in gene therapy. Split editors solve size, provided the halves find each other inside cells.

Programmable coiled coil peptides act as the velcro, pairing the halves on arrival. The split editors worked efficiently in living animals, sometimes beating intact versions. Delivery limits have stalled base editing's clinical path, so a modular self assembling design could widen treatable diseases.
pmc-13416751:
Eisendrath and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare heart event during a hip replacement operation. A 63-year-old man had an elective right total hip replacement, and monitoring later showed his ventricles had stopped contracting for twenty seconds during surgery. This event, called ventricular standstill, means the heart's main pumping chambers pause completely.

This patient stayed asymptomatic, with steady blood pressure before, during, and after the pause. No treatment emergency followed, and the event was found only on the heart monitor record. The authors discuss possible triggers, including a vasovagal response, where a nerve reflex slows the heart, and inflammation linked to surgery and anaesthesia. They note that no earlier case in their search described standstill during an operation. The report adds a data point on how long a pause a stable patient can tolerate.
pmc-13418051:
Ma and colleagues report a 2026 study of a chemical tagging system that restrains sugar burning and bowel cancer growth. Many tumors run aerobic glycolysis, a fast but wasteful way to burn sugar. The team found that an enzyme called UFL1 attaches a small tag, UFM1, to enolase 1, a core sugar-burning enzyme, at two specific sites on the protein.

The tag breaks up enolase pairs and lowers its activity, which cuts the flow of sugar burning. Tumors with active tagging grew more slowly in dishes and in animals. A licensed antibiotic, torezolid, strengthened the tagger's grip on enolase and sharply boosted the standard drug 5-FU in lab models, patient-derived tumor organoids, and grafts, without visible toxicity. The work names a new control point in cancer metabolism and a drug pairing ready for further testing.
pmc-13418251:
Yanli Lin, Marne L White, Jihong Zhang, and Todd S Braver track brain networks during mindfulness training, in a 2026 longitudinal study. Sixteen beginners completed up to 24 lab sessions of two meditation styles: focused attention on one object, and open monitoring of whatever arises. Brain waves and self rated mindfulness quality were collected each session, then modelled as networks over time.

The two styles produced distinct brain and experience networks, supporting their theoretical split. Both shared strong carry over of mindfulness skill between sessions, plus opposing effects of front versus back brain alpha rhythms. One size EEG markers mislead, the authors argue; meaning depends on practice type and stage.
pmc-13420651:
Yasunaga and co-authors describe a surgical technique for controlling blood flow during open repair of a chest-and-abdomen aortic aneurysm. Their patient was a man whose aorta had earlier been treated from inside with a stent graft. Clamping the old graft directly looked difficult. So they used inflatable occlusion balloons to seal the aorta from within.

The patient was a 76-year-old man whose earlier repair had developed a pseudoaneurysm, a contained leak beside the original stent. Guided by X-ray imaging, the team placed balloons into each graft limb through leg artery sheaths. Blood kept flowing to the legs through side branches during the operation. A composite graft bridged the size mismatch, and an inner cuff stopped bleeding at the lower join. He survived without major complications. Scans at 12 months showed no recurrence.
pmc-13421151:
Linn Renman, Lotta Andréen and Sahruh Turkmen report a 2026 study from northern Sweden on how women want to be followed up after surgery for endometrial cancer. They compared newly operated patients who had not yet entered follow-up with patients already attending a standard hospital-based programme.

Ninety patients completed questionnaires about their preferences and quality of life. Newly operated patients showed more varied wishes, with about half favouring doctor-led hospital visits, while more than four in five of the experienced group preferred that format. Quality-of-life scores did not differ clearly between the groups. The findings suggest that follow-up plans may need to adapt as patients gain experience of the programme.
pmc-13421251:
Simona S Ghanem, Tara Al-Barazenji, Rehab Badi and Essam M Abdelalim show in a 2026 study that growing stem-cell-derived liver cells as three-dimensional organoids helps them mature. Human pluripotent stem cells can be turned toward liver cells in flat dishes, yet those cells often stay immature, which limits their value for disease modelling and drug testing.

The team grew liver progenitor cells in flat culture, then either kept them flat or gathered them into organoids for the final maturation stage. Organoid cells expressed higher levels of mature liver markers and performed better, secreting more albumin and producing more urea and stored glycogen. Gene sequencing found 1,266 genes differing between the two formats, pointing to the pathways behind the improvement.
pmc-13421451:
Matteo Montalbano and eight colleagues characterise, in a 2026 study, oesophageal adenocarcinomas that have lost one or both of two chromatin-remodelling proteins, SMARCA2 and SMARCA4. These proteins keep DNA packaging dynamic, and their loss marks aggressive cancers elsewhere, yet the pattern in this cancer was undefined.

The team stained 722 removed tumours from a large Western cohort and classed each as intact or deficient. Tumours lacking one or both proteins made up 11.2 percent of cases. They clustered in patients aged 65 and over. They carried MET gene amplification more often, especially after pre-surgery therapy. Digital pathology measured the surrounding scar-like and immune tissue in detail. Survival analysis completes a portrait of a distinct subtype that may need its own treatment logic.
pmc-13422351:
Lu Peng leads an eleven-author team building, in a 2026 study, a living vaccine against the bacterium behind pig pleuropneumonia, a costly disease of swine worldwide. Existing vaccines cover only some of the nineteen known serovars, while a weakened live strain might protect broadly — if it can be told apart from wild infection later.

Starting from a virulent strain, they defanged its three main toxins while keeping them visible to the immune system and deleted a fourth toxin as the tell-tale marker. The strain proved far milder in mice and protected most animals against three different serovars. Pigs tolerated high doses without fever or lung damage, and vaccination protected two thirds to all of the pigs depending on challenge strain.
pmc-13422751:
Pusec and colleagues present in 2026 the case of a patient whose tumor was an IDH-mutant grade 2 astrocytoma, a slow-growing brain tumor. The patient's scans seemed to worsen soon after starting an IDH inhibitor drug, ivosidenib. New bright areas appeared on MRI four months into treatment.

Surgeons removed the bright region one month later and tested it closely. The tumor was still grade 2, with no rise in cell division, no dead tissue, and no new aggressive features. Its growth marker stayed near two percent of cells in samples taken both before and after treatment began. After surgery the patient had radiation and temozolomide chemotherapy and stayed stable for more than 18 months. The case warns that scan changes can mimic true progression.
pmc-13423151:
Nanna Lind, Patricia DeCosta, and Jannet Svensson report translating a United States questionnaire on life with type 1 diabetes into Danish for parents of young children. The parent version of the measure, called T1DAL, asks how the condition shapes daily family life, and moving such a tool across languages demands care to keep its meaning intact.

Following the ten-step international good-practice method, two bilingual Danes produced forward translations, which were merged, then translated back by two native English speakers. Mismatches led to small wording and cultural adjustments, including debate over the answer scale and items reflecting United States health care. Face validation with the target group completed the process, yielding a Danish version ready for wider testing.
pmc-13425851:
Yujun Chen and colleagues ran a 2026 randomized trial of speaking valves for intensive care patients recovering after tracheostomy. A speaking valve redirects air through the upper airway, supporting speech and breathing mechanics, and the team tested whether valve use speeds early mobilization. Reports from the trial link valve use with improved respiratory measures during recovery.

Patients using valves also scored higher on the EQ-5D-5L quality-of-life scale in the study highlights. For intensive care teams, the results support fitting valves early as part of getting tracheostomy patients moving sooner. Care teams can fit the valve check in with the daily round, since the gear is small and the steps are few once staff learn the way.
pmc-13425951:
Svärding and colleagues follow in 2026 adults recovering from surgery for a distal radius fracture, a break near the wrist. They ask whether two psychological traits predict lasting hand disability. The traits are self-efficacy, confidence in handling tasks, and sense of coherence, a feeling that life is manageable and meaningful.

The prospective study tracked 74 patients to three months and 61 to one year after surgery, measuring disability, pain, grip strength, and wrist motion. Disability scores improved greatly over the year, and pain at rest settled, though grip and one bending motion had not fully returned by twelve months. Sense of coherence never predicted disability. Higher self-efficacy for reaching goals linked to lower disability only at the six-month check, so neither trait consistently forecast recovery.
pmc-13426351:
Mohammed Ali Qasem Al-Soufi and coauthors surveyed complementary medicine knowledge among health students in Sana'a, Yemen, in a 2026 single-centre cross-sectional study. Complementary and alternative medicine is widely used in Yemen, while formal teaching for future clinicians stays limited. Their questionnaire reached 318 final and pre-final year medical and pharmacy students at the University of Science and Technology, a 53 percent response.

Knowledge, attitude, and practice scores were split at sixty percent of the maximum to define good knowledge and positive attitude. Results show how prepared Yemeni graduates feel to counsel patients who already use traditional and alternative remedies.
pmc-13427751:
Singh, Singh, and Shukla built LightGastroFormer, a lightweight transformer network. It classifies gastrointestinal diseases from endoscopy and capsule images. It stays small enough for hospital use in practice. Existing deep learning systems often miss either fine local lesion detail or broad context. They also struggle on the field's large, heavily imbalanced image sets.

The model combines a multi-resolution patch tokenizer, lean self-attention, and a gated feed-forward network. That mix catches small lesions without heavy math. It scored 0.94 accuracy on the Kvasir v1 benchmark and 0.95 on Kvasir v2 in the reported tests. On the highly imbalanced Kvasir-Capsule set it reached 0.97 accuracy, with a matching 0.97 F1-score. It did so with no special class-balancing tricks. The whole network carries only 6.42 million trainable parameters. Ablation studies showed each component helps.
pmc-13428151:
Katrin Conen and colleagues surveyed internal medicine residents at McMaster University about training in palliative care, meaning care that eases symptoms and supports people with life-limiting illness. They paired a survey of junior residents with interviews of senior ones to map training gaps.

Twenty-four residents answered the survey, and just over half called palliative care very important for their future work. Only half felt happy with the training they now get, though most felt at ease managing symptoms and talking with patients. Residents felt unsure about local resources and about discussing feeding tubes with patients and families. Senior residents praised hands-on learning but cited weak role models and timetable clashes, and backed required rotations and case-based teaching.
pmc-13428251:
Cibele R. Bonvicino, Maria Julia Cardoso, and Filipe Souza-Gudinho trace, in a 2026 study, the family history of olingos, small tree-dwelling carnivores of Central and northern South America. Olingos are rarely seen and are often confused with kinkajous, their larger relatives. The team read a mitochondrial gene from animals in eastern Amazonia and compared it across the genus. Populations from the Guiana Shield formed a well-separated branch from those in western Amazonia.

The genetic gap between those branches rivals gaps between recognized subspecies elsewhere in the genus. Combined with body differences noted earlier, the authors argue the Guiana Shield animals merit subspecies rank under the name beddardi. Kinkajous caught at the same sites used different local spots, hinting at habitat splits. Field guides and conservation lists for a shy genus get firmer lines.
pmc-13428351:
Lötzsch and colleagues look past neurons to astrocytes, the star shaped support cells of the brain, in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, the commonest drug resistant epilepsy. Surgery tissue offers a direct view. Their 2026 study stains dentate gyrus samples from patients grouped by scarring grade, plus postmortem controls. Four astrocyte proteins that handle glutamate, a key brain signal, and water balance are the targets. The team maps which cell subtypes carry which mix.

In healthy tissue the subtypes kept layer bound protein patterns. In epilepsy those identities survived, but three of the four proteins shifted in amount and place, pointing to faulty glutamate clearance and water control. The fourth protein stayed steady, so the team used it to count cells, and counts matched controls, against claims of astrocyte growth. Reactivity in this disease is a subtype rewiring, not a uniform surge, which matters for drug design aimed at glia.
pmc-13428451:
Fu and team compared six combined triglyceride-glucose and obesity indices as predictors of stroke in 3,400 Chinese adults with early-stage cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, drawn from a national aging cohort. Each index multiplies a blood-based insulin resistance marker by a different body-shape measure, and the study weighed baseline, cumulative, and changing values over time.

During a median follow-up of 8.6 years, 232 participants suffered an incident stroke in the cohort. Two indices stood out consistently: the visceral adiposity version and the body roundness version of the combined score. Each standard deviation rise in the visceral version carried a hazard ratio of 1.36, and the roundness version a hazard ratio of 1.32 at baseline. People whose levels stayed high over time faced roughly double the risk, with hazard ratios of 2.28 and 2.01 respectively, and associations were strongest at syndrome stage 2.
pmc-13428551:
Jui-Fan Kao and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 Taiwanese study, a five-level triage scale used by ambulance crews before hospital arrival. Sorting patients by urgency early can mobilize the right hospital resources in advance. The study covered 9,698 adults carried by ambulance to one major medical center in Taoyuan City during 2023. Researchers compared the newer five-level scale with the older two-level approach on admission, death, and time spent in the emergency department.

The highest urgency level covered about one in ten patients yet accounted for about four fifths of emergency deaths. The new scale predicted death more accurately than the old one by standard measures. Crews labeled far more patients high-acuity than hospital staff later did, a gap the authors note openly. Even so, they cast the scale as an early warning system that shifts emergency care from reaction to preparation.
pmc-13433951:
Amin Sharifi and co-authors brewed a soap-like flood mix in 2026 to squeeze more oil from tight chalk rock under hot, salty strain. Such rock holds vast oil yet yields poorly to plain water floods. Their mix centers on a fresh salt-liquid, blended with twin-tail soaps to pool each kind's strengths.

A screen chain ran from shelf life through mix acts, touch angles, phase play, rock soak, and core floods. The best mix cut oil-water skin pull to a whisper and halved the wet angle, while holding firm at fierce salt and hardness loads. Core floods won near a fifth more oil past sea water. A cheap plastic cut the hero part's rock loss to a low mark. Full checks backed the wet shift and its gears.
pmc-13434151:
Xuan Xue and coauthors offer a 2026 computer method for tracing how old shophouse styles in Singapore grew and changed. Past work relied on hand sorting and gut feeling, which can miss links across many buildings. Their method uses front photos to group styles in a more open and testable way.

The study covers 1,276 old shophouses in Chinatown. Its groups differ from the time order set by city planners in the 1990s. The new order gives more weight to the mixed roots of the buildings across ethnic groups. Urban historians get a model for joining field study with computing.
pmc-13434451:
Leoš Shivaya Valášek and coauthors review a surprise in cell biology in 2026: RNAs long classed as non coding can in fact make small proteins. These long RNAs were once seen as mere regulators that never build anything. New tools now catch tiny products that old screens missed.

The review asks which products are real, how cells choose to build them, and what jobs they do in growth and disease. Some tiny proteins may add a second role to RNAs already known for control work. The authors suggest a fresh name for the coding subset. Field leaders get a map of open tests to run.
pmc-13434651:
Yuhan Zhou and a large team find a choke point in fat burning that can kill tumor cells in 2026. Blocking one late enzyme in the fat burning chain floods cells with a altered fat carrier. Blocking earlier steps does not have the same effect, the team shows.

The piled up carrier harms the cell power units and sparks a rust like cell death. Tumors shrank in mice, immune attack rose, and a common immune drug worked better. Blood levels of the carrier track better outcomes in lung cancer patients. A heart drug that hits the same enzyme mimics the benefit.
pmc-13436451:
János B Biró and coauthors show that an mRNA cleanup system is vital for legume roots and their bacterial partners in 2026. The system, nonsense mediated decay, destroys faulty messages before they do harm. Roots of a model clover lacking the system were tested under low nitrogen.

Crippled roots grew poorly and formed far fewer working nodules. Partner bacteria normally move into root lumps and fix nitrogen for the plant. Many symbiosis pathways shift when cleanup fails, the team reports. Message quality control thus guards a key farm symbiosis. Stronger cleanup might one day lift yields on poor soils.
pmc-13436551:
Loizou, Aharonson, and Hajigeorgiou published a 2026 survey on AI tools in medical school. First-year students now meet chatbots and study apps from day one. Little was known about how new students judge these tools so early. The survey covered 102 students in three classes at one Cyprus university.

Nearly all students knew the tools, and most used ChatGPT on a regular basis. Students rated the tools high for grasping hard topics and saving study time. Trust in medical facts from AI stayed middling, well below the usefulness scores. Wrong answers from chatbots were a common complaint in open comments. Students who had AI training reported spotting fewer errors, a pattern worth follow-up. The authors back adding clear AI guidance into the medical school curriculum.
pmc-13437751:
Anna Wajda led a seventeen-author probe of why methotrexate, the anchor drug for rheumatoid arthritis, helps some and fails others. The team focused on the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, a sensor shaping immunity and drug breakdown. Their 2026 study mixed computer docking, blood cells from patients and donors, and a liver cell model. Cell sorting measured the receptor across immune cell types, and a second drug, tocilizumab, was tested too.

Good responders carried far more of the receptor on these cells than poor responders or patients who could not tolerate the drug. Adding tocilizumab tended to trim receptor-positive monocytes, while pairing it with methotrexate nudged the pattern back toward the good-responder look. The authors float the receptor as a possible blood marker for likely response. They stress the work is exploratory, built on layered lab models rather than a patient trial.
pmc-13437851:
Torrey and co-authors describe a 5-year-old boy whose congenital myasthenic syndrome, a genetic failure of nerve-to-muscle signaling, came from a previously unreported variant in the GFPT1 gene. He presented with low muscle tone, progressive weakness including head drop, cognitive delay, and visual impairment, a combination broader than the classic picture for this gene.

A neuromuscular gene panel found a homozygous missense variant, catalogued as c.1154G>A, and trio sequencing confirmed the recessive inheritance pattern in the family. Brain imaging showed white matter abnormalities with shrinkage of the corpus callosum and cerebellum, features resembling a severe muscular dystrophy group called alpha-dystroglycanopathy. Electrical jitter testing of an eye muscle proved the transmission defect at the neuromuscular junction, while his muscle biopsy notably lacked the tubular aggregates typical of GFPT1 disease. The authors define a muscle-eye-brain form of the syndrome from this case.
pmc-13439351:
Shah and colleagues ask which early warning scores still work for liver transplants kept on a warm perfusion machine. Machine perfusion holds the organ near body state, which may break scores built in the cold storage era. Their 2026 study reviews 126 perfused livers from 2022 to 2024. Seven judged unusable were set aside. Three scores were checked against survival in the 107 livers transplanted.

Two trajectory based scores failed to predict early graft loss at all. The simpler early dysfunction label did. It flagged 40 percent of grafts. Those livers had lower six month survival than the rest, 89 percent against 100 percent. Donor body weight, longer dying and sewing times, and weak pump readings, such as slow lactate clearing, tracked with dysfunction. Some livers past pump cutoffs still did well, so scores should guide, not dictate, organ use.
pmc-13439951:
Fu, in a solo 2026 study, measures whether stored barley seed quietly accumulates harmful mutations. Genebanks keep germplasm, the seed collections that preserve crop diversity, in cold storage for decades. Seeds are periodically regrown to refresh them, and Fu asked how much the harmful mutation burden changes over one such regeneration cycle.

Fu compared RNA sequencing data from paired samples of 90 barley accessions, taken at original storage and after the first regeneration. Two variant-calling methods together identified 1,642 harmful variants spread across all seven chromosomes, mostly rare and carried in single-copy form. More variants appeared after regeneration than before. The estimates suggest each accession gained roughly 28 to 37 harmful variants over the period, showing such accumulation can be measured in practice.
pmc-13440051:
Cheng and Park use first-principles calculations in 2026 on a multiferroic compound, a material that is both magnetic and electrically polar. They argue it actually takes a tetragonal crystal form rather than its widely assumed cubic form. The compound is a lithium iron oxide studied for solar and spintronic uses.

Their computed structure belongs to a tetragonal symmetry group, with the lattice stretched more along one axis than another. It also has a direct band gap, the energy needed to free electrons for current, smaller than in the cubic version. The authors trace the distortion to strong magnetic exchange interactions running along the stretched axis and to iron-oxygen-iron coupling between neighboring atoms. Strong mixing of iron and oxygen electronic states supports that picture. The result could change how the material's light response is modeled.
pmc-13440451:
Carlos Alberto Conceição Santana and colleagues review what happens when faulty cochlear implant electrodes are switched off, reporting a 2026 records study. Implant arrays carry up to twenty-two contacts, and clinicians sometimes deactivate one that misbehaves. Whether hearing suffers was the open question. Charts for 46 users covered hearing tests in quiet and noise, speech recognition at set levels, and electrical measures taken before and after deactivation.

Speech recognition and overall hearing averages held steady after deactivation. Some frequency thresholds shifted on paper without changing daily function. Electrical checks did change: more electrodes showed abnormal resistance, and fewer produced the expected nerve response. Reflex testing was too sparse to judge. The authors conclude that deactivation, when clinically indicated, preserves hearing while still demanding close electrical follow-up for each user.
pmc-13441851:
Chunxiao Zhao, Jinghua Qi, and Yuxiang Chen survey burnout among managers on Chinese metro construction sites, testing a classic demands-and-resources model in a 2026 study. Burnout research hugs healthcare and teaching, leaving high-risk project work thinly covered. A pilot round of 140 replies tuned the scales, then a formal survey gathered 274 valid responses. Burnout was scored through exhaustion, cynicism, and fading professional efficacy.

Exhaustion and cynicism scored clearly higher than lost efficacy. Heavier job demands tracked with more burnout, while richer job resources tracked with less. Workload carried the largest single weight on the demand side. On the resource side, social support, fair distribution, and career development chances protected most strongly. The authors say the model travels well to metro sites, and they name workload control plus those three resources as the practical levers, while noting that one-off surveys show association, not cause.
pmc-13442851:
Justine Gantzer and colleagues sort an ultra-rare tumor, PEComa, by its gene marks in a 2026 study. No gene-based class system guides care for these growths, which spring from vessel-wall cells. Full multi-layer profiling covered an unselected set of tumors from varied body sites.

Joins in the MITF gene family stood out, often fused to actin genes such as ACTA2, ACTG1, and ACTB. Tumors from womb sites carried cell-cycle gene faults, while soft tissue and gut tumors lacked faults in the mTOR path. Gene-use reads split tumors into four subtypes with distinct roots and acts. One stem-like subtype, thick with TP53 and RB1 faults, grew fast, shrugged off mTOR drugs, and may answer immune drugs. The authors offer the map as a first frame for matched care.
pmc-13443851:
Zheyao Gu and colleagues test an AI helper for problem-based glaucoma teaching in a 2026 pilot study. Seventy-four fourth-year medical students split into two arms for the same glaucoma course with the same teacher. One arm learned through problem cases with the DeepSeek assistant at hand, while the twin arm took standard teaching.

The AI arm scored higher on theory tests, with a gap marked at P of 0.003 in their checks. Clinic skill drills also favored the AI arm on questioning, diagnosis logic, and overall craft. Student surveys praised pace and ease gains. Learners did flag a real worry: AI medical advice can err, so trust needs checks. The authors call for bigger cohorts and longer follow-up before wide rollout.
pmc-13444251:
Chuan Zhang and colleagues profile blood fatty acids in very preterm infants in the first day of life in a 2026 study. Early birth cuts the mother's fatty supply short, yet age-tied profiles stayed sketchy. Serum from 105 infants born before 32 weeks faced gas and mass scans that class fats by chain length and bonds.

Younger infants showed deeper fat gaps in the reads. Short-chain fats rose with gestational age, marked at p of 0.003 in their tests, led by butyric and caproic acids. Saturated and single-bond fats also rose with age. Mother's high blood pressure and diabetes left their own marks on fat shares. Twin birth and infant sex shifted shares too. The authors map first-day fats to guide feed plans.
pmc-13446351:
Lizzy Olsen and colleagues watch what a lone fruit fly motor neuron does when every input to a patch of larval muscle is wiped out, in a 2026 study. Most fly muscles take two neuron kinds, a steady tonic one and a burst phasic one. The team cut both kinds from a back muscle field and tracked the survivor over days.

The surviving tonic neuron sprouted fresh branches and built working junctions on the bare muscles, a reach across its own turf. Mere silencing of neighbors, without their loss, sparked no such growth, so physical loss is the trigger. The tonic cell grew its total contact patch only a bit, spreading it thin over home and foreign ground. The phasic kind barely remodeled, a split in talent by cell type.
pmc-13447351:
Aoyi Li and colleagues pool trials of music for people with disorders of consciousness in a 2026 meta-analysis. After severe brain injury, some patients remain in coma or minimally aware states for long periods. Music is safe, cheap and easy to deliver at the bedside, yet its effect on awakening needed a combined verdict.

Twelve randomised trials with nine hundred twenty-six patients, found across databases spanning decades, met the rules. Music groups scored higher on a standard coma scale than control groups and awakened at higher rates. A recovery scale for consciousness also favoured music, while a stroke severity scale favoured music modestly. Trial counts for several outcomes were small, so the authors present music as a promising nursing aid that still needs stronger trials to confirm effects and explain how it works.
pmc-13447451:
Bryan Ford leads a team expanding a web tool that links implementation science frameworks to measurement instruments in 2026 work. Researchers who study how proven practices reach real settings often struggle to find a fitting questionnaire or interview guide for each framework concept. Older repositories were scattered, narrow and uneven in access, prompting a rebuild of an existing models webtool.

Expert review settled thirty-eight descriptive fields for each instrument, and abstraction followed agreed checks for accuracy. The first phase holds fifty-one instruments spanning surveys, interviews and worksheets across quantitative, qualitative and mixed formats. Users can browse by instrument, concept or model, with filters for setting, audience and equity relevance. Guidance on choosing and applying tools is built in, and community input will grow the collection over time.
pmc-13448051:
Lu Sun and co-authors review DNA methylation in bipolar disorder in a 2026 synthesis of mechanism and translation. The disorder cycles between mania and depression, with high relapse and suicide risk, yet its biology stays partly obscure. Methylation, a chemical tag that tunes gene activity without changing DNA code, may form a regulatory layer behind that variety.

Altered tags appear in genes for dopamine, serotonin and other messenger systems, plus growth and ion channel genes tied to brain plasticity and excitability. Candidate signatures include a growth factor pattern, specific sites in a receptor gene and faster epigenetic ageing. Mood stabilising drugs may partly act through such pathways, though evidence stays tentative. Most findings are associations, not causes, and blood tags may not mirror brain, the authors stress.
pmc-13448551:
Dandan Li and colleagues evaluate a one-week mindfulness plus ear acupressure programme before surgery for spinal metastases in a 2026 before-and-after study. Cancer spread to the spine fragments sleep and heightens anxiety and pain before an already major operation. A short, home-practised programme guided by phone audio offered a low-drug option worth testing against standard care alone.

Ninety-two patients treated at one hospital across two years split evenly between the programme era and the earlier standard era. Programme patients reached surgery with lower anxiety and pain scores and lower saliva cortisol, a stress hormone, than controls. Wearable sleep measures also favoured the programme on waking time and night awakenings in the reported results. Since groups came from different time periods rather than random assignment, the authors frame gains as associations needing prospective confirmation.
pmc-13448951:
Changyi Zhou and a large team trace in 2026 how dissolving artery scaffolds provoke the late inflammation that can re-narrow the vessel they were meant to open. These scaffolds, made of poly-lactic acid, support the artery briefly and then break down. Using gene profiling of stented pig arteries and tissue sections over time, the team found the late response dominated by neutrophil extracellular traps, webs of DNA that neutrophils cast out.

Breakdown products overload a calcium channel in neutrophils, triggering those traps, which then push vessel wall muscle cells into a growth state through the TLR2 receptor. To break the loop, the team coated a scaffold with C29, a selective TLR2 blocker. In rabbit arteries the coated device cut neutrophil buildup and reduced the thickened inner layer that causes restenosis. The authors offer the coated scaffold as a precise way to keep lumens open longer.
pmc-13449251:
S Lorena Ament-Velásquez and colleagues trace the evolution of NOD-like receptor genes, intracellular immune sensors, in the Podospora anserina fungus species complex. Some fungal versions of these receptors trigger regulated cell death when the fungus meets a non-self strain, but most remain uncharacterised. Their 2026 study asks how the repertoire changes over evolutionary time.

Most of the receptors carried domains known to execute cell death. Compared with random genes, they turned over faster, carried more protein-changing variation, and evolved more quickly overall. One subgroup, marked by repeat segments with very high internal similarity, arose independently several times. These genes sat near transposable elements, showed high diversity partly driven by a fungal mutation process, and carried signs of balancing selection, with repeat swapping between genes creating new variants. The authors argue fungal immune receptors evolve under diversity-enhancing pressure, consistent with a general immune role.
pmc-13449351:
Vincent Dutreuil and José Paulo Pinheiro present in 2026 full build plans for a laboratory device that stirs liquid samples while holding their temperature steady, printed largely on a 3D printer. Commercial circulation thermostats do this job but are bulky, slow to settle, and costly. Their open-source unit combines a magnetic stirrer with thermoelectric temperature control aimed at electroanalytical and spectroscopic measurements, where samples typically need holding anywhere between minus ten and eighty degrees Celsius.

One unit costs roughly 350 euros to build without chemical probes, controlled by Arduino electronics. The design files sit in a public repository under a Creative Commons license that allows reuse with attribution for noncommercial purposes. The authors frame the device as teaching and research infrastructure: a cheaper, faster-responding alternative that small laboratories can fabricate themselves, adapt to macroscopic or microfluidic cells, and repair without vendor support.
pmc-13449451:
Samuel Lam and a multispecialty panel publish in 2026 a systematic review and practice guideline on imaging children who arrive at emergency departments after blunt chest trauma. Computed tomography finds chest injuries superbly, yet injuries needing intervention are rarer in children than adults, and radiation carries extra lifetime risk for the young. The panel framed four structured questions about when screening chest X-ray or bedside ultrasound can stand in for the scanner.

Screening 10,447 articles left only three retrospective studies fit for pooling, and the quality of proof graded very low. On that thin base the group could answer just one question. For children under eighteen whose first screening chest imaging shows nothing or only minor findings, they conditionally recommend against routine chest CT to hunt injuries needing procedures or surgery. The guideline's honesty about its own limits is part of its message.
pmc-13449651:
Ramon Joel Seastres and colleagues pool in 2026 fifteen studies of 4,948 adults to find what predicts a good neurological outcome for people who survive a cardiac arrest inside a hospital. Predicting recovery in this group is notoriously hard, and the survivors are a selected slice of all arrests. Quality and certainty were graded formally, and most evidence landed at low certainty.

A first shockable heart rhythm tripled the odds of favorable recovery, the single strongest rhythm signal. Cardiac causes, an admission diagnosis of heart attack or heart failure, male sex, and shorter resuscitation all helped. After circulation returned, emergency heart catheterization carried the largest association, an odds ratio of 4.55, with intensive monitoring and membrane oxygenation also favorable. The authors stress that findings apply only to patients discharged alive, and that better prospective studies are needed before these factors guide family conversations.
pmc-13452151:
Pandey and colleagues reviewed in 2026 why HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria medicines run out in low- and middle-income countries, and what those stock-outs cause. Their systematic review screened over ten thousand records and included 56 studies on antiretroviral, anti-tuberculosis, and antimalarial drug shortages.

Causes clustered around inefficient supply chains, slow procurement, weak funding, poor governance, and bad demand forecasts. The harm was direct: patients missed doses, drug resistance grew, and illness and deaths rose, while families paid more out of pocket and programs paid emergency prices. Fixes ranged from emergency buying and redistribution in the short term to buffer stocks, more suppliers, and digital inventory systems for the long term. The authors stress that most causes are preventable with stronger, better financed supply systems.
pmc-13453951:
Alicja Braczko and nine co-authors show a way to watch mitochondria breathe in a piece of living human artery, in real time. The tissue is the left internal mammary artery, a vessel often borrowed for heart bypass grafts. Their 2026 study takes segments during bypass surgery and tests them on a Seahorse analyzer, a bench tool that tracks oxygen use.

A standard stress test read out the artery's base and peak breathing rates while the tissue stayed intact. In parallel, a liquid separation method measured the tissue's energy carrying nucleotides, which report on energy status and redox balance. Pairing the two reads gave a fuller picture of the graft's energy health than either alone. The authors present the workflow as a first for intact human vessel tissue and a base for vessel metabolism studies.
pmc-13454051:
Richard Chilipa and Clement Nyirenda review neuro fuzzy systems, which marry neural learning with fuzzy rule based reasoning, for the Internet of Medical Things. Connected health gear needs analytics that adapt in real time and can explain their calls. Their 2026 review gathers 55 journal papers from 2020 to July 2025 across six publisher libraries.

Half the papers used neural tuned designs, while hybrid and deep variants split most of the rest, and only seven used evolving systems that learn on the fly. Prediction tasks led the uses, ahead of detection tasks. Reporting was thin: 61.8 percent of papers never said where the system runs, and only 10.9 percent timed its speed. Nearly all proof was retrospective or simulated. The authors list open gaps in live adaptation, device fit, and bedside clarity.
pmc-13454651:
Hiroki Sato and colleagues, writing for a Japanese resuscitation study group in 2026, ask whether regions that test hearts more often suffer fewer cardiac arrests outside hospitals. Cardiac arrest away from care remains a major public danger, and rates vary by place. The team ran a prefecture-level ecological study covering 2014 to 2023.

Cases came from the national Utstein registry, which logs nearly every ambulance-treated arrest in Japan. The analysis kept arrests of presumed cardiac origin in adults aged 40 to 74. Testing intensity came from national insurance claims data, which record outpatient heart tests per prefecture. Risk profiles for each prefecture, such as metabolic health, came from the same source. By joining the two datasets, the authors test whether heavier local testing aligns with lower arrest rates after accounting for those risk profiles.
pmc-13454751:
Sofija Ivanova and six colleagues explore, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how diet relates to gut leakiness and inflammation in people with type 1 diabetes. Food choices can stir gut imbalance and low-grade inflammation in this condition. Participants logged a day of eating, kept three-day food records, and answered a frequency questionnaire, while blood and stool markers were measured.

Higher intake of hot drinks and legumes paired with higher levels of a key inflammation marker. Lower intake of protein, fat, energy, and fiber paired the same way. Red meat intake tracked with higher levels of a bacterial toxin marker in blood. Stool inflammation readings rose with protein intake. The authors call the study exploratory and ask for feeding trials that test whether changing diet can tighten the gut barrier in type 1 diabetes.
pmc-13454951:
Goryanin and colleagues present a computer model of aging in 2026 that treats aging itself as an outcome drugs can change. Their model joins four parts. It tracks drug action on body chemistry, side effects, and damage and repair states tied to frailty. It also tracks blood markers of metabolic health, meaning how the body handles sugar and fat. The drugs are semaglutide, SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin, and rapamycin.

The team tuned the semaglutide part against STEP trial results, matching weight loss, blood sugar gains, and nausea within limits. Wider tests showed strong metabolic effects for semaglutide but almost none on blood sugar for rapamycin. Simulations found two best mixes. One joined a GLP-1 drug, an SGLT2 inhibitor, and metformin for metabolic gain. The other added rapamycin to that base for aging related gain. The two goals, the authors stress, do not point to the same treatment.
pmc-13456651:
Jialin Fan leads an eleven-author review, from 2026, of tiny RNA molecules that help set how fast bodies age and how long they live. MicroRNAs are short strands that tune whole gene networks at once. Across worms, flies, and mammals, their levels shift with age, and they grip conserved pathways covering insulin signals, growth control, cell cleanup, and inflammation.

Eating less, the most reliable life-extending trick known, rewrites these RNA programs toward stress resistance and metabolic thrift. The review weighs that evidence species by species. It also tours the diagnostic promise of microRNAs floating in blood and urine, which could betray biological age without a biopsy. The authors close by imagining combined RNA networks and aging clocks as the next tools for measuring, and perhaps slowing, the aging process.
pmc-13457351:
Saifullah and colleagues in Chicago scanned in 2026 the kept brains of 912 old folk to split the shrink marks of two late life brain ills. One ill is Alzheimer's change, the plaque and tangle path.
