Brains were classed by post death reads: one ill, the twin, both, or none.

Each ill alone left the mid time zone thin against clean brains. Both ills at once spread the loss to front and side zones too. The twin ill alone cut the front of the sea horse zone, the memory hub, most. Step ups in the twin ill shrank that hub more than step ups in the first ill. The split may sharpen scans in life, the team says.
pmc-13457451: Heavier comorbidity burden steering initial treatment choices in older women with gynecologic cancer. Lin Tang, Yuhang Liu, and others study the retrospective cohort. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is gynecologic oncology. It links comorbidity burden to initial treatment allocation decisions in the cohort.
pmc-13458151:
Daniel Lagos and co-authors studied skin cells from patients with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A, an inherited nerve disorder caused by mutations in the MFN2 gene. MFN2 normally helps mitochondria, the cell's power stations, merge, while a partner protein called DRP1 splits them apart. In their 2026 study, the team compared two disease mutations, L248H and M376V, in patient cells and mouse cells, filming living mitochondria and measuring energy production.

Both mutations broke mitochondrial merging, but they pushed splitting in opposite directions. Cells with L248H formed overly long mitochondria with stalled fission and burned more oxygen, while cells with M376V fragmented their mitochondria with excessive fission and leaned more on sugar fermentation. The difference tracked with distinct chemical tagging of the DRP1 splitting protein. Therapies adjusting mitochondrial dynamics, the authors argue, must account for which mutation a patient carries.
pmc-13458351: The team construct a massive public database to support ending the HIV outbreak. The project provides thorough data resources for the national EHE initiative. The 2026 Europe PMC paper shares useful lessons from large-scale database making. It addresses privacy protection, data quality, and accessibility hurdles in full.
pmc-13459251:
Bingbing Tuo and co-authors measured how evenly China's price negotiated cancer drugs are spread across its 31 provinces. Since 2016, national negotiations have cut prices and expanded insurance coverage of anticancer medicines, but availability can still depend on local wealth. Their 2026 study collected province level data on which hospitals and pharmacies stock the negotiated drugs. It computed gap indices tied to provincial income and broke those indices down to find what drives them.

Both indices showed pro rich gaps: hospitals scored 0.125 and pharmacies 0.139 on the concentration measure used. Medical insurance spending and inpatient costs together explained much of the hospital side gap, while pharmacist numbers drove the pharmacy side gap. Even within one disease the pattern held, with two breast cancer drugs showing higher gap scores of 0.244 and 0.223. The authors urge targeted supply measures for poorer, remote areas.
pmc-13459451:
Yang Fu and co-authors investigated low platelet counts, called thrombocytopenia, in children with lupus, an autoimmune disease that attacks many organs. Their 2026 study reviewed 236 children diagnosed with childhood onset systemic lupus erythematosus at a Fudan University children's hospital between 2020 and late 2025. The team compared children who had low platelets at diagnosis with those who did not. Blood counts, complement levels, and autoantibody patterns were examined to find what predicts the complication and what it signals clinically.

That group showed more white cell reductions and more frequent positivity for antiphospholipid antibodies, anti-beta2-glycoprotein antibodies, and lupus anticoagulant, all markers tied to clotting problems. pmc-13460051:
Meng Zhang leads a Beijing team reporting in 2026 on six patients whose hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, an inherited vessel disorder, was complicated by pulmonary hypertension and treated with bevacizumab. Experience with this drug in that rare pairing is scarce. Charts from Beijing Anzhen Hospital between 2021 and 2024 were reviewed, and matched comparison groups with other forms of high lung blood pressure set the context. Five patients completed follow-up after a three-month starter course.

Compared with the other groups, these patients pumped far more blood per minute while their vessels offered unusually little resistance. After that course, every followed patient improved in activity class, hemoglobin, a heart strain marker, and a combined scan measure of right heart performance. Two patients improved despite starting with lower cardiac output.
pmc-13460951:
Shahdad Ahmadi and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a probiotic bacterium taken from camel milk can ease acute inflammatory pain in rats, benchmarking it against acetaminophen. Forty-two male Wistar rats were split into seven groups, including pain controls and three groups fed Lactobacillus plantarum strain NIMBB003 at rising doses. Only the highest dose worked, cutting pain behavior in both phases about as strongly as the painkiller did, while lower doses showed nothing significant. The high dose and acetaminophen each lowered the inflammatory signals IL-1 beta, IL-2, and IL-6. The authors propose the strain as a candidate alternative for inflammatory pain.
pmc-13461351:
Federico Caporaletti and co-authors used an X-ray technique that watches molecular motion at specific length scales to settle how two kinds of movement in supercooled liquids relate. When a liquid is cooled fast enough to skip crystallization, its molecules rattle inside cages of neighbors in a fast secondary process, then escape in the slow process that sets flow. Their 2026 study examined a hydrogen bonded glass former. It found the two processes are not independent: the fast rattling is the prelude to escape.

Before diffusion begins, the mean squared displacement of molecules grows more slowly than linearly, the signature of this constrained rattling in their measurements. The team reads the secondary relaxation as molecules testing the cage walls just before breaking out, linking it directly to the onset of flow. Tying this relaxation to diffusion sharpens predictions for pharmaceutical glasses and other materials that must not crystallize in storage.
pmc-13461851:
Zhichang Liu and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, that the gene PLAU helps head and neck cancer reshape its surroundings and spread. The cancer type starts in flat cells of the mouth, throat, and voice box. A halfway change, called partial epithelial-mesenchymal transition, lets cells loosen from neighbors and move. The team screened changed genes in public data to find drivers of that change.

Twelve candidate genes emerged, and PLAU stood out as tied to the halfway state. PLAU levels tracked closely with two marker proteins of that state in 75 tumor samples. Turning PLAU down slowed growth, invasion, and movement in lab dishes. Survival models named PLAU a sign of worse outlook, and high levels went with spread to neck lymph nodes. The authors conclude PLAU speeds the rebuilding of tissue around the tumor through that change, marking it as a target for blocking spread.
pmc-13462051:
Fukuda, Kobayashi, and Wakashima built in 2026 a scale to measure how Japanese adults explain mental disorders to themselves. People differ in whether they see such illness as medical, moral, psychological, social, or spiritual, and those views shape what help they accept. The team drafted a scale from an older three-style framework, added social and spiritual styles, and tested it in an online survey of 928 adults using five disorder stories.

Fukuda's analysis settled on 24 items in six factors. Two of them, biologising and medicalising, split apart even though they began as one idea, which the authors flag as exploratory. Most subscales held together well and scored stably over time, but the psychologising part was weak inside and needs better items. Scores lined up with related attitude measures as predicted. The authors present the scale as a first tool for mapping lay views of mental illness in Japan.
pmc-13462251:
Baifeng Chen and colleagues reviewed how infected urachal cysts in babies respond to treatment without surgery. A urachal cyst is a leftover pouch near the bladder that can infect; the study covered first-time infections in infants under one year.

The series covered 49 infants treated between 2012 and 2026 with antibiotics alone or antibiotics plus needle drainage. Belly-button signs were the commonest presentation, in about 79.6 percent, and three quarters had formed an abscess. Overall, 79.6 percent of cysts cleared fully without surgery, and only 12.2 percent of infants eventually needed an operation. Younger babies needed drainage more often, Chen notes, and every surgical case declared itself within three months.
pmc-13462551:
Zhiyan Li and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, a lactate-shuttling protein called SLC16A3, also known as MCT4, as a driver and target in liver cancer. Liver cancer remains lethal, with high rates of return, spread, and drug resistance. Tumors rewire their fuel use, and this protein helps dump acid so cancer cells keep burning sugar fast. It runs high in cancers and tracks with aggressive behavior.

High levels mark worse outlook, giving it prognostic value. Blocking it could starve tumors of their metabolism and reopen them to therapy. The authors frame the protein as a window into tumor metabolism and a target. They call for strategies built around it to improve outcomes in liver cancer.
pmc-13463151:
Yixiang Qian and Chenli Zhang review, in a 2026 article, microecological agents, meaning prebiotics, probiotics, and their combined synbiotic forms, as treatments aimed at the gut-kidney axis in kidney disease. Diseased kidneys often come with disturbed gut microbes, a build-up of uremic toxins healthy kidneys would clear, and body-wide inflammation. Feeding helpful microbes or their food may rebalance the gut, seal its barrier, lower toxin entry, and calm inflammation and oxidative stress.

Across chronic kidney disease, trials suggest these agents can slow the slide in kidney function. They may also ease companion problems such as mineral and bone trouble, heart and brain vessel events, and high uric acid. Evidence is patchy: products, doses, and timing differ so much between studies that firm verdicts blur. The authors sort the findings by disease, weigh their uneven quality, and sketch strategies for turning gut-based support into standard kidney care.
pmc-13463551:
Chi and colleagues build a star-shaped carrier that loads boron for a type of cancer care. The care, called boron neutron capture therapy, kills tumour cells with beams once boron sits inside them. Boron-rich units called carboranes hold much boron. Yet they mix poorly with water. The team tied twenty carboranes to one star-shaped chain. The result still mixed well with water. It could dissolve at high strength in water too.

The carrier did not harm head and neck cancer cells in lab tests. A tagged form lit up on PET scans in healthy mice. Blood held the tag well, and the kidneys cleared it. That path sets up later tumour tests.
pmc-13464051:
Soares, Barbosa, and Stolf ask whether a host's immune response can change a parasite's strength in this 2026 study. The parasite, Leishmania amazonensis, causes skin disease and lives inside host cells in a form called the amastigote. The team compared parasites taken from normal mice with those from nude mice, a strain that lacks T cells, the immune cells that coordinate attacks on invaders.

Both mouse groups were infected for 13 weeks before parasites were collected from footpad lesions. Parasites from normal mice survived better and multiplied more once cultured. They also infected cells more aggressively, forming larger internal compartments, and caused stronger disease when placed into new hosts. The authors conclude that living under T-cell pressure had, paradoxically, produced hardier and more virulent parasites.
pmc-13464251:
Jeremy Wells and four co-authors report an emergency valve-in-valve rescue for a failed artificial heart valve. Tests showed his placed valve leaking badly backward, flooding his lungs and starving his heart.

The leak stopped at once, and pressure steadied. Emergency valve-in-valve work, the authors show, can rescue patients too unstable for open surgery.
pmc-13464751:
Abdilahi Abdi Ibrahim and three co-authors build a warning model for a rare flare-up after cryptococcal meningitis, a fungal brain infection. Small numbers mean the tool needs wider testing, the authors caution, before clinics can lean on it.
pmc-13466651:
Qiumei Gu and colleagues review eyes with wet macular disease that responded poorly to standard injections and were switched to double doses of the same drug, in a 2026 real-world study. The drugs block a vessel growth factor that drives leaking in the back of the eye. Eyes qualified only after at least three standard injections left active leaking or swelling.

Evidence for this doubling strategy has been thin, which is the gap the authors set out to fill.
pmc-13466751:
Linda Ficociello and colleagues compare hospital use between dialysis clinics that monitor blood volume during treatment and matched clinics that do not, in a 2026 study. Nearly twenty-five thousand patients entered the analysis. Adjusted rates of hospital visits overall and of fluid-related visits ran lower where monitoring was routine, as did days spent in hospital. Monthly clinical measures were tracked as secondary outcomes. Real-world proof for this monitoring has been limited, which the authors aim to supply.
pmc-13466951:
Seal and colleagues ran a double-blind trial in 2026 to test whether bisphenol A, a chemical in many consumer plastics, directly lowers insulin sensitivity in healthy adults. pmc-13468851:
Marco Meloni and co-authors report in 2026 long-term results for injecting a patient's own blood cells into the legs of people with ischemic diabetic foot ulcers. pmc-13469251:

pmc-13469751:

pmc-13470151:

pmc-13471451: Coastal botanists conduct comprehensive integrated environmental, phytochemical, and genetic assessment of Avicennia marina mangrove populations. pmc-13471551:

pmc-13471651:

pmc-13473251:

pmc-13473751:

pmc-13474651:

pmc-13474851:

pmc-13474951:
Walshe and a large team report a scandium-based porous material in this 2026 chemistry study. pmc-13478051:

pmc-13478251:

pmc-13479551:

After adjusting for how old each district's population was, that link faded to non-significance, while the models explained far more variation. Stronger exercise showed its own pattern in the adjusted results. The author cautions city policymakers that raw district comparisons mostly reflect demographics, and walking promotion should be judged with age structure in view.
pmc-13479951:

The pandemic caused a temporary dip in treatment starts, visible in the yearly counts. rochester-knockings-1851:
Raps in a farm house launch a faith in Rochester Knockings!, a brief tract of 1851. No name stands on the tract. It tells of the Fox girls of Hydesville, near Rochester, whose house raps seemed to reply to asks in code. A dead pedlar, they claimed, spoke from the grave through the knocks on wall and floor.

Crowds flocked to hear the raps in halls. Sages came to test and scoff. The tract is the first print cry of the whole wave. It is the birth note of a world faith.
ruskin-stones-venice-vol-1-1851:
John Ruskin published The Stones of Venice, Volume 1, in 1851, subtitled The Foundations. Ruskin studies Venetian buildings as records of moral and social life. This volume lays out the elements of architecture: walls, roofs, openings, and ornament. He judges each form by truth to nature and to its materials.

Ruskin praises Gothic craft against the machine-made work of his own century. Imperfection, for him, is a sign of free and living labor. The book began his campaign to remake English taste. Architects and reformers took its lessons to heart. It remains a founding text of the Arts and Crafts spirit.
smith-pearl-great-price-1851:
Franklin D. Richards published the first Pearl of Great Price at Liverpool in 1851, a slim pamphlet with lasting weight. He gathered pieces of Joseph Smith's work for British Saints who lacked the American prints and papers. Extracts from the Book of Moses and the Book of Abraham stand at its heart, word for word.

Smith's own history and the Articles of Faith, his crisp list of beliefs, complete the little book for its first readers. What began as a missionary pamphlet grew into one of Mormonism's four standard works in time. The 1851 edition shows that scripture in embryo, before canonization fixed its place in the church.
spencer-social-statics-1851:
Herbert Spencer published Social Statics in 1851, his first statement of a social system. The book sets out the law of equal freedom. Each person, Spencer argues, may do as he wills so long as he does not infringe the equal freedom of others. From that law he derives rights to property, speech, and trade.

He opposes state churches, state education, and state poor relief as breaches of the law. Land ownership receives a radical chapter that he later softened. The book became a bible of classical liberalism in its strictest form. Later Spencer revised some claims, yet the core principle endured. It remains his most quoted early work.
the-american-phrenological-journal-and-r: The American Phrenological Journal and Repository, 1851. The repository. This book preserves that periodical. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume one of Casanova's memoirs: childhood in Venice. The great adventurer's beginnings, frankly told. Where the legend starts. First volume: a Venetian childhood, where the legend begins, a Venetian childhood frankly told, childhood in Venice frankly told.
the-winds-of-the-world-pg6751: Talbot Mundy — the master of Indian adventure — sets this novel in the Northwest Frontier during the Great War. British officers, native princes, and German agents collide in a tale of loyalty tested by intrigue. Mundy's deep knowledge of India gives the excitement an authentic, exotic flavor.
tob-10051:
Genesis stands first in the Old Testament, in the King James Version's 1611 English, with Moses named in the catalog as its traditional author. God forms the world and humankind, Adam and Eve fall, and Cain kills his brother Abel. Noah rides out the flood that wipes the slate nearly clean.

After the flood and the scattering at Babel, attention narrows to one family. Abraham receives the promise of a great nation, and his line carries the story through Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph into Egypt. These founding stories of Judaism and Christianity are told here in the stately wording generations of English readers knew by heart.
tob-13151:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton published The Coming Race in 1871, sending a fictional explorer deep underground into a hollow earth. There rules the Vril-ya, a superior race wielding vril, a psychic energy that powers their utopia and their weapons alike. The narrator tours their cities as guest, student, and eventually a problem to be solved.

Part satire of Victorian society, part prophecy of energy weapons and a master race, the novel coined a word that haunted occultists for decades. Some later readers took vril literally, which Bulwer-Lytton may not have intended. The book stands as science fiction before the genre had a name, and as a warning dressed as a wonder tale.
tob-4151:
Al-Ghazali, the great theologian of Islam, wrote the Alchemy of Happiness in Persian as a short form of his Revival of the Religious Sciences. Claud Field translated it into English in 1910. Ghazali treats the soul as a kingdom to be ruled: its diseases are pride, envy, and greed, and its cure is disciplined worship.

Self-knowledge opens the book, since a person who does not know his own soul cannot know God. Marriage, food, and friendship all receive a physician's calm advice. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. The little work remains Ghazali at his most pastoral.
tob-4185-78851:
Plutarch's table talk, political counsel, and words of comfort fill much of volume three in Goodwin's Moralia. Friends at dinner debate questions large and small, from why leaves change color to what music suits a feast. The talk shows philosophy as good company.

Other essays advise rulers, console the grieving, and discuss the training of children. Plutarch moves easily between the state and the nursery. His range explains why later ages kept copying him when other essayists vanished. Goodwin's middle volume gives the fullest taste of that range, in steady Victorian prose that lets the Greek shine through.
un-ga-res-a-69-51:
The illicit trade in small arms fuels wars far from any factory, and Resolution A/69/51, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, renews the world plan against it. The text recalls the vote of the year before, and the first of the chain, passed on Christmas Eve 2001. At its heart stands the Programme of Action of 2001, the world deal to bar, fight, and wipe out the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons.

Full work on that plan is pressed as a must. So is work on its twin, the world tracing tool of 2005, which lets states mark arms and track the illicit ones fast and with trust. States had pledged themselves to both plans at past review meetings, and the vote holds them to it.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/51 of the General Assembly is the annual review of work against the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons. It stresses full implementation of the 2001 Programme of Action and the International Tracing Instrument. It endorses the report of the Fifth Biennial Meeting of States held in June 2014. It fixes the follow-up calendar: an open-ended meeting of governmental experts in New York on 1–5 June 2015, and a third review conference in 2018. States are urged to report nationally, control brokering, and match assistance needs with resources.
un-sc-res-1351:
UNDOF, the observer force on the Golan Heights, won a routine renewal in May 2001. On 30 May 2001 the Security Council extended its mandate for six months. The term ran until 30 November 2001. The Secretary-General had reported on the force earlier that month. The Council restated its standard terms without change.

The parties again had to carry out resolution 338 right away. That text from 1973 called for a ceasefire and peace talks. The Secretary-General owed a report when the term closed. It would describe events and steps taken toward 338. These six-month renewals had kept a thin blue line between Israel and Syria since 1974.
un-sc-res-1451: Filed in the official record under number 1451, this Council resolution is catalogued with a 2002 date. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1551:
Bosnia and Herzegovina was taken up by the Security Council in Resolution 1551, adopted on 9 July 2004. NATO planned to end its stabilization force, SFOR, by the end of 2004. The European Union would launch its own mission, with troops, from December 2004. Refugee returns still lay at the heart of lasting peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps SFOR running for six more months under one command. Member states may take all necessary measures to enforce the peace deal and defend the force. The existing status rules will cover the new European mission while it builds up. Local leaders bear the main duty for carrying out the Dayton deal, including handing suspects to the war crimes tribunal.
un-sc-res-1651:
Sudan's wars frame this short decision of 21 December 2005. The Council backed the African Union peace talks at Abuja on Darfur. It also backed full use of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement for the south. At the same time it deplored the violence and atrocities in Darfur. Earlier resolutions had placed sanctions on Sudan and set up a panel of experts to track them.

Here the Council extends that panel's mandate until 29 March 2006. The panel must report before its term ends. Its report goes through the sanctions committee. It covers how the arms and travel measures are working in practice.
un-sc-res-1751: Resolution 1751, from 2007, records a Security Council decision in the official wording held by English Wikisource. The document's structure is disciplined: what the members recalled, what they noted, and then what they decided, in numbered steps. Preserving that structure is preserving the decision, which is the work this entry does for later readers in this collection.
un-sc-res-1851:
Members of the Council adopted Resolution 1851 on Piracy off Somalia on 16 December 2008. Pirate attacks had grown bolder in the past six months. The tanker Sirius Star had been seized far off the coast of Kenya. Somalia's weak government could not police its own waters or try captured pirates.

The text lets states working with that government take all needed steps inside Somalia against piracy. The power runs for twelve months from an earlier vote that month. It backs deals that place law officers from regional states aboard foreign warships. Those shiprider deals help put captured pirates on trial instead of setting them free.
un-sc-res-251: Israel held a military parade in Jerusalem on 2 May 1968, and the Security Council answered the same day. In resolution 250 (1968), adopted on 27 April, the Council had unanimously decided against the parade. The Secretary-General reported on 26 April and again on 2 May. The Council deeply deplored that Israel went ahead in disregard of that unanimous decision. The whole text is this single act of censure, with no further order attached.
un-sc-res-351:
Security Council Resolution 351, adopted on June 10, 1974, recommended Bangladesh for membership in the United Nations. Bangladesh had broken from Pakistan in 1971 after a war marked by mass killing and a vast flight of refugees. Its first bid for a seat had met a Chinese veto in 1972, cast in support of Pakistan; by 1974 the path had cleared.

Pakistan itself had come to accept Bangladesh, and the Assembly seated the new state that September. The resolution is short and formal, yet it closed one of the sorest disputes left from the partition of British India. Bangladesh took its place as one of the world's most populous nations.
un-sc-res-451:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed in June 1979 with talks in view. On 15 June 1979 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 December. The parties had agreed the force should stay. Cyprus's government said the island's conditions still required it. The Secretary-General's May report guided the decision. A ten-point agreement had just set terms for new intercommunal talks.

The parties had to pursue those talks without delay. The Council wanted them steady and aimed at results. The Secretary-General kept his good offices mission. He owed a report by 30 November 1979. China did not take part in the vote. The renewal was routine in form, but the talks it backed soon stalled again.
un-sc-res-51:
Kashmir's fate was still being fought over in the spring of 1948. On 3 June 1948 the Security Council returned to the dispute between India and Pakistan. It restated its three earlier Kashmir resolutions of that year. A United Nations commission for the two countries already existed. Resolution 47 had given that commission its main duties. Those duties centered on ending the fight and arranging a free vote.

The Council now directs the commission to travel to the disputed areas without delay. The work set by resolution 47 comes first. The commission must also study points raised by Pakistan's foreign minister. It would report on those points when it judged the time right. The vote passed with three abstentions.
un-sc-res-651:
The observer group watching the Iran-Iraq cease-fire received a new term on 29 March 1990. The group, called UNIIMOG, had been set up in 1988. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 22 March, covered its work. The settlement plan of Resolution 598, from 1987, still had not been carried out in full. Resolution 651 records the renewal.

The Council called once again on the parties to carry out Resolution 598 at once. That text had set the terms for ending the Iran-Iraq war. UNIIMOG's mandate was extended for six more months, until 30 September 1990. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the steps taken toward the 1987 settlement. The observers stayed on the border line while the peace they guarded remained unfinished.
un-sc-res-751:
Somalia's collapse brought the first United Nations operation there in April 1992. On 24 April 1992 the Security Council established the United Nations Operation in Somalia. Fighting factions had signed a ceasefire in Mogadishu on 3 March. Letters of agreement followed in other towns. The Secretary-General reported on the plan days before the vote.

The Council first sent fifty observers to watch the Mogadishu ceasefire. It also agreed in principle to a security force under the Secretary-General's special representative. That force would guard relief work as aid groups faced a famine. The mission, UNOSOM, was the start of a much larger involvement. Its limits soon showed as the country slid further into war.
un-sc-res-951: United Nations Security Council Resolution 951, adopted on 21 October 1994, is a brief procedural text about the International Court of Justice. A Russian judge of the court, who had served since 1985, died on 28 September 1994. His seat stood open for a term that ran until February 1997. The Council sets 26 January 1995 as the day to elect his replacement. The Council and the General Assembly, at its forty-ninth session, vote on that day.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The Golan watch gained its usual six months in the spring of 2001. On 30 May, the Council adopted Resolution 1351 without dissent. The Secretary-General's report on the observer force had come in that month. The force, UNDOF, keeps Israel and Syria apart along the truce line. It has done so since 1974.

The text calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 at once. That 1973 order pairs a truce with peace talks. The mandate then runs to 30 November 2001. A report from the Secretary-General is due at the end. It must cover events in the area and steps toward Resolution 338. The chain of such renewals has never broken.

The Golan Heights observer force is renewed once more on 17 December 2002. UNDOF stays in place for six months, until 30 June 2003, watching the separation between Israeli and Syrian forces. The Council called on the parties to carry out its resolution 338 of 1973 without delay. It also asked the Secretary-General to report at the end of the period on developments and on steps taken toward that goal.

Chad's seat was handled in the same busy sitting as its neighbors' bids. On 23 August 1960, the Council adopted Resolution 151 without dissent. The Republic of Chad had claimed freedom from France twelve days before. It was one of a string of French African lands reaching self-rule that summer.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Chad. Chad was seated the next month. The landlocked state added its vote to a reshaped Assembly. Seventeen new members joined in that one 1960 session. Most of them were African. Their bloc gave the body's debates a new center of weight.

Bosnia's stabilization force is extended one last time by Resolution 1551, adopted unanimously on 9 July 2004. NATO had decided at its Istanbul summit to end its SFOR operation by the end of 2004. The European Union planned to launch its own mission from December 2004, with a military component. The Peace Agreement's civilian side still depended on the High Representative.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes SFOR to continue for a further planned six months under unified command. It may use all necessary measures to enforce Annex 1-A of the Peace Agreement and control Bosnia's airspace. It welcomes the handover path to the EU mission and decides the existing status-of-forces agreements will apply provisionally to the EU force from its build-up. The parties are reminded that full cooperation with the Yugoslavia tribunal, including surrendering indictees, is part of their duty to implement the peace.

Darfur's sanctions watchers gained three more months in late 2005. On 21 December, the Council adopted Resolution 1651. It acted under Chapter VII. Peace talks on Sudan ran in Abuja, Nigeria, at the time. The new peace deal for the south had just taken hold. Atrocities in Darfur, though, had not stopped.

The text extends the Panel of Experts until 29 March 2006. The panel was built under Resolution 1591. Its job is to police the Darfur arms ban and targeted sanctions. It must report before its term ends. It also sends advice on how the measures are working. Panels like this one built the proof trail for later sanctions steps.

One further month is granted to MONUC, the United Nations mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on 13 April 2007. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council kept the mission at the strength set by its earlier resolutions until 15 May 2007. The bridge extension held the operation steady while a longer renewal for the post-transition period was prepared.

Piracy off Somalia takes a new turn in Resolution 1851, adopted on 16 December 2008. Attacks had grown more daring in six months, reaching a hijacked supertanker 500 nautical miles off Kenya. Somalia's Transitional Federal Government could not patrol its waters or prosecute pirates, and captured pirates were often released for lack of courts. The EU operation Atalanta and NATO were already responding at sea.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council lets cooperating states and regional groups take all necessary measures on Somali territory for twelve months from Resolution 1846 to suppress piracy at sea. They may act with the Transitional Government's notice and consent. It backs 'shiprider' deals so regional officers can sail with foreign navies and bring suspects home for trial. It calls for a contact mechanism and a regional coordination centre, and notes that rising ransoms and the unenforced arms embargo were fuelling piracy's growth.

Four days before a tense election run-off in Côte d'Ivoire, the Council lent troops across a border. On 24 November 2010, it adopted Resolution 1951 under Chapter VII. The Secretary-General had warned that the UN mission in Côte d'Ivoire needed backup. The mission next door in Liberia, UNMIL, still had its own job to do.

The text lets the Secretary-General shift troops from Liberia for no more than four weeks. The package caps help at three infantry companies. It adds an air unit with two utility helicopters. Such lending between missions let the UN surge guards around a risky vote. No new force had to be built from scratch.

A military parade in Jerusalem provoked Resolution 251, adopted unanimously on 2 May 1968. Israel held the parade that day, marking twenty years since its founding, through a city divided since the 1967 war. Days earlier the Council had unanimously decided, in resolution 250, against such a display.

The resolution does one thing: it deeply deplores Israel's holding of the parade in disregard of that unanimous decision. There are no demands or deadlines, which makes the text a pure statement of institutional protest. It still matters as an early sign of how the status of Jerusalem would test the Council's authority, since a member state had openly ignored a direct and unanimous call.

Bangladesh joins the United Nations in the record of Resolution 351, adopted without a vote on 10 June 1974. Bangladesh had applied to join, and the Council had weighed the young state's request. The South Asian country had fought its way out of Pakistan in 1971, but its UN entry waited while recognition politics, including a Chinese veto in 1972, blocked the path.

The resolution recommends that the General Assembly admit Bangladesh to membership. That recommendation cleared the way for the Assembly to seat Bangladesh later in 1974. The two-line text is a reminder that admission is often the end of a long diplomatic struggle rather than the beginning of one.

Fresh hope for Cyprus talks bloomed in May 1979. Chiefs of both halves of the isle met in Nicosia on 18 and 19 May. They set a ten-point plan to restart talks. The UN force, UNFICYP, had kept the peace since 1964. Its host state agreed it should stay. Resolution 451 passed on 15 June 1979 by fourteen votes to none. China sat the vote out.

The force stayed to 15 December 1979. Both sides were urged to seize the ten points. Talks had to be steady, kept up, and aimed at real fruit. No drift would do. The chief's good offices would run on. A report on the work was due by 30 November. The chief's Cyprus report of 31 May had set the stage for the vote.

Kashmir's UN panel was told to get moving in this text of 1948. On 3 June, the Council adopted Resolution 51. Eight members voted yes and none voted no. China and the two Soviet republics held back. Fighting between India and Pakistan over Kashmir ground on. Earlier texts had set up a UN panel for the dispute. Resolution 47 had sketched a vote-based path as well.

The text restates those earlier steps. It directs the panel to head to the disputed areas without delay. The duties from Resolution 47 come first in its work. The panel must also study the extra matters raised by Pakistan's foreign minister. Reports go back to the Council as the panel sees fit. Its mission failed within a year.

Observers on the Iran-Iraq border gained six more months in 1990. On 29 March, the Council adopted Resolution 651. The observer group had watched the truce line since the 1988 halt to the eight-year war. The peace text behind it, Resolution 598, was still not carried out. Neither side had fully complied with its terms.

The text calls once more on both parties to act on Resolution 598 at once. It extends the observer mandate to 30 September 1990. A report from the Secretary-General is due at the end of that stretch. The quiet renewals ended the next year. The observers were then withdrawn for good.

Fifty observers were the seed of the UN's Somalia effort in 1992. On 24 April, the Council adopted Resolution 751 without dissent. Ceasefire deals had been signed in Mogadishu that March. They covered UN watch over the truce. They also set fair ways to share relief aid. Suffering across the stateless land stayed vast all the same.

The text sets up a United Nations Operation in Somalia under the Council's own charge. It backs the Secretary-General's work in the country. He must send fifty observers to the capital at once. Their job is to watch the ceasefire hold. That small mission, UNOSOM I, grew within a year into a vast relief effort. Famine and faction war swamped its first design.

Resolution 951, adopted on 21 October 1994, is a short procedural text on the International Court of Justice. The Council notes the death of Judge Nikolai Konstantinovitch Tarassov on 28 September 1994, which left a vacancy on the Court for the remainder of his term. Under Article 14 of the Court's Statute, the election date is fixed by the Council. It decides the election will take place on 26 January 1995, at a meeting of the Security Council and at a meeting of the General Assembly during its forty-ninth session.
un-un-res-fifth-report-of-the-secretary-:
By 2000 the small observer effort in Sierra Leone had grown into a full peacekeeping mission, UNAMSIL, and this fifth report of the Secretary-General, document S/2000/751, tracks its work. The mission had just survived a grave crisis. Rebels had seized hundreds of UN troops as hostages that spring.

The report reviews the rescue of the mission, the state of the ceasefire, and plans to disarm rebel fighters. It also weighs the force's size and the risks ahead. Council members used reports like this one to decide how much backing the mission would get.
vaughan-lumen-de-lumine-1651:
Thomas Vaughan, writing as Eugenius Philalethes, published Lumen de Lumine in London in 1651. Its subtitle promises a new magical light thrown upon the world. Vaughan wrote at the height of the Interregnum's occult ferment, when civil war had loosened every certainty in England, religion included.

The book is the foundational text of the English Rosicrucian revival. Vaughan mixes natural philosophy, alchemy, and theology in a prose of fire and riddling. He presents magic as a sacred science of nature's hidden light. His twin brother Henry the poet shared the family's mystical bent. Lumen de Lumine made Philalethes the leading English voice of the new occult learning.
zoist-vol-09-1851:
March 1851 to January 1852 is the span of The Zoist's ninth volume. The Great Exhibition year finds Elliotson still editing his journal of mesmerism. Painless operations, trance cures, and clairvoyant sittings fill the reports. Cerebral physiology articles continue the journal's scientific frame.

Spiritualism, newly landed from America, competes for the same public wonder. Elliotson's pages treat the older mesmeric gospel as the true key. The thirteen volume set preserves the English movement from 1843 to 1856. Volume nine shows its ninth year of stubborn print. Few fringe sciences left so full a record. The detail here is dense and direct.
